descriptors.title: Manipulate elements and devices
descriptors.description: manipulate the elements of dance and/or choreographic devices to choreograph dances that communicate ideas, perspectives and/or meaning
descriptors.knowledge: Students can use elements of dance to choreograph dance that communicates ideas, perspectives and/or meaning (Y3-4). They can structure dances with beginning-middle-end, generate and combine movement material, and use choreographic intent to guide decisions.
descriptors.endpoint: Students manipulate the elements of dance and/or choreographic devices to choreograph dances that communicate ideas, perspectives and/or meaning.

nodes.label: Choreographic devices as tools
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and intentionally use choreographic devices — such as repetition, contrast, unison — to shape how their dance communicates.
criteria: Student can name at least one choreographic device used in their dance
Student can explain what effect that device creates in their dance
nodes.hinge_reason: Choreographic devices are the compositional vocabulary of Y7-8 and Y9-10 Creating strand work. Students who have not internalised devices as intentional tools will approach composition as movement arrangement rather than structural craft.

width.minimum: Using at least one choreographic device (e.g. repetition or contrast) intentionally in a movement sequence — can name the device and explain its effect.
width.typical: Exploring and applying choreographic devices: repetition, contrast, unison; using a repeating section that alternates with contrasting sections; structuring a dance using devices to create sections; exploring how devices change the audience experience.
wider: Investigate how choreographic devices are used in a dance they are studying or have experienced — applying the same device in their own work
Experiment with combining multiple devices in a single dance — examining how layered device use deepens communicative effect

modes.reason: Devices need naming and analysis before they become tools. Use examples from dances students have experienced — 'this section repeats, and here's what that does' — before expecting intentional application.

nodes.label: Generating material through manipulation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can manipulate elements of dance and choreographic devices to generate and develop movement material — exploring multiple possibilities before selecting.
criteria: Student generates at least three distinct movement possibilities from one starting point
Student can explain why they selected the movements they used (connects to communicative intent)

width.minimum: Generating at least three movement variations from one starting movement using element manipulation (space, time, dynamics, relationship); selecting among them for a choreographic purpose.
width.typical: Exploring stimuli and other dances to devise movement possibilities (different ways to jump/land, roll/stand, spiral to ground); selecting, combining, arranging and refining; experimenting with characters and mood through element manipulation; exploring technical-expressive focus (control, coordination, balance).
wider: Use positive and negative space as a choreographic consideration — exploring how spatial relationships between dancers change meaning
Develop movement material from a theme or issue (sustainability, identity) — using element manipulation to represent ideas abstractly

modes.reason: Students at this level should be developing choreographic range — the habit of generating many possibilities before committing. Reward exploration over early closure.

nodes.label: Structuring a complete dance
nodes.checkpoint: Students can structure a dance using choreographic devices that communicate a clear idea, perspective or meaning — with technical and expressive skill considerations integrated.
criteria: Student produces a dance that uses at least one choreographic device to structure communication of an idea
Student can identify how technical-expressive skill choices contribute to the dance's communicative effect
Student can describe what their dance communicates and explain at least one structural decision
nodes.hinge_reason: Producing a complete structured dance using devices — not just movement arranged in order — is the capability milestone of this standard. Without this, students enter Y7-8 without the compositional experience to work with more complex structural forms (binary, ternary, narrative) and genre-specific techniques.

width.minimum: A structured dance using at least one device; clear communicative intent; attention to at least one technical-expressive skill (control, coordination, balance).
width.typical: Creating structured dances: narrative dances retelling a story, dances exploring themes or issues; using choreographic devices to create sections; focusing on technical and expressive skills; reflecting on and refining using Viewpoints questions ('How is the body used to represent the story?', 'How can space communicate meaning?').
wider: Create a dance using production elements (music, costume, props) to enhance communication of the theme or idea
Choreograph a dance that explores a sustainability or social issue — using device choices to structure an argument or narrative arc

modes.reason: Structuring integrates device knowledge (N1), generated material (N2), and technical-expressive attention into a communicative whole. Use Viewpoints questions throughout the process — not just at the end.

descriptors.title: Technical and expressive skills
descriptors.description: develop and practise technical and expressive skills using safe dance practice and the elements of dance
descriptors.knowledge: Students can experiment with and practise skills for moving safely and expressively (Y3-4). They demonstrate habitual safe practice and can use elements to communicate ideas through movement.
descriptors.endpoint: Students develop and practise technical and expressive skills using safe dance practice and the elements of dance.

nodes.label: Developing technical skill range
nodes.checkpoint: Students can refine technical execution of fundamental movements — improving control, coordination, accuracy and expressive quality across a range of movement types.
criteria: Student can demonstrate improved technical quality in a target movement following sustained practice
Student applies safe dance practice consistently across all technical skill development activities

width.minimum: Refining technical execution of at least three movement types (e.g. galloping, jumping, rolling, spinning) — demonstrating improvement over time in at least one.
width.typical: Developing technical and expressive skills in fundamental movements: galloping, jumping, sliding, rolling, slithering, spinning, shrinking, exploding, collapsing; developing focus, clarity, confidence and facial expression/character; applying safe dance practice throughout.
wider: Choose one technically demanding movement as a sustained practice focus — setting specific quality targets and tracking improvement across sessions
Explore how the same movement (e.g. jumping) is executed differently in different dance styles — developing style-awareness alongside technical skill

modes.reason: Technical skill development requires deliberate, repeated practice with targeted feedback. Students benefit from sustained focus on specific movements rather than constant variety.

nodes.label: Expressive skills and communicative clarity
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use expressive skills — focus, clarity of movement, confidence, facial expression — to communicate ideas through performance.
criteria: Student uses at least two expressive skills in a performance — visible to an observer
Student can explain how each expressive skill serves the communicative intention of the dance
nodes.hinge_reason: Expressive skill in performance is the bridge between technical execution and communicative impact. Students without expressive skill development will produce technically competent but communicatively flat performance — this limits their work in Y7-8 Performing strand where technical and expressive integration is foregrounded.

width.minimum: Demonstrating at least two expressive skills in a movement sequence — can name each and explain its communicative function.
width.typical: Developing expressive skills of focus, clarity of movement, confidence and facial expression/character; improvising new movement in response to stimuli to practise communicative expressiveness; exploring element of dance choices (positive/negative space, contrasting dynamics) to develop expressive range.
wider: Use video self-review to identify expressive skill strengths and development areas — setting specific goals for a subsequent performance
Explore how contrasting expressive skill choices (e.g. confident vs hesitant, focused vs distracted) change what a movement communicates

modes.reason: Expressive performance integrates technical skill (N1) with communicative intent and audience awareness. Frame expressiveness as a skill that can be practised and refined — not a personality trait.

descriptors.title: Elements of dance communicate meaning
descriptors.description: explore ways that the elements of dance are combined to communicate ideas, perspectives and/or meaning in dance across cultures, times, places and/or other contexts
descriptors.knowledge: Students can explore where, why and how dance is choreographed and/or performed across cultures, times, places and/or other contexts (Y3-4). They can compare dances and identify purpose and meaning using Viewpoints questions.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explore ways that the elements of dance are combined to communicate ideas, perspectives and/or meaning in dance across cultures, times, places and/or other contexts.

nodes.label: Reading element use in observed dances
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and describe how elements of dance and choreographic devices are combined in dances they experience — connecting element choices to communicative effect.
criteria: Student can describe how at least two elements combine in an observed dance to create a specific communicative effect
Student connects at least one element choice to the mood, meaning or audience relationship in the dance
nodes.hinge_reason: Reading element combinations as communicative — not just aesthetic — is the analytical move that distinguishes appreciation from analysis. Students who cannot yet do this will engage with dances at a descriptive surface level in Y7-8 investigating work.

width.minimum: Identifying how at least two elements of dance are used together in one observed dance — and describing the communicative effect of those choices.
width.typical: Exploring how dances use elements and choreographic devices (repetition, unison, contrast); discussing purpose of movements, elements, production elements, technical and expressive skills and their effect on mood and audience relationship; using Viewpoints to explore similarities and differences across choreographers and contexts.
wider: Explore how dance communicates cultural traditions — examining a dance from a country or region in Asia and asking how it reflects cultural ways of being
Investigate how elements of dance in a specific dance style (e.g. hip hop, contemporary, classical) reflect the cultural or historical context of that style

modes.reason: Element-to-meaning reading requires an explicit interpretive move — students need Viewpoints questions with analytical scaffolding: 'How does the use of slow dynamics here change the mood?', 'What does the unison say about the relationship between dancers?'

nodes.label: Comparing element use across cultural contexts
nodes.checkpoint: Students can compare how elements of dance are combined across different cultural and temporal contexts — identifying how context shapes element use.
criteria: Student can compare element use in two dances from different cultural or temporal contexts
Student offers a culturally contextualised explanation for at least one difference observed

width.minimum: Comparing element use in two dances from different cultural or temporal contexts — identifying at least one difference in how elements are combined and suggesting why.
width.typical: Exploring similarities and differences in how choreographers use elements across genres, styles, cultures and times; using Viewpoints to develop questions about how main ideas are communicated; seeking feedback about how audience perceived choreographic intent; considering how cultural traditions shape element use.
wider: Investigate how dance-on-screen (film, music video) uses production elements alongside dance elements — examining how the combination changes what is communicated
Explore how a dance from a country or region in Asia uses elements in ways that differ from familiar Western dance styles — discussing what this reveals about cultural values and aesthetics

modes.reason: Genuine comparison requires genuine diversity of examples. Students who have encountered only one or two cultural dance contexts cannot make meaningful comparative observations.

descriptors.title: Perform with technical skills
descriptors.description: practise and perform dances using technical and expressive skills in informal and/or formal settings
descriptors.knowledge: Students can practise and perform dances in informal settings (Y3-4). They use expressive skills (projection, focus) and can communicate intent to an audience and reflect on performance.
descriptors.endpoint: Students practise and perform dances using technical and expressive skills in informal and/or formal settings.

nodes.label: Technical and expressive skill in rehearsal
nodes.checkpoint: Students can apply technical and expressive skills in rehearsal — working within their body capabilities and improving quality across multiple attempts.
criteria: Student can identify at least one technical and one expressive skill they are working on in rehearsal
Student shows improvement in a target skill across multiple rehearsal sessions

width.minimum: Rehearsing a dance with awareness of technical skill application (e.g. landing alignment, balance) and at least one expressive skill — able to identify what they are working to improve.
width.typical: Rehearsing learned and/or self-choreographed dances with awareness of body capabilities; applying technical and expressive skills; creating tension through slow controlled movements with neutral facial expression; using Viewpoints questions to reflect on spatial placement, focus, musicality, clarity.
wider: Use video to review rehearsal — identifying specific technical and expressive skill development areas and setting targeted goals
Rehearse across multiple sessions with a documented improvement focus — tracking change in a performance journal or checklist

modes.reason: Rehearsal skill — the capacity to use repetition productively and target improvements — is itself a learnable practice. Students benefit from explicit rehearsal strategy instruction alongside content.

nodes.label: Performing for audiences in varied settings
nodes.checkpoint: Students can perform dances in informal and/or formal settings — using technical and expressive skills and appropriate production elements to communicate ideas to an audience.
criteria: Student performs a dance using at least two identifiable technical-expressive skills
Student can use at least one production element purposefully in performance
Student can reflect on their performance using a Viewpoints question — identifying one strength and one area for development
nodes.hinge_reason: Performance in varied settings — including formal contexts — is the experiential foundation for the more demanding performance requirements of Y7-8. Students who have only ever performed in highly informal single-class settings lack the performance confidence and audience awareness that formal contexts require.

width.minimum: Performing one dance in an informal or formal setting using at least two technical-expressive skills; using at least one production element where appropriate.
width.typical: Performing in informal and/or formal settings: using specific technical and expressive skills to communicate ideas, perspectives or meaning; using production elements (music, costumes, props) to enhance different contexts; performing with cultural community representatives using traditional music where appropriate; using Viewpoints questions to reflect on performance.
wider: Perform a dance for an audience beyond the class — a school assembly, community event, or online platform — adapting performance presence for the context
Perform a dance using traditional music when presenting with representatives of the cultural group from the community — following relevant cultural protocols

modes.reason: Performance integrates rehearsal skill (N1), technical-expressive skill, and production element choices into a communicative event. The audience relationship is the critical new element at this node — frame performance as communication, not demonstration.

descriptors.title: Develop characters and dramatic action
descriptors.description: develop characters and situations, and shape and sustain dramatic action to communicate ideas, perspectives and/or meaning in improvised, devised and/or scripted forms
descriptors.knowledge: Students can improvise and devise drama using elements of drama to communicate ideas and meaning (Y3-4). They can shape improvisations using voice, movement and language, and devise drama collaboratively with communicative intent.
descriptors.endpoint: Students develop characters and situations, and shape and sustain dramatic action to communicate ideas, perspectives and/or meaning in improvised, devised and/or scripted forms.

nodes.label: Developing character
nodes.checkpoint: Students can develop a character with consistent physical, vocal and relational qualities, distinguishable from their own default behaviour.
criteria: Student creates a character distinguishable from their own default through at least two consistent choices (voice and physical)
Student sustains character across a scene including during reactions to others
Student can describe the character's perspective or intention
nodes.hinge_reason: Consistent character development is the anchor for sustaining dramatic action; if characters collapse under pressure (breaking in and out of role or losing character consistency), the dramatic action cannot be sustained across longer or more complex forms — particularly in scripted drama.

width.minimum: Student creates and sustains one character across a short scene, making at least two distinct characterisation choices (voice and physicality).
width.typical: Students explore physical, fictional or emotional spaces to create characters; they vary voice (projection, dynamics, pace, pause, pitch) and use movement and gesture to communicate characters' intentions; they rehearse and negotiate with others to interpret scripts and create characters and their relationships.
wider: Students use empathy to develop characters from different perspectives, considering situations from multiple characters' viewpoints and challenging stereotypes
Students develop a 'new scene' to include in a dramatic re-telling of a known narrative, creating a character who was not in the original

modes.reason: Character consistency develops through rehearsal and deliberate practice; students need repeated opportunities to 'inhabit' a character across different scenarios before they can sustain it through a full drama.

Developing characters across different contexts — improvised, scripted, empathy-based, culturally situated — builds transferable characterisation skills and prevents students from defaulting to a single character type.

nodes.label: Shaping dramatic action across forms
nodes.checkpoint: Students can shape dramatic action — developing situation, tension and resolution — across improvised, devised and/or scripted forms.
criteria: Student shapes a dramatic sequence with a recognisable dramatic arc (beginning, complication, resolution)
Student demonstrates sustained dramatic action across a complete piece in at least one form
Student can articulate what idea, perspective or meaning the drama is communicating

width.minimum: Student shapes a dramatic sequence with an identifiable beginning, complication and resolution across one form.
width.typical: Students shape and sustain dramatic action across improvised, devised and/or scripted drama; they use rehearsal, interaction and negotiation with others; they use props, costumes and available technologies (light, sound, multimedia) as dramatic symbols; they develop drama for school rituals or community events with a specific purpose.
wider: Students devise drama based on research about a school or local community project, using drama to present different perspectives in a debate or issue
Students explore how a devised drama for a specific community audience (e.g. school assembly, cultural ceremony) requires adapting form and content to purpose
Students use Viewpoints to frame questions about their own drama: 'How did the performers use elements effectively?', 'What was the purpose?'

modes.reason: Shaping sustained dramatic action across forms is the integration point — character, situation, tension, purpose and audience awareness all converge. Structured reflection and feedback during rehearsal is the key scaffold.

descriptors.title: Combine elements to communicate
descriptors.description: explore ways to combine the elements of drama to communicate ideas, perspectives and/or meaning in improvisations, devised drama and/or scripted drama
descriptors.knowledge: Students can use elements of drama — voice, movement, language, space — in combination to develop dramatic action in improvisations and devised drama (Y3-4). They can make deliberate element choices and describe their effect.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explore ways to combine elements of drama to communicate ideas, perspectives and/or meaning in improvisations, devised drama and/or scripted drama.

nodes.label: Using empathy and perspective to develop combination choices
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use empathy to explore how combining elements differently communicates different perspectives and challenges stereotypes.
criteria: Student makes at least one element combination choice informed by a specific character perspective
Student can explain how their combination choice communicates that character's viewpoint or intention
nodes.hinge_reason: Empathy-informed element choice is what distinguishes purposeful dramatic crafting from mechanical application of techniques; without this, combinations may be technically correct but lack communicative power — particularly critical in scripted drama where character interior is essential.

width.minimum: Student makes at least one element combination choice that is informed by a character perspective other than their own default.
width.typical: Students experiment with empathy when combining elements in improvised and scripted drama; they consider situations from multiple characters' perspectives; they use Viewpoints to explore how cultures shape element use ('How are relationships, language and symbols shaped by cultures?').
wider: Students imagine themselves in the time/place of a historical event, considering why participants made particular decisions, and explore this through deliberate element combinations
Students explore how the same dramatic situation produces different element-combination choices for characters from different cultural backgrounds

modes.reason: Use structured empathy activities before script or devising work — 'hot-seating', role-on-the-wall, or perspective-taking exercises — to give students the interior perspective that informs element choices.

nodes.label: Combining elements across forms — improvised, devised and scripted
nodes.checkpoint: Students can combine elements of drama purposefully across improvised, devised and scripted forms, evaluating which combinations communicate most effectively.
criteria: Student combines elements of drama purposefully in at least two different forms
Student evaluates the effectiveness of a specific element combination and suggests an alternative

width.minimum: Student compares how element combinations produce different effects in at least two different dramatic forms.
width.typical: Students use improvisation or process drama to compare how improvised and scripted drama create characters and action; they explore how elements combine differently across forms; they consider how cultural understandings shape meaning through element combinations.
wider: Students evaluate drama they experience in live performance, identifying specific element combinations, and consider how to apply those techniques in their own work
Students explore drama from another culture or historical period and investigate how element combinations reflect that culture's dramatic conventions

modes.reason: Exploring element combinations across multiple forms and cultural contexts builds the flexible, transferable skill of combining intentionally rather than habitually.

descriptors.title: Elements combine to communicate meaning
descriptors.description: explore ways that the elements of drama are combined to communicate ideas, perspectives and/or meaning in drama across cultures, times, places and/or other contexts
descriptors.knowledge: Students can explore where, why and how drama is created across cultures, times and places; they can identify features from other drama contexts and connect them to their own practice (Y3-4).
descriptors.endpoint: Students explore ways that elements of drama are combined to communicate ideas, perspectives and/or meaning in drama across cultures, times, places and other contexts.

nodes.label: Identifying how elements combine in specific drama
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and describe how specific elements of drama are combined in a drama work to communicate ideas or meaning.
criteria: Student identifies at least two elements in combination in a specific drama and describes what each communicates
Student can connect an element combination choice to a communicative intention or cultural context
nodes.hinge_reason: If students cannot identify and describe specific element combinations in a drama they observe, they cannot make the cross-cultural comparison the descriptor requires; 'across cultures' demands a precise enough analytical lens to identify what varies.

width.minimum: Student identifies and describes at least two elements used together in a specific drama they have observed, and explains what they communicate.
width.typical: Students identify and discuss the use of elements (space, time, language, movement, character, relationships) in drama using Viewpoints questions ('What did you see?', 'How did actors make characters believable?', 'What was the purpose?'); they consider how cultural understandings shape meaning through element use.
wider: Students analyse drama from another culture or historical context, identifying how element combinations reflect specific cultural purposes or values
Students investigate how drama is used in their own community to maintain, continue and revitalise culture — and identify the element combinations that carry this meaning

modes.reason: Use Viewpoints-based questioning protocols systematically before asking students to compare — 'What did you see?', 'How was X element used?' — to ensure they have the observation vocabulary for comparison.

nodes.label: Comparing element combinations across contexts
nodes.checkpoint: Students can compare how element combinations communicate differently across diverse cultural, historical and contextual drama examples.
criteria: Student identifies at least one meaningful difference in how elements are combined across two different cultural or historical drama contexts
Student explains how cultural understandings shape that difference

width.minimum: Student compares element combinations in two drama examples from different cultural or historical contexts and identifies at least one meaningful difference.
width.typical: Students explore drama from other places and times, discussing how it might contribute to their own drama and how cultural understandings shape meaning; they explore how drama is used to share cultural knowledge in celebrations, ceremonies and rituals in different communities including Asia.
wider: Students investigate a specific drama tradition from a country or region in Asia in depth — exploring its conventions, element combinations, and how these reflect cultural values
Students investigate how drama from another cultural tradition uses elements to carry knowledge that wouldn't translate through Western dramatic conventions

modes.reason: Genuine cross-cultural comparison requires experiencing diverse examples — not just one 'other' culture; width here is the pedagogical goal, not a bonus.

descriptors.title: Rehearse and perform in varied settings
descriptors.description: rehearse and perform improvised, devised and/or scripted drama in informal and/or formal settings
descriptors.knowledge: Students can perform improvised and devised drama in informal settings, demonstrating role-commitment and making deliberate performance choices (Y3-4). They understand the purpose of audience and can reflect on performance experience.
descriptors.endpoint: Students rehearse and perform improvised, devised and/or scripted drama in informal and/or formal settings.

nodes.label: Understanding rehearsal as purposeful preparation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain the purpose of rehearsal and demonstrate collaborative rehearsal practices — remembering lines, cues and moves.
criteria: Student can explain at least one purpose of rehearsal
Student demonstrates improvement in a specific performance skill (line recall, movement, cue response) across rehearsal sessions
nodes.hinge_reason: Understanding rehearsal as purposeful iteration — not just repeated run-throughs — is the gateway to the formal performance context introduced in this band; without a rehearsal discipline, performance in formal settings cannot achieve the communicative precision the descriptor implies.

width.minimum: Student participates in at least two rehearsal sessions for a piece, demonstrating improvement in line/cue recall and movement between sessions.
width.typical: Students show understanding of the purpose of rehearsing and the need for collaboration; they focus on communication with the audience by remembering lines, moves and cues in rehearsal and performance; they share ideas about their drama with audiences through performance space choices or introductory presentations.
wider: Students take on a specific rehearsal role (director, stage manager, prompt) and reflect on how each role contributes to production
Students create a pre-show introduction — a podcast, poster, or programme note — that frames the drama for their audience before the performance

modes.reason: Make the purpose of each rehearsal explicit: 'Today we are rehearsing to fix X' — give each rehearsal session a specific focus so students understand that rehearsal is analytical problem-solving, not just practice.

nodes.label: Performing in informal and formal settings
nodes.checkpoint: Students can perform with communicative intent in both informal and formal settings, adapting their performance to the audience and context.
criteria: Student performs in at least one formal or semi-formal setting with sustained communicative intent
Student demonstrates use of at least one technical element (prop, costume, lighting/sound, space) to enhance dramatic meaning
Student reflects on the performance against their rehearsal intentions, identifying one success and one area for improvement

width.minimum: Student performs in at least one formal or semi-formal setting (beyond classroom presentation) with clear communicative intent.
width.typical: Students use props, costumes and technologies to create dramatic symbols and enhance dramatic action; they demonstrate communication with the audience; they share ideas about their drama through their performance choices, introductions or pre-show presentations.
wider: Students devise and perform drama for a specific community audience (school assembly, cultural event, community gathering), adapting the work to purpose and audience
Students evaluate their own performance against their rehearsal intentions — noting what communicated as intended and what they would change

modes.reason: Performance in varied settings is the integration event — character, technical skills, rehearsal discipline and audience awareness converge. Structured reflection after performance completes the learning cycle.
Performing in different settings (informal/formal, different audiences, different purposes) builds adaptability and deeper understanding of how context shapes performance choices.

descriptors.title: Construct works for specific audiences
descriptors.description: use media languages, media technologies and production processes to construct media arts works that communicate ideas, perspectives and/or meaning for specific audiences
descriptors.knowledge: Students can construct representations using media languages and production processes, communicating ideas and perspectives. They have applied shot types, sound, sequencing and pre-production planning. They have not yet designed works specifically for audiences — applying genre codes and conventions deliberately, or using chroma key, special effects and more advanced editing.
descriptors.endpoint: Students use media languages, media technologies and production processes to construct media arts works that communicate ideas, perspectives and/or meaning for specific audiences.

nodes.label: Audience and genre
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify the relationship between audience, purpose and genre — explaining how codes and conventions of an established genre serve specific audiences.
criteria: Student can identify the genre of a media arts work and name at least two defining codes or conventions
Student can explain how those conventions serve the intended audience
nodes.hinge_reason: Understanding the audience-genre relationship is the prerequisite for all subsequent production decisions — without it, production choices serve personal preference rather than communicative intent for a specific audience.

width.minimum: Identify the genre of one media arts work, name two codes or conventions that define it, and explain how those conventions serve the intended audience.
width.typical: Analyse genre codes and conventions across two or more media forms (genre film, music video, advertisement, game design); explain how conventions create audience expectations and relationships; identify story structures and technical/symbolic elements that contribute to genre formation.
wider: Identify the genre conventions of a music video and explain how they structure the audience experience differently from a narrative film — applying findings to original genre analysis or production planning

Analyse game genre conventions (character design, level design, dialogue conventions) and investigate how each convention builds a specific audience relationship — applying analysis to original character or level design

modes.reason: Use Viewpoints questions to build the reasoning chain: 'How can I adapt and manipulate story principles to make my intention clear for this audience?' Students need explicit practice connecting genre conventions to audience expectation.

nodes.label: Production planning for audiences
nodes.checkpoint: Students can plan a media arts production using pre-production tools — designing for a specific audience and making pre-production decisions that serve that audience relationship.
criteria: Student produces a pre-production plan (storyboard, shot list, or equivalent) for a media arts work
Student can explain at least two audience-directed decisions in the plan

width.minimum: Produce a storyboard or shot list for a key scene in a planned media arts work — including at least two audience-directed decisions (e.g. camera angle choice, sound choice) with written justifications.
width.typical: Design using pre-production tools (storyboard, shot list, game design plan, script) for specific audiences; apply genre conventions to planning decisions; reflect on the storyboard using Viewpoints questions ('What is working well?', 'What do I need to improve?'); plan permissions and documentation requirements.
wider: Design a storyboard for a short genre film — including camera angles, transitions, edits, voice and soundtrack decisions — and evaluate the storyboard against the intended audience relationship before producing

Design a game character for a specific genre — considering costume, mannerisms, cultural background and typical dialogue for the target audience — and justify each design decision in terms of genre conventions

modes.reason: Pre-production planning is a discipline habit that requires practice — students who skip or rush storyboarding produce works that drift from their communicative intent. Invest in thorough planning cycles, not just capture.

nodes.label: Constructing for specific audiences
nodes.checkpoint: Students can construct a media arts work using advanced production techniques — applying genre conventions and reflecting on whether the work communicates its intended meaning to the specific audience.
criteria: Student produces a media arts work for a specific audience applying at least two genre conventions deliberately
Student can explain whether and how the work successfully communicates its intended meaning to that audience

width.minimum: Produce one media arts work for a specific audience, applying at least two genre conventions deliberately, and reflect on how successfully the work communicates to that audience.
width.typical: Produce media arts works across two or more genres and forms (genre short film, advertisement, game design, music video section) using chroma key, special effects, editing, sound effects and film language; apply genre conventions deliberately; reflect using Viewpoints questions on whether production choices serve the audience.
wider: Create a short genre film using chroma key, special effects, editing, sound effects and film language — applying all five elements deliberately and evaluating how each serves the intended genre audience

Create a section of a music video that brings together music, dance and media arts — considering how the codes and conventions of music videos structure the audience experience, and reflecting on what was successfully communicated

modes.reason: Construction for specific audiences integrates genre knowledge, pre-production planning and production skills — the produced work should be evaluated against the intended audience relationship, not just as an object.

descriptors.strand: Media arts: developing practices and skills
descriptors.title: Develop production skills for meaning
descriptors.description: develop media production skills to communicate ideas, perspectives and/or meaning through manipulation of media languages, including images, sounds, texts and/or interactive elements, and media technologies
descriptors.knowledge: Students can experiment with production techniques and evaluate how changes affect meaning. They can apply Foley sound, storyboarding and image review. They have not yet manipulated media languages across multiple forms to communicate perspectives — or applied genre conventions deliberately to create humour, mood or meaning.
descriptors.endpoint: Students develop media production skills to communicate ideas, perspectives and/or meaning through manipulation of media languages and media technologies.

nodes.label: Manipulating media languages to change meaning
nodes.checkpoint: Students can manipulate at least two media language elements (sound, framing, editing, text, augmented environment) and explain how each manipulation changes the meaning or perspective communicated.
criteria: Student can manipulate at least two media language elements (sound, framing, editing, text)
Student can explain how each manipulation changes the meaning or perspective communicated
nodes.hinge_reason: If students cannot connect specific manipulation choices to their communicative effect, production decisions remain accidental — they cannot evaluate or refine their work against communicative intent.

width.minimum: Manipulate one media language element (e.g. add or modify a soundtrack to an existing image sequence) and describe how the change affects the perspective or meaning communicated.
width.typical: Manipulate media languages across images, sounds and texts — framing to change status/power, sound and music to change mood, genre conventions applied to everyday events to create humour; use Viewpoints questions to evaluate the effect of each manipulation; experiment with augmented reality or chroma key to change environments.
wider: Trial applying the conventions of an established genre to an everyday event to create humour (e.g. a visit to the library as an action movie) — experimenting systematically with framing, music and sound effects, and evaluating how genre conventions create comic effect through audience expectation

Use augmented reality, virtual reality or chroma key to transport the same content into three different environments — comparing how the environment change creates different meaning and evaluating which is most effective for a specific audience

modes.reason: Use Viewpoints questions as an explicit evaluation frame: 'How can I change the meaning of a story by adding or modifying a soundtrack?' This builds the reasoning habit that distinguishes deliberate production from accidental production.

nodes.label: Production skills across forms
nodes.checkpoint: Students can apply production skills across multiple media forms — capturing, sequencing, scripting or documenting with deliberate communicative intent in at least two different task contexts.
criteria: Student applies production skills in at least two different media forms or task contexts
Student makes deliberate manipulation decisions in each and can explain the communicative intent behind those decisions

width.minimum: Apply production skills in two different media forms or task contexts (e.g. stop motion animation and radio script, or green screen film and podcast) — demonstrating deliberate manipulation of media languages in each.
width.typical: Develop production skills across a range of forms — comic book/animation/stop motion with green screen, genre conventions applied to everyday events, radio production script with permissions documentation, image-music meaning experiments; practise selecting the most effective approach from multiple options.
wider: Create a script for a radio production and document the permissions required for music and voice talent in a real-world community radio setting — practising the professional production workflow from scripting through to permissions documentation

Produce a stop motion animation or green screen work that retells a familiar story in a new environment — applying all stages of the production process and reflecting on how environment choice serves the communicative intent

modes.reason: Build students' production skill repertoire across multiple forms — animation, film, radio, print. The wider the repertoire, the more informed future production choices will be.

descriptors.title: Media languages across contexts
descriptors.description: explore ways that media languages and media technologies are used in media arts works and practices across cultures, times, places and/or other contexts
descriptors.knowledge: Students can compare media arts works made for different purposes and explain how context shapes representations. They have not yet explored how media languages and technologies construct power relationships, stereotyping and bias — or systematically compared media representations across historical and cultural contexts.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explore how media languages and media technologies are used to construct representations across cultures, times, places and contexts — including analysis of stereotyping, power, bias and cultural values.

nodes.label: Representations and power
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how media language choices (framing, colour, costume) construct power relationships and status in representations of characters.
criteria: Student can identify at least two media language choices (framing, colour, costume, setting) that construct a character's status or power
Student can explain how each choice communicates that status to the audience
nodes.hinge_reason: Understanding how media languages construct power and status is the conceptual foundation for media literacy at Y5-6 — without it, students cannot critically analyse stereotyping, bias or ideological positioning in media.

width.minimum: Identify how framing, colour or costume is used in one media work to establish a character as high or low status — explaining the specific language choices that create that power relationship.
width.typical: Explore how status and power relationships are constructed through framing, colour, costume and setting (hero/villain creation); investigate stereotyping and bias in game characters and media representations; apply Viewpoints questions to analyse power: 'How can I use framing to demonstrate a power relationship between characters?'
wider: Investigate how status and power relationships are constructed through framing, colour and costume in a specific media form (e.g. advertising, game design, TV) — applying findings to original character design that deliberately constructs or challenges a power relationship

Compare how the same type of character (hero, villain, authority figure) is constructed differently in media works from different cultural contexts — identifying what the differences reveal about cultural values and assumptions

modes.reason: Students need explicit scaffolding to move from 'this character looks powerful' to 'the low-angle shot and dark costume construct power because...' Use Viewpoints questions as an analytical framework.

nodes.label: Context, values and comparison
nodes.checkpoint: Students can compare media representations created in different times, places and cultural contexts — explaining how context influences the values, characters and stories portrayed.
criteria: Student can compare two media representations of the same topic from different contexts
Student can explain how context influenced at least two differences between the representations

width.minimum: Compare two media arts works representing the same topic (e.g. family, youth, heroes) from different times or cultural contexts — identifying at least two differences and explaining how context influenced each.
width.typical: Research and compare media representations from different times and places (e.g. family in TV across decades, safety campaigns across cultural contexts); explain how context influences values; investigate how media arts works share cultural information about communities; discuss the role of media arts in cultural knowledge sharing.
wider: Research and compare representations of a topic (e.g. family, youth, heroes) across multiple historical periods or cultural contexts — explaining what forces (social, economic, political) shaped each representation, and evaluating how audiences might have responded differently

Investigate how media arts works from different cultural contexts share information about people's relationships with their environment and community — comparing two culturally distinct examples and discussing what values are communicated

modes.reason: Vary the comparison contexts — different decades, different countries, different cultural contexts — so students develop genuine analytical range rather than a single comparison that may reinforce existing assumptions.

descriptors.title: Present with responsible media practice
descriptors.description: present media arts works in informal and/or formal settings using responsible media practice
descriptors.knowledge: Students can share media arts works in informal settings applying permission and credits. They have not yet presented in formal settings, used internet-based platforms for distribution, or reflected systematically on how different audiences receive the same work.
descriptors.endpoint: Students present media arts works in informal and/or formal settings using responsible media practice, considering how audiences and platforms shape reception.

nodes.label: Responsible media practice for formal and digital settings
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and apply responsible media practices appropriate to formal or digital presentation contexts — including legal, ethical and cultural considerations.
criteria: Student can identify at least two responsible media practice requirements for their planned presentation context
Student applies both requirements when presenting and can explain why each is needed in this context
nodes.hinge_reason: Responsible media practice for digital and formal settings requires explicit application — without it, online sharing creates legal, ethical and cultural compliance gaps that cannot be remedied after the fact.

width.minimum: Identify at least two responsible media practice requirements for a formal or digital sharing context (e.g. online safety, cultural protocols, copyright) and apply them when preparing to present.
width.typical: Apply responsible media practices across informal and formal contexts and digital platforms — legal, ethical and moral considerations; online safety protocols; cultural protocols for representing community or cultural stories; copyright and attribution; engaging appropriately with audience responses online.
wider: Investigate protocols for representing community or cultural stories in media arts works before creating and presenting a work — documenting the protocol decisions made and reflecting on how cultural understandings shaped the final presentation choices

Research responsible media practice requirements for sharing on a specific digital platform (school LMS, community website) — developing a checklist that addresses legal, ethical and cultural considerations specific to that platform

modes.reason: Use scenario-based reasoning to build transferable responsible media practice: 'Before we upload this to the school website, what do we need to check? Why does each check matter?' Apply to real planned sharing activities.

nodes.label: Presenting across settings and audiences
nodes.checkpoint: Students can present a media arts work to audiences in more than one setting — reflecting on how and why the work may be received differently across settings.
criteria: Student presents a media arts work to at least one audience applying relevant responsible media practices
Student can reflect on at least one aspect of how the audience or setting shaped the reception of the work

width.minimum: Present a media arts work to at least one audience and reflect on at least one way the setting or audience affected how the work was received.
width.typical: Present media arts works in informal and formal settings (classroom, school assembly, online platform); reflect on differences in reception across settings; engage with audience responses on digital platforms applying online safety; consider how understandings of culture shape audience experience.
wider: Present a short film to multiple audiences in different settings (classroom, school assembly, digital platform) — reflecting systematically on how and why the work was received differently in each context, and what this reveals about the relationship between audience, setting and meaning

Present a media arts work using internet-based technologies on a curated digital platform (school LMS) — applying online safety and responsible media practice, engaging with audience responses thoughtfully, and reflecting on how the online audience differs from a live audience

modes.reason: Presenting across settings integrates production, responsible media practice and audience awareness — support students in treating reception differences as information about communication, not just approval ratings.

Vary the presentation settings — informal classroom, formal assembly, digital platform, community context — so students develop genuine experience of how setting and audience shape reception across multiple contexts.

descriptors.title: Manipulate elements and use compositional devices
descriptors.description: manipulate elements of music and use compositional devices to communicate ideas, perspectives and/or meaning when composing and practising music for performance, and notate, document and/or record the music they compose
descriptors.knowledge: Students can manipulate elements of music to communicate ideas and practise for performance, using notation to document work (AC9AMU4C01). They can use multiple documentation formats and work collaboratively on accompaniments. They have not yet applied formal compositional devices (form, contrast, repetition) to structure compositions, or composed for specific instruments within technical constraints.
descriptors.endpoint: Students manipulate elements of music and apply compositional devices to communicate ideas, perspectives and/or meaning, notating, documenting or recording the work in a format that supports rehearsal and performance.

nodes.label: What compositional devices are
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and describe at least two compositional devices (e.g. repetition, contrast, a given form such as verse/chorus or binary) and recognise them when listening.
criteria: Can name at least two compositional devices and describe what each does
Can identify at least two compositional devices when listening to a musical example
nodes.hinge_reason: Compositional devices are the new conceptual demand of this standard. Students who can manipulate elements but have no understanding of compositional devices as structural tools cannot 'use' them — they can only accidentally reproduce them. Without this conceptual foundation, the higher-order compositional work in AC9AMU8C01/C02 and AC9AMU10C01/C02 is inaccessible.

width.minimum: Identify at least two compositional devices in a piece of music; describe what each device does to the music's structure or effect.
width.typical: Identify and describe compositional devices in diverse musical examples — repetition, contrast, verse/chorus form, binary, ternary, ostinato; explain how each device structures the music and serves the communicative purpose.
wider: Compare two pieces in different forms (e.g. verse/chorus vs binary) and describe how the structural difference affects the listener's experience

Listen to examples of the same compositional device used in different genres or cultural contexts — how does repetition function differently in a pop song vs a West African drum pattern vs a Bach invention?

modes.reason: Introduce compositional devices through analysis before application. Listen to a verse/chorus song and identify the structural pattern before asking students to compose in that form. 'What repeats? What contrasts? What is the effect of that repetition/contrast?' Analysis first, composition second.

nodes.label: Using compositional devices to structure a composition
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use at least one compositional device to structure a composition with a clear communicative intention.
criteria: Composes a piece using at least one identified compositional device
Can explain how the device serves the stated communicative intention

width.minimum: Compose a piece using at least one compositional device (e.g. verse/chorus form or deliberate repetition); state the communicative intention and explain how the device serves it.
width.typical: Compose pieces using multiple compositional devices across different contexts — structuring a song with verse/chorus, using repetition and contrast to shape a melody, composing in binary or ternary form; connect each structural decision to the communicative or expressive intention; compose in response to a theme, image or cross-curricular question.
wider: Work collaboratively to compose a song for a cross-curricular presentation — use both element manipulation and compositional devices, and explain why each choice serves the communication task
Arrange or re-imagine a known work by applying a different compositional device — compose new lyrics and restructure the form, then compare the original and re-imagined versions

modes.reason: Compositional device application is richer across multiple purposes and contexts. Composing for different reasons (a cross-curricular song, a song with personal meaning, a soundscape for a ceremony) requires different device choices — context breadth develops flexible structural thinking.

nodes.label: Composing within technical constraints
nodes.checkpoint: Students can compose a melody or instrumental part within a defined technical constraint (e.g. a limited pitch range, specific instruments) and use digital tools to complete the work.
criteria: Composes a melody or part that respects a stated technical constraint
Documents the composition in a format (notation or recording) that supports rehearsal

width.minimum: Compose a melody or part for a specific instrument within a stated constraint (e.g. using only the notes they can play); use at least one digital tool to supplement or complete the work.
width.typical: Compose for specific instruments within technical constraints — using a pitch range matching their instrumental skill level; combining live performance with digital tools (loops, notation software); composing voices and instruments parts that are within the players' technical capability.
wider: Combine loops constructed from melodic or rhythmic patterns with live performance — design the loop and live components so they complement each other
Use notation software to create a score for voice and instruments — perform from the score and evaluate whether the notation accurately captures the intended performance

modes.reason: Composing within constraints integrates element manipulation, compositional devices and technical knowledge of instruments. The teaching investment is in making constraint-based composition a creative discipline rather than a limitation: 'Within these five notes, what can you create?'

nodes.label: Notating, documenting and recording compositions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can notate, document or record a composition in a format appropriate to the type of music and suitable for use in rehearsal and performance.
criteria: Documents a composition in a format matched to its type
Documentation is detailed enough to guide a rehearsal without relying entirely on memory

width.minimum: Document a composition using a format matched to the music type (e.g. lead-sheet for a song, graphic/staff notation or recording for an instrumental piece) with sufficient detail to reconstruct it in rehearsal.
width.typical: Use a combination of notation formats, audio recording and digital tools to document compositions; ensure documentation captures element manipulation decisions and structural devices; use documentation in rehearsal to maintain fidelity to compositional intent.
wider: Create a combined graphic and staff notation document for a piece — use graphic notation for soundscape sections and staff notation for melodic sections; evaluate which format works better for each section
Use digital loop and notation tools to create a multi-track recorded and notated score — compare the information captured by each format

modes.reason: Y5-6 students benefit from consolidating and extending their documentation repertoire. Different composition types require different documentation approaches — the goal is fluent selection of appropriate tools, not mastery of one format.

descriptors.title: Develop aural and expressive skills
descriptors.description: develop listening/aural skills and skills for manipulating elements of music to achieve expressive effects when composing, singing and playing instruments
descriptors.knowledge: Students can manipulate elements during performance and use evaluative listening to compare effects (AC9AMU4D01). They can read from notation and demonstrate developing technique. They have not yet developed the specific aural-skills lens of hearing and adjusting to other parts in real time, or used digital tools systematically for technical development.
descriptors.endpoint: Students develop listening/aural skills and skills for manipulating elements of music to achieve expressive effects when composing, singing and playing instruments.

nodes.label: Aural skills in ensemble contexts
nodes.checkpoint: Students can listen to other parts when singing or playing in a group and adjust their own volume, tempo or pitch to achieve a balanced ensemble sound.
criteria: Demonstrates at least one real-time aural adjustment during ensemble performance (not prompted by teacher)
Can describe what they heard and what they adjusted in response
nodes.hinge_reason: Aural monitoring during performance — listening and adjusting simultaneously — is the compound skill that distinguishes capable ensemble performers from individual players performing in proximity. Students who cannot do this remain dependent on external feedback from teachers. This is foundational to all ensemble performance work in Y7-8 and beyond.

width.minimum: Demonstrate one real-time aural adjustment during group performance (e.g. reducing volume when their part is too loud, or adjusting pitch toward the group).
width.typical: Combine listening and performance skills in ensemble contexts — listening to other parts while playing, adjusting volume for balance, monitoring pitch relative to the group, responding to dynamic signals from conductors or other performers.
wider: Focus on ensemble balance across a full rehearsal — practise listening for specific parts (melody, accompaniment, bass) and adjusting accordingly
Record an ensemble rehearsal, listen back focusing on balance, and identify three specific moments where adjustment improved the sound

modes.reason: Real-time aural adjustment requires the underlying performance skills to be automatic enough that cognitive bandwidth is available for listening. Build this through repeated ensemble practice with explicit listening focus: 'This rehearsal, focus only on hearing the melody part and matching your dynamic to it.'

nodes.label: Vocal and instrumental techniques for expressive effect
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use vocal or instrumental techniques to manipulate elements of music and create expressive effects — contrast, repetition or balance — in composition and performance.
criteria: Demonstrates at least one vocal or instrumental technique that achieves a described expressive effect
Can explain how the technique creates the effect and how it could be applied in a different musical context

width.minimum: Demonstrate at least one technique that creates an expressive effect (e.g. changing timbre to create mood, or using articulation to create contrast) and describe the effect.
width.typical: Explore vocal and instrumental techniques for creating contrast, repetition and balance — timbre manipulation for mood, articulation techniques, dynamic control, range extension; use focused listening and Viewpoints questions to evaluate effects and set improvement goals; practise and refine techniques for accuracy.
wider: Focus on timbre manipulation: compare how changing tone colour changes mood across different styles — e.g. the same melody played with different articulation, or sung with different vocal quality
Use Viewpoints to analyse how a professional performer achieves a specific expressive effect — develop a practice plan to replicate or adapt that technique

modes.reason: Expressive technique development is richer when applied across multiple musical styles and contexts. Each style or context brings different technique priorities — legato playing in classical music differs from staccato articulation in jazz which differs from ornamentation in folk. Breadth of application builds transferable expressive skill.

nodes.label: Using digital tools for skill development
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use digital tools (tuner, metronome, recording software) to develop specific technical skills — setting goals, monitoring progress and refining accuracy.
criteria: Uses at least one digital tool to monitor a specific technical aspect of their performance
Can describe what the tool revealed and one adjustment they made in response

width.minimum: Use at least one digital tool to monitor a specific technical aspect of their performance (e.g. intonation or tempo accuracy); describe one thing the tool revealed.
width.typical: Use digital tools systematically for technical development — digital tuner for pitch accuracy, metronome for tempo control, recording software to monitor dynamic range and articulation; set specific technical goals, use tools to track progress, make adjustments.
wider: Use a recording to compare technique before and after a targeted practice period — document what changed and what the digital feedback revealed
Set a specific technical goal (e.g. maintaining consistent dynamics across a full phrase), practise with digital monitoring for two or three sessions, and evaluate progress

modes.reason: Digital tools provide feedback that replaces teacher monitoring, but students need to know what to do with the feedback. Build a feedback-action loop: 'The tuner shows you're flat on that note — what will you try to fix it?' The tool's value is in generating data; the skill is in interpreting and acting on it.

descriptors.title: Elements of music across cultures and contexts
descriptors.description: explore ways that the elements of music are combined in music across cultures, times, places and/or other contexts
descriptors.knowledge: Students have explored music for similar purposes across cultures and compared performance and audience expectations (AC9AMU4E01). They can identify how elements are used in a piece and describe purposes. The new demand is specifically on how elements are combined — and on evaluation of personal response and musical preferences using music terminology.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explore ways that elements of music are combined in music across cultures, times, places and other contexts, evaluating personal responses and describing how structural features create effects.

nodes.label: How elements are combined in diverse music
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe how multiple elements of music are combined in a piece and identify the effect of those combinations.
criteria: Can describe how at least two elements are combined in a piece of music
Can name the effect of those element combinations on the music's mood or meaning

width.minimum: Listen to one piece and describe how at least two elements are combined (e.g. fast tempo with loud dynamics, repeated melodic pattern with changing timbre); name the effect of that combination.
width.typical: Listen to music with diverse instrumentation, forms and cultural origins; describe how elements are combined across whole works and sections; identify which instruments play melody vs accompaniment; compare original versions with arrangements and covers to explore how changing element combinations changes the effect.
wider: Compare an original version of a song with a cover or arrangement — identify which elements changed, which stayed the same, and how the combination differences change the overall effect
Listen to music from an Asian culture and describe how elements are combined — use music terminology and your own words to explain the effect and your personal response

modes.reason: Understanding element combinations is built through encountering many examples. Different genres, styles and cultural traditions use element combinations in distinctly different ways — the range of examples determines how flexible and nuanced students' analytical listening becomes.

nodes.label: Evaluating personal responses with reasons
nodes.checkpoint: Students can evaluate and share personal preferences for music from diverse contexts, using both their own words and music terminology, and giving reasons.
criteria: Shares a personal response to a piece using at least one music term
Gives at least one reason grounded in a specific musical feature

width.minimum: Share a preference for or response to one piece of music using at least one music term and give at least one reason grounded in the music.
width.typical: Evaluate and discuss personal preferences across music from multiple contexts — leisure music, ensemble music, music important to family or community, music from specific genres; use music terminology to describe what creates the preference; give reasons grounded in the music's features rather than vague impressions.
wider: Compare preferences for music from two different cultural contexts — discuss what each communicates and why one is preferred, using specific terminology
Evaluate a piece of game or screen music — describe what the music does for the product and whether it succeeds, using element analysis as evidence

modes.reason: Personal response becomes analytically meaningful when grounded in specific musical evidence. Build a response framework: 'I like/don't like this piece because [specific musical feature] creates [specific effect]. I know because [what I listened for].' This bridges felt response and analytical observation.

nodes.label: Structural features and music in social contexts
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify structural features (riffs, strumming patterns, song forms) and describe how music is used in celebrations, ceremonies or rituals in at least two contexts.
criteria: Can identify at least one structural feature in a piece of music and describe its function
Can describe how music is used in at least one celebration, ceremony or ritual context

width.minimum: Identify one structural feature (e.g. a riff, a chorus, an ostinato) in a piece and describe its function; identify one way music is used in a celebration or ceremony they know.
width.typical: Identify and describe structural features across diverse music (riffs, ostinatos, strumming patterns, verse/chorus, theme and variations); explain how these features create effects; explore how music gives structure to celebrations, ceremonies and rituals in different community contexts; demonstrate understanding of popular song form through parody.
wider: Use parody to demonstrate understanding of popular song structure — compose new lyrics to a known song, justify how the structural form was used, and perform the parody
Investigate how music structures a specific ceremony or ritual in two different cultural contexts — compare the role music plays in each

modes.reason: This node integrates structural analysis (identifying devices), cultural context (how music functions in community life) and personal application (parody). It brings together the analytical and contextual threads of the descriptor into a demonstration of integrated musical understanding.

descriptors.title: First Nations music and cultural continuity
descriptors.description: explore ways First Nations Australians use music to continue and revitalise culture
descriptors.knowledge: Students have explored how First Nations Australians use music to communicate connection to and responsibility for Country/Place (AC9AMU4E02), including engaging with First Nations Australian voices directly. The new focus is cultural continuity and revitalisation — music's role in maintaining living culture, language, and knowledge, including in contemporary contexts.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explore ways First Nations Australians use music to continue and revitalise culture, investigating diverse styles, language preservation, and how cultural knowledge is shared through performance.

nodes.label: Diverse contemporary styles and instruments
nodes.checkpoint: Students can investigate the diverse music styles and instruments that living First Nations Australian composers and performers are using, including in contemporary genres.
criteria: Can name at least two different music styles used by living First Nations Australian artists
Can describe how each style is connected to First Nations Australian identity or cultural expression
nodes.hinge_reason: A narrow image of what First Nations Australian music 'is' — limited to traditional or ceremonial contexts — prevents students from engaging with living cultural continuity. If students associate First Nations Australian music only with the past, they cannot understand how music continues and revitalises culture in the present. This conceptual block makes the rest of the descriptor inaccessible.

width.minimum: Identify at least two different music styles or genres being used by living First Nations Australian composers or performers; describe one instrument or musical feature of each.
width.typical: Investigate the range of music styles used by living First Nations Australian composers and performers — contemporary pop, hip-hop, classical, orchestral, ceremonial, folk; identify instruments including both traditional instruments and contemporary ones; recognise the diversity of what First Nations Australian music is and can be.
wider: Compare a First Nations Australian artist working in a contemporary genre (e.g. hip-hop or pop) with one working in a more traditional context — describe how each serves cultural continuity in different ways
Investigate the work of a specific First Nations Australian composer or performer in depth — identify their style, instruments, cultural context and what they say about their music

modes.reason: Deliberately expose students to First Nations Australian musicians working across diverse contemporary genres alongside traditional contexts. The breadth itself challenges the assumption that First Nations Australian music is a single, historical thing — each new genre context adds evidence for living, diverse cultural expression.

nodes.label: Language revitalisation through music
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe how music is being used to maintain and revitalise knowledge and use of First Nations Australian languages.
criteria: Can describe at least one way music is being used to maintain or revitalise a First Nations Australian language
Can explain why music serves this purpose effectively

width.minimum: Identify one example of First Nations Australian music that uses or teaches a specific language; describe how the music contributes to language knowledge.
width.typical: Investigate how First Nations Australian musicians are using music to maintain and revitalise languages — songs that teach vocabulary, performances that model pronunciation and usage, recordings that preserve language from Elders; discuss the role music plays in keeping languages alive that might otherwise be lost.
wider: Research a specific First Nations Australian language that music is helping to revitalise — find and listen to examples of that music, then discuss how music serves language learning differently from formal instruction
Investigate how musicians balance the use of English and First Nations Australian languages in their music — what choices do they make and why?

modes.reason: Language revitalisation through music is a concept most students will encounter for the first time at Y5-6. Build understanding through specific examples and guided questioning: 'How does singing a song in a language help you learn that language?' 'Why might music be a more effective vehicle for language preservation than textbooks?' Connect to what students know about how music helps people remember things.

nodes.label: Sharing cultural knowledge through performance
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe how First Nations Australian composers and performers share cultural knowledge as part of their performances — including acknowledgements and explanations.
criteria: Can identify at least one way a First Nations Australian performer shares cultural knowledge in a performance
Can explain what that practice communicates to audiences about culture and identity

width.minimum: Identify at least one way a First Nations Australian performer shares cultural knowledge as part of a performance (e.g. acknowledging Country/Place, sharing language information, explaining inspiration).
width.typical: Investigate how First Nations Australian composers and performers share cultural knowledge in performances — acknowledging Country/Place before performing, sharing information about the language used in a song, explaining the inspiration for a composition, connecting the music to specific cultural stories or knowledge; discuss what this practice communicates to audiences.
wider: Compare how cultural knowledge is shared in two different performance contexts (e.g. a mainstream festival vs a community ceremony) — what is shared in each, and what is different?
Investigate how First Nations Australian musicians who create music for animations or screen works incorporate cultural knowledge into the work itself — analyse one specific example in depth

modes.reason: This node integrates the understanding of living cultural diversity with language revitalisation and the specific practice of knowledge-sharing in performance. It brings the exploration of First Nations Australian cultural continuity together in the concrete act of a performer choosing to make their cultural knowledge part of the performance event.

descriptors.title: Perform in informal and formal settings
descriptors.description: perform music in a range of forms they have learnt and/or composed in informal and/or formal settings
descriptors.knowledge: Students can perform from notation in informal settings, use rehearsal recordings and basic sound reinforcement, and plan/introduce performances (AC9AMU4P01). They have not yet performed in formal settings, presented via digital platforms, or engaged in systematic peer feedback cycles.
descriptors.endpoint: Students perform music in a range of forms in informal and/or formal settings, using expressive elements, peer feedback and digital platforms to refine and present performances.

nodes.label: Expressive elements in rehearsal and performance
nodes.checkpoint: Students can focus on specific expressive elements (e.g. dynamics and balance) during rehearsal and demonstrate them in performance to engage audiences and communicate ideas.
criteria: Can identify at least one expressive element targeted in rehearsal
Demonstrates that element in performance with a recognisable effect on the audience experience

width.minimum: Identify at least one expressive element to focus on in rehearsal; demonstrate that element in the subsequent performance.
width.typical: Rehearse and refine performances with a focus on expressive elements — dynamics, balance, tone colour, articulation (phrasing, staccato, legato); connect expressive choices to the mood and meaning of the music; focus on songs from cultural groups or in a language being learnt.
wider: Rehearse the same piece with different expressive interpretations — compare recordings and decide which interpretation best communicates the mood, with justification
