Focus on tone colour and articulation across a cultural context the class is exploring — how do the expressive conventions of that style differ from what students typically apply?

modes.reason: Expressive performance requires the technical aspects to be automated enough that expressive intention can be maintained throughout. Rehearsal that explicitly separates technical accuracy work from expressive focus work — drilling technique first, then adding expression — builds this layered competence.

nodes.label: Providing and responding to peer feedback
nodes.checkpoint: Students can provide specific, music-based feedback on a peer's performance and use feedback received to make documented refinements.
criteria: Provides at least one music-specific piece of feedback on a peer's performance
Makes at least one documented change to their performance in response to feedback received
nodes.hinge_reason: Peer feedback as a rehearsal tool — rather than post-performance commentary — is a new practice at Y5-6. Students who cannot give or use specific music-based feedback remain dependent on teacher evaluation for performance improvement. This skill underpins the self-directed rehearsal and evaluation practices required in Y7-8 and Y9-10.

width.minimum: Provide at least one specific music-based piece of feedback on a peer's performance; respond to at least one piece of feedback received by making a documented change.
width.typical: Provide and respond to feedback systematically — discussing how the composer indicates dynamics and how the performer/s interpret this; describing how tone colour and articulation communicate mood; making specific adjustments based on feedback and evaluating their effect.
wider: Conduct a structured peer feedback session using a specific framework (e.g. 'I noticed... I wondered... I suggest...') and track how feedback is used across three rehearsals
Compare feedback from a peer vs a recording vs the teacher — how does each source offer different perspectives on the performance?

modes.reason: Effective peer feedback requires a framework that keeps observations music-specific. Without structure, students give vague or personal feedback ('I liked it', 'it was too quiet'). Build a feedback protocol: 'Name a specific moment, describe what you heard using a music term, suggest one specific change.' Practise before applying in performance contexts.

nodes.label: Performing in formal and digital contexts
nodes.checkpoint: Students can present performances in formal settings and via digital platforms, adapting their approach to suit the context and audience.
criteria: Performs in at least one context beyond the usual classroom setting
Can describe at least one way the context changed the performance decisions made

width.minimum: Perform in at least one context beyond the classroom (formal or digital); reflect on how the context changed the performance experience.
width.typical: Present performances via digital platforms (school intranet or website) including, if age-appropriate, interacting with audiences; stream or upload recordings; pose questions for online audiences; present performances in formal settings such as assemblies or community events; consider online safety protocols.
wider: Upload a performance recording with discussion questions for the audience — collect and evaluate responses, then reflect on how the online audience experience differed from in-person
Perform for an audience in a different year level or community group and adapt the introduction and performance approach for that specific audience

modes.reason: Performing in different contexts (classroom, assembly, online, community event) teaches students that performance decisions — pacing, introduction, engagement strategies — are context-dependent. Each new context adds to their repertoire of performance adaptations.

descriptors.title: Plan and create artworks that communicate ideas and meaning
descriptors.description: use visual conventions, visual arts processes and materials to plan and create artworks that communicate ideas, perspectives and/or meaning
descriptors.knowledge: Students can create artworks that communicate specific ideas and perspectives using compositional choices and deliberate selection of conventions and materials (AC9AVA4C01). They can generate and select ideas and explain their choices. They have not yet planned artworks systematically, applied aesthetic criteria, or created works that combine digital and analog materials intentionally.
descriptors.endpoint: Students use visual conventions, visual arts processes and materials to plan and create artworks that communicate ideas, perspectives or meaning — making and documenting deliberate choices about how elements serve aesthetic and communicative intentions.

nodes.label: Planning with intention
nodes.checkpoint: Students can plan an artwork systematically — generating ideas, identifying visual conventions and processes that will serve their intent, and documenting decisions before making.
criteria: Produces a plan that identifies the idea, at least one convention, and a material or process
Explains how at least one planned choice will serve the communicative intent
nodes.hinge_reason: Systematic planning is the new demand at Y5-6 compared to Y3-4. Students who skip planning and rely on intuition produce works that can communicate but cannot be refined or defended — subsequent nodes about refining and evaluating choices are inaccessible.

width.minimum: Produce a simple plan for an artwork — identify the idea, at least one convention to be used, and one material or process — before beginning the work.
width.typical: Plan artworks using brainstorming, Viewpoints questions and compositional sketches; identify and document how visual conventions, materials and processes will serve the communicative intent; make and justify choices before making.
wider: Create a logbook comparing analog and digital versions of the same material — document what each can and cannot do and explain which will serve the artwork's intent
Plan an artwork inspired by a text's illustrative approach — analyse how the illustrator's choices serve the narrative, then design your own approach for a different scene

modes.reason: Planning is a reasoning process — students need to think forward (what will this produce?) not just backward (why did I make this?). Structured planning prompts build the habit of intentional decision-making before the work begins.

nodes.label: Aesthetic choices and material knowledge
nodes.checkpoint: Students can make and explain choices about materials, joining techniques and visual conventions based on the aesthetic qualities they want the artwork to have.
criteria: Makes at least one material or process choice based on an aesthetic quality wanted
Explains the reasoning in terms of what the material or process does — not just personal preference

width.minimum: Make at least one material or process choice based on an aesthetic quality wanted (e.g. durability, texture, translucency, gestural quality) and explain the reasoning.
width.typical: Apply knowledge of material properties to make aesthetic choices (joining techniques, brushstroke qualities, surface effects); compare virtual and analog simulations of the same material; select combinations that communicate intended aesthetic qualities.
wider: Explore how different brushstrokes communicate different meanings — compare long smooth horizontal lines in watercolour wash with textural thick paint strokes; explain what each communicates
Investigate how First Nations Australian artists use specific materials and processes to produce particular visual and cultural effects — with guidance from culturally authoritative resources

modes.reason: Material knowledge is built through comparative experience — students who have tried only one material type cannot reason about aesthetic choice. Comparing analog/digital, different paint techniques, and sculptural materials reveals how properties map to aesthetic effects.

nodes.label: Creating with coordinated intent
nodes.checkpoint: Students can create an artwork in which planning, aesthetic choices and communicative intent are coordinated — the work delivers what was intended.
criteria: Creates an artwork that realises at least one planned intention
Explains how at least two visual choices (convention, material, composition) work together to serve the communicative intent

width.minimum: Create an artwork that realises at least one planned intention; explain how the visual choices made serve that intention.
width.typical: Create artworks using planned visual conventions, materials and processes; make choices that serve both aesthetic quality and communicative intent; combine multiple elements coherently; include digital and analog combinations where appropriate.
wider: Create an artwork that combines at least one digital and one analog material — document in a logbook and explain how each contributes to the final work
Form modular patterns using grid paper or digital tools (glyphs, pixels, shapes) — remove the grid and transform into a final form such as a poster or printmaking template
Create an artwork in response to a site-specific inspiration — document how the site shaped material and compositional choices

modes.reason: Planning, aesthetic judgment and material execution are coordinated here. The integration is not just technical — it is the student demonstrating that what they made matches what they intended.

descriptors.strand: Visual arts: developing practices and skills
descriptors.title: Experiment, document and reflect on visual arts practice
descriptors.description: experiment with, document and reflect on ways to use a range of visual conventions, visual arts processes, and materials
descriptors.knowledge: Students can experiment with a range of materials and processes, document discoveries through annotation, and use visual arts language to reflect (AC9AVA4D01). They have begun investigating composition. They have not yet produced systematic logbook-style documentation, experimented with Augmented Reality or cross-arts visual mapping, or applied observational drawing across multiple representational modes.
descriptors.endpoint: Students experiment with, document and reflect on ways to use a range of visual conventions, visual arts processes and materials, using their documentation as a source for informed making choices.

nodes.label: Systematic documentation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can document experiments systematically — recording what was tried, what resulted, and what it means for future making.
criteria: Produces at least one documented experiment that records what was tried and what resulted
Draws at least one implication for future making from the documentation
nodes.hinge_reason: Systematic documentation is the key new demand at Y5-6 — students who do not maintain records of experiments cannot make informed choices in subsequent making. The documentation is what converts experiments into a knowledge base.

width.minimum: Document at least one experiment in a logbook or visual diary — record what was tried, what the result was, and one implication for future making.
width.typical: Maintain a developing documentation record across multiple experiments; use Viewpoints questions to annotate processes; connect discoveries to informed future choices; build a body of documented practice.
wider: Create a systematic comparison of analog and digital simulations of the same material — record findings in a logbook and draw conclusions about when each is preferable
Document the steps of a printmaking process — record variations (colour changes, progressive texture additions) and reflect on what each variation produces

modes.reason: Documentation habits require consistent expectation across multiple sessions to become genuinely systematic. Students who document only when required develop superficial records — the habit needs consolidation through repeated practice.

nodes.label: Multiple approaches to representation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use multiple approaches to represent the same subject — observational drawing, gestural drawing, photographic overlay, abstract — and reflect on what each approach can and cannot communicate.
criteria: Uses at least two different approaches to represent the same subject
Describes at least one thing each approach can communicate that the other cannot

width.minimum: Use at least two different approaches to represent the same subject; describe what each approach communicates differently.
width.typical: Explore and reflect on observational and gestural drawing as different ways to describe an object; combine imaginative drawing over realistic photographs; investigate printmaking, Augmented Reality and 3D as additional representational modes; reflect on how approach shapes meaning.
wider: Map the movements of a dance sequence visually — represent shapes, levels and energy as an abstract artwork; reflect on how colour, tone and composition communicate the mood and emotions of the dance
Explore Augmented Reality face filters — identify key asset types, design an analog concept for a filter communicating an intended idea, consider how it could extend a performance context

modes.reason: Students who have only used one representational approach (typically observational drawing) cannot reason about which approach is best suited to a given communicative purpose. The range of approaches — gestural, photographic, abstract, digital — reveals that mode is a choice, not a given.

nodes.label: Informed making choices
nodes.checkpoint: Students can draw on documented experiments and reflection to make informed choices about visual conventions, processes and materials for a specific artwork.
criteria: Identifies at least one making choice that is directly informed by a documented experiment
Explains the connection between the discovery and the choice

width.minimum: Identify at least one choice (convention, material or process) for an artwork that is directly informed by something discovered in a documented experiment.
width.typical: Use documented experiments to make and justify multiple informed choices for artworks; connect discoveries about representational approaches, material properties and visual effects to specific making decisions.
wider: Develop a range of 3D hand-building techniques in earthenware or modelling clay — document surface decoration experiments and reflect on how form and surface choices communicate ideas
Review a full set of documented experiments and identify a pattern in your choices — describe an emerging preference or approach that could define a personal style direction

modes.reason: The connection between documented discovery and future making is the core integration at this level — students demonstrate that experimentation is not separate from creating but feeds it.

descriptors.title: Visual arts communicating ideas across cultures and contexts
descriptors.description: explore ways that visual conventions, visual arts processes and materials are combined to communicate ideas, perspectives and/or meaning in visual arts across cultures, times, places and/or other contexts
descriptors.knowledge: Students can compare artworks across cultures, times and places and explain how an artist's context shapes their approach (AC9AVA4E01). They can identify multiple perspectives on events. They have not yet examined how social and historical forces shape artworks, or engaged critically with multiple-perspective readings of the same artwork.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explore ways that visual conventions, processes and materials are combined to communicate ideas, perspectives and meaning across cultures, times, places and other contexts — examining multiple perspectives and discussing how artworks develop social awareness.

nodes.label: Multiple perspectives on artworks
nodes.checkpoint: Students can critically navigate multiple perspectives on the same artwork — recognising that viewers bring different backgrounds and that these differences produce different interpretations.
criteria: Shares one interpretation of an artwork
Explains why two different interpretations of the same artwork could both be valid
nodes.hinge_reason: The move from 'one correct meaning' to 'multiple valid perspectives' is the foundational conceptual shift for this descriptor. Students who cannot hold two different interpretations of the same artwork simultaneously cannot engage with the social and critical dimensions the descriptor requires.

width.minimum: Share one interpretation of an artwork; listen to a different interpretation; explain why the two differ.
width.typical: Use Viewpoints questions to examine, compare and contrast observations across multiple students; discuss why the same artwork produces different responses; explore how background, experience and perspective shape interpretation.
wider: Compare how different artists present multiple perspectives on colonisation in Australia — examine works from First Nations Australian, British and other perspectives; discuss how artworks develop social awareness
Listen to audio descriptions of artworks by Australian artists — compare the audio description with your own visual interpretation; create your own audio description of a selected work

modes.reason: Multiple-perspective thinking is cognitively demanding and needs explicit scaffolding — structured discussion protocols (share one interpretation, listen to another, explain the difference) prevent students from treating the first interpretation as definitive.

nodes.label: Social and historical context in artworks
nodes.checkpoint: Students can investigate how social, historical and environmental concerns are expressed in artworks, and how artworks can develop social awareness.
criteria: Identifies at least one social, historical or environmental concern expressed in an artwork
Explains how at least one visual choice (convention, material, composition) communicates that concern

width.minimum: Identify one social, historical or environmental concern expressed in an artwork; explain how the visual choices communicate it.
width.typical: Investigate how Australian and international artists have expressed historical, social and environmental concerns; compare how different artists approach the same concern from different contexts; explore artworks from countries in Asia relevant to class topics.
wider: Explore a range of artworks from different cultural contexts that address sustainability — compare how land art, recycled-material works and climate visualisations each use visual conventions to communicate environmental concern
Explore artworks that communicate perspectives on migration to Australia — investigate how artists' backgrounds shape what they emphasise and how they use visual conventions

modes.reason: Students who examine only Australian artists or only one issue type develop limited understanding of how visual arts function socially. International and cross-cultural comparisons are essential for understanding that the relationship between art and social concern is universal.

nodes.label: Cross-cultural comparison and social awareness
nodes.checkpoint: Students can compare how artists from different cultures, times and places use visual conventions, processes and materials to communicate ideas and perspectives on the same topic.
criteria: Compares artworks from at least two different cultural contexts on the same topic
Identifies how visual choices serve different social or cultural purposes in each

width.minimum: Compare how two artworks from different cultural contexts address the same topic; identify one similarity and one difference in how visual choices serve the purpose.
width.typical: Compare artworks from a range of cultural contexts on the same topic; discuss how artworks develop social awareness; explore perspectives on colonisation, migration, sustainability or identity from different cultural viewpoints; create a personal visual response to an issue in a series of sequential panels.
wider: Investigate how colonisation of Australia is represented across multiple cultural perspectives — create a personal sequential visual response without text that expresses your own view
Investigate and compare artworks from Australian and Asian contexts on a shared topic from another learning area — discuss how cultural context shapes emphasis and visual choices

modes.reason: Students bring together their understanding of multiple perspectives and social context to produce a comparative analysis — demonstrating that visual choices serve social and cultural purposes that differ across contexts.

descriptors.title: Select and present visual arts practice in informal and formal settings
descriptors.description: select and present documentation of visual arts practice, and display artworks in informal and/or formal settings
descriptors.knowledge: Students can share and display artworks in informal settings, produce artist statements and make audience-driven decisions about format (AC9AVA4P01). They have curated basic displays and produced written or spoken statements. They have not yet prepared artworks for formal display, created professional exhibition materials, or used digital encoding methods to accompany their work.
descriptors.endpoint: Students select and present documentation of visual arts practice and display artworks in informal and/or formal settings — making deliberate decisions about space, labelling, audience and format.

nodes.label: Preparing artworks for display
nodes.checkpoint: Students can prepare artworks for physical display — attending to measurement, framing, labelling and spatial arrangement.
criteria: Prepares at least one artwork for display, attending to at least one presentation element
Labels the artwork with relevant information about the work and the artist

width.minimum: Prepare one artwork for physical display — attend to at least one presentation element (framing, mounting, positioning, labelling).
width.typical: Prepare artworks for display within the school environment; measure and make frames or stands using repurposed materials; position artworks at consistent heights and intervals; write and position labels with appropriate information.
wider: Plan and prepare a class exhibition space — make decisions about layout, spacing, label design and audience flow; reflect on how spatial choices affect the audience's experience
Adapt a physical display for a digital platform — consider what changes and what can be preserved; add QR codes or image coding to link audiences to additional information

modes.reason: Physical display preparation involves practical skills (measurement, framing, labelling) that require practice to execute at a level that serves the artwork. Consolidation across multiple display tasks builds the precision that formal exhibition demands.

nodes.label: Selecting documentation to communicate development
nodes.checkpoint: Students can select and arrange evidence of their learning — investigations, experiments, reflections — to communicate the development of their ideas and understanding.
criteria: Selects at least three pieces of documentation from their practice
Arranges them to show development and can explain what the sequence communicates

width.minimum: Select at least three pieces of documentation (experiment, reflection, work-in-progress, final work) and arrange them to show how ideas developed.
width.typical: Select and arrange comprehensive documentation of visual arts practice — investigations, experiments, reflections and final works; share with teacher and peers; explain how the sequence communicates the development of ideas and understanding.
wider: Consider how a work's meaning changes depending on how it is positioned in space — experiment with Augmented Reality or physical arrangement to explore how point of view affects audience experience
Create a short moving image work that maps how visual assets change depending on the audience's point of view

modes.reason: Selecting and arranging documentation to communicate development requires curatorial reasoning — students need to think about sequence, emphasis and what to include/exclude. Structured prompts support this reasoning rather than leaving selection arbitrary.

nodes.label: Exhibition materials and public sharing
nodes.checkpoint: Students can create exhibition materials that support audience engagement — labels, introductions, advertising, reviews — and consider options for sharing work in public spaces.
criteria: Creates at least one exhibition material (label, statement or introduction) for a class exhibition
The material provides relevant information about the artwork and the artist's intentions

width.minimum: Create at least one exhibition material (label, artist statement or introduction) for a class exhibition.
width.typical: Create a set of exhibition materials for a class exhibition — labels with artist information, an exhibition introduction, advertising or review material; work collaboratively on an online exhibition; consider options for sharing in public or community spaces.
wider: Develop a complete set of exhibition materials for a class show — labels, introduction, advertising and press statement — evaluate each element's effectiveness for the intended audience
Explore options for sharing work in public spaces (café galleries, community arts events) — plan what would need to change about the work and its presentation to suit a public audience

modes.reason: Students bring together physical display skills, documentation selection and audience awareness to produce a complete exhibition — where every element (artwork, label, arrangement, statement) serves the audience's experience.

descriptors.title: Choreograph dance for meaning
descriptors.description: choreograph dance by selecting and manipulating elements of dance and choreographic devices to communicate ideas, perspectives and/or meaning
descriptors.knowledge: Students can use elements of dance and simple choreographic devices in own dance works (AC9ADA6C01). They have not yet selected and manipulated devices with a clear rationale for how each choice communicates specific ideas, perspectives or meaning.
descriptors.endpoint: Students choreograph dance where selections of elements and devices are deliberate and connected to intended ideas, perspectives and meaning.

nodes.label: Improvising to generate choreographic material
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use improvisation as a generative tool to produce movement material that can be selected and developed for choreographic purposes
criteria: Generates movement material through at least one focused improvisation
Selects at least two movement phrases with a reason for their potential
Improvisation has a clear focus — not just free movement

width.minimum: Generate movement material through at least one improvisation with a specific focus (e.g. mood, theme, relationship); select at least two movement phrases worth developing
width.typical: Use improvisation with different focuses (mood, social relationships, thematic ideas) to generate a range of choreographic material; document and evaluate what each improvisation produces
wider: Improvise using movements and techniques from diverse styles — evaluate how importing movement vocabulary from other traditions generates unexpected choreographic possibilities
Use improvisation focused on communication of specific emotions or social relationships — document how the improvisation generates movement that carries expressive content
Experiment with using improvisation for a specific production context (music video, VR experience) — evaluate how the intended context shapes what movement is worth generating

modes.reason: Students need to build a repertoire of improvisation approaches — focused on different themes, emotions, contexts and movement sources — before they can select intelligently from improvised material. A single improvisation produces a narrow range of material; diverse improvisation approaches build the generative bank needed for purposeful choreographic selection.

nodes.label: Selecting and developing movement with choreographic devices
nodes.checkpoint: Students can select movement from improvisation and develop it using choreographic devices to communicate intended ideas or meaning
criteria: Uses at least one choreographic device to develop selected movement
Explains how the device serves the intended meaning or idea
Device choice is deliberate — not just applied by default

width.minimum: Select movement from improvisation and develop it using at least one choreographic device; explain how the device serves the intended meaning
width.typical: Select, combine, refine and sequence movement using choreographic devices such as transitions, variation and contrast, and forms such as binary, ternary or narrative; document how each device choice serves the choreographic intent
wider: Experiment with multiple structural forms (binary, ternary, narrative) and evaluate how each changes what the dance communicates — select the form that best serves the intended meaning
Develop movement sequences that portray characters or social relationships respectfully and empathetically — evaluate whether the choreographic choices achieve the intended portrayal
Create choreography for a specific production context (music video, immersive VR experience) — analyse how the context constrains and shapes choreographic decisions

modes.reason: Students commonly apply a single familiar choreographic device (e.g. repetition) without exploring whether other devices better serve the intended meaning. Working across multiple devices and structural forms — in different contexts with different communicative goals — builds the habit of purposeful device selection rather than defaulting to the familiar.

nodes.label: Documenting and evaluating choreographic choices
nodes.checkpoint: Students can document their choreographic process and evaluate whether their choices successfully communicate the intended ideas, perspectives or meaning
criteria: Documents at least two choreographic decisions
Evaluates whether each decision contributed to the intended communication
Documentation uses dance terminology — not just 'it worked' or 'it didn't'

width.minimum: Document at least two choreographic decisions made during the process; evaluate whether each decision contributed to the intended communication
width.typical: Document the choreographic process using journals, blogs, video or audio recordings; analyse and evaluate structural choices; explain what worked and what would change
wider: Analyse own choreographic process to identify the decisions that had most impact — evaluate what they reveal about own strengths and developing areas as a choreographer
Use video documentation of own choreography to evaluate structural choices against choreographic intent — identify specific moments where choices succeed or fall short
Compare two versions of the same choreographic material — one developed with extensive documentation and reflection, one without — and evaluate what the documentation process produced

modes.reason: Documenting and evaluating choreographic decisions is a reflective practice habit that develops through sustained cycles of making, documenting and evaluating. Students need repeated practice with the documentation cycle until it becomes integrated into the creative process rather than an afterthought.

This node brings together improvisation and material generation (Node 1), device selection and development (Node 2), and reflective practice from D02 into a documented evaluation of the whole choreographic process. Students who can make choreographic choices but cannot evaluate and document them have not met the standard's full demand.

descriptors.title: Apply skills to communicate meaning
descriptors.description: apply technical and expressive skills and/or genre- or style-specific techniques to communicate ideas, perspectives and/or meaning
descriptors.knowledge: Students can use technical and expressive skills in own dance works (AC9ADA6C02). They have not yet applied skills with a clear rationale for how each contributes to communicating specific ideas, perspectives or meaning.
descriptors.endpoint: Students apply technical and expressive skills deliberately to communicate intended ideas, perspectives and meaning, using feedback to refine their application.

nodes.label: Applying technical skills to intensify communication
nodes.checkpoint: Students can apply specific technical skills to intensify the communication of mood, atmosphere or meaning in a dance
criteria: Applies at least one technical skill with a specific communicative purpose
Explains how the skill contributes to mood or meaning
Technical choices are connected to intent — not just demonstrations of ability

width.minimum: Apply at least one technical skill (e.g. balance, strength, coordination) with a specific communicative purpose; explain how the skill contributes to the mood or meaning communicated
width.typical: Apply a range of technical skills across a dance to communicate choreographic intent; explain how each technical choice intensifies or clarifies the intended communication
wider: Investigate how mastery of a specific technical skill (e.g. controlled stillness, sustained movement quality) changes what a dance communicates — experiment with developing that skill to expressive purpose
Apply strength, balance and coordination simultaneously — evaluate the challenge of coordinating multiple technical demands while maintaining expressive clarity
Experiment with applying style-specific techniques from a dance genre that uses those techniques with different communicative purposes than own familiar style

modes.reason: Students commonly apply technical skills for their own sake — demonstrating what they can do — without connecting technical choices to communicative intent. Scaffolding the reasoning (what am I trying to communicate, which technical quality serves that, how does this skill intensify the intended effect?) builds the habit of purposeful technical application.

nodes.label: Using feedback to refine expressive and technical application
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use feedback to evaluate and refine how technical and expressive skills are communicating choreographic intent
criteria: Responds to at least one piece of feedback with a documented change
Explains what the feedback revealed about the technical or expressive application
Refinement is specific and connected to communicative intent

width.minimum: Respond to at least one piece of feedback about technical or expressive skill application; document what changed and why
width.typical: Use feedback from peers and teachers to evaluate clarity of movement, projection, focus and musicality; refine technical and expressive application; document decisions using dance terminology
wider: Use Viewpoints questions alongside peer feedback to evaluate whether movement choices are communicating what is intended — 'What did you think the dance expressed?'
Use video to evaluate and refine spatial placement or articulation — compare video observation with own proprioceptive sense of the movement
Develop criteria for evaluating own technical and expressive application — articulate what 'clear communication' looks like across multiple technical and expressive dimensions

modes.reason: Using feedback to refine technical and expressive application requires sustained cycles of performing, receiving feedback, adjusting and performing again. The refinement habit develops through iteration, not through exposure to more feedback types or dance contexts.

nodes.label: Integrated application of skills across a complete dance
nodes.checkpoint: Students can apply technical and expressive skills consistently across a complete dance to communicate intended ideas, perspectives or meaning
criteria: Demonstrates at least two deliberate technical and expressive applications in a complete dance
Applications are connected to intended meaning — not just demonstrations of skill
Can evaluate whether the application communicated the intended ideas

width.minimum: Perform or present a dance that demonstrates at least two deliberate technical and expressive skill applications connected to intended meaning
width.typical: Perform or present a dance demonstrating consistent and deliberate application of technical and expressive skills across the whole work; evaluate whether the application successfully communicates the intended meaning
wider: Apply genre- or style-specific techniques with sufficient mastery that they carry the expressive content of the style — evaluate whether technique has moved from imitation to genuine stylistic expression
Perform the same dance material with deliberately different technical and expressive choices — evaluate how the changes alter what the dance communicates
Reflect on the relationship between technical mastery and expressive freedom — evaluate how technical development has expanded rather than constrained expressive possibilities

modes.reason: This node integrates purposeful technical application (Node 1), feedback-driven refinement (Node 2), and material developed through AC9ADA8C01 into a complete performed work. The coordination of technical and expressive skills across a whole dance is the learning — students who can apply skills in isolation but cannot sustain them across a complete work have not met the standard.

descriptors.title: Develop safe dance practice and skills
descriptors.description: develop safe dance practice and use of expressive and technical skills and, as appropriate, genre- or style-specific techniques
descriptors.knowledge: Students can use technical and expressive skills with some control (AC9ADA6D01). They have not yet systematically extended movement vocabulary across diverse styles or applied safe dance practice principles deliberately across different physical demands.
descriptors.endpoint: Students develop technical and expressive skills and movement vocabulary through sustained deliberate practice, applying safe dance practice principles appropriately.

nodes.label: Developing technical competence through deliberate practice
nodes.checkpoint: Students can develop specific technical skills through deliberate practice, using feedback to guide improvement
criteria: Practises at least one technical skill with a clear improvement goal
Describes what improved and how it affects the dance
Uses feedback from self, peer or teacher to direct practice

width.minimum: Practise at least one technical skill (e.g. balance, alignment, coordination) with a clear improvement goal; describe what changed and how the improvement affects the dance
width.typical: Develop technical competence across multiple skills through sustained practice; use self, peer and teacher feedback to guide practice direction; document progress and remaining goals
wider: Extend technical competence across control, coordination, accuracy, alignment, balance, flexibility, strength and endurance — develop a personal practice plan targeting specific skills
Investigate how safe dance practice principles apply differently across styles and physical demands — develop own safe practice protocol
Experiment with style-specific techniques from a dance style distinct from own experience — document what the technique demands technically and how it extends own range

modes.reason: Technical skill development in dance is fundamentally a consolidation task — the skills (balance, alignment, coordination, strength) develop through sustained repetition with feedback, not through exposure to more contexts. Students who practise deliberately across a sustained period build genuine technical competence; students who rotate through many styles without sustained practice do not.

nodes.label: Extending movement vocabulary through diverse styles
nodes.checkpoint: Students can extend their movement vocabulary by experimenting with movements and techniques from diverse dance styles
criteria: Experiments with at least one style beyond own familiar range
Describes what the experimentation added to own movement vocabulary
Movement vocabulary extension is connected to expressive possibility — not just technical novelty

width.minimum: Experiment with movements or techniques from at least one dance style beyond own familiar style; describe what the experimentation added to own movement vocabulary
width.typical: Improvise using movements and techniques from diverse dance styles; document what each style adds to available expressive range; reflect on how extended vocabulary informs own choreography and performance
wider: Develop a personal movement vocabulary archive — document movements and techniques from different styles with annotations about their expressive qualities and technical demands

Investigate how a specific dance style from another cultural context uses expressive skills (gesture, facial expression, use of space) differently — experiment with integrating these into own movement vocabulary
Create an improvisation that deliberately draws on movements from three or more distinct dance styles — evaluate how the combination creates new expressive possibilities

modes.reason: Students who improvise only within familiar movement vocabulary cannot access the expressive range the descriptor requires. Experimenting with diverse styles — each with different technical and expressive demands — genuinely expands what students can do and say through movement. Breadth here is the mechanism of growth, not just enrichment.

nodes.label: Using expressive skills to communicate
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use expressive skills — including gesture, facial expression and use of space — to communicate relationships, emotions or ideas in dance
criteria: Uses at least one expressive skill with a clear communicative purpose
Explains how the skill serves the intended communication
Does not rely on generic expression — choices are connected to specific intent

width.minimum: Use at least one expressive skill deliberately to communicate a relationship, emotion or idea; explain how the skill serves the communicative intent
width.typical: Use a range of expressive skills across a dance to communicate ideas with consistency and clarity; evaluate whether the expressive choices achieve the intended communication
wider: Explore how expressive skills carry different meanings in different cultural dance traditions — investigate and experiment with expanding own expressive range
Develop an extended improvisation focused entirely on expressive skills — gesture, facial expression, spatial relationship — without relying on technical virtuosity
Evaluate the difference between expressive skills that communicate clearly and those that are generic — develop criteria for evaluating own expressive choices

modes.reason: Students commonly use expressive skills by habit — smiling, making eye contact — without reasoning through whether those choices serve the intended communication. Scaffolding the reasoning (what am I trying to communicate, what expressive skill serves that, does the audience receive what I intend?) builds deliberate expressive practice rather than default behaviour.

descriptors.title: Reflect on dance works to inform practice
descriptors.description: reflect on own and others' dance works and/or practices to inform choreographic choices and use of technical and expressive skills
descriptors.knowledge: Students can use teacher feedback to reflect on own dance practice (AC9ADA6D02). They have not yet systematically investigated others' dance works as a source of influence, or used reflection to document and direct practice development over time.
descriptors.endpoint: Students reflect on own and others' dance works to make and document informed choices about choreography and technical/expressive skill use.

nodes.label: Investigating others' dance works as influence
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify how other dancers' and choreographers' use of elements, devices and techniques influences own practice choices
criteria: Investigates at least one example of another artist's use of an element or technique
Explains how the example informs a specific choice in own practice
Does not reduce influence to 'inspiration' — connects specific observation to specific decision

width.minimum: Investigate at least one example of how another dancer or choreographer uses an element of dance or style-specific technique; explain how this informs a specific choice in own practice
width.typical: Document a range of examples of how others use elements of dance or style-specific techniques in a journal; explain how each example informs choices in own choreography or performance
wider: Develop a personal archive of influences — journal entries documenting how specific examples of others' work open new directions in own practice

Investigate how two choreographers with contrasting approaches to the same element of dance make different expressive choices — analyse what each reveals and use the comparison to sharpen own approach
Research a choreographer whose work has directly influenced a dance style and trace the chain of influence into contemporary practice

modes.reason: Students need to build a personal repertoire of influences — documented examples of how others use elements and techniques — before reflection on influences can become a genuine practice habit. A single example is insufficient; accumulated references build the vocabulary for informed choreographic decision-making.

nodes.label: Using feedback to refine dance
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use feedback from peers, self-observation and teachers to identify specific refinements to choreography and technical/expressive skills
criteria: Responds to at least one piece of feedback with a documented change
Explains what the feedback revealed and what changed as a result
Change is specific — not a vague 'I improved'

width.minimum: Respond to at least one piece of feedback with a documented change in choreography or skill use; explain what the feedback revealed and what changed
width.typical: Use feedback from peers who have observed a workshop or rehearsal to identify refinements; document how feedback leads to specific changes in dance; evaluate outcomes
wider: Use video self-review alongside peer feedback — compare what each reveals and evaluate how video feedback identifies things that peer observation misses
Develop criteria for evaluating own rehearsal footage — go beyond 'it looked good/bad' to articulate specific technical and expressive standards
Evaluate how different feedback sources (self, peer, teacher) reveal different aspects of dance — develop a personal feedback integration strategy

modes.reason: Using feedback productively — receiving it, interpreting it against dance criteria, and translating it into changed practice — is a reflective habit that develops through repeated cycles. Students need sustained practice with the feedback loop, not exposure to more feedback contexts.

nodes.label: Sustained reflection on practice development
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use sustained reflection on own and others' dance to show how practice has developed over time and where it is heading
criteria: Shows at least one example where reflection led to changed practice direction over time
Documentation demonstrates development — not just a single reflection moment
Reflection on others' work and own feedback is connected to increasingly informed practice choices

width.minimum: Show at least one example where reflection led to a changed practice direction over time; explain what changed and what the reflection revealed
width.typical: Document how practice has developed across a unit as a result of sustained reflection on own and others' dance; evaluate how movement vocabulary and technical/expressive range have grown
wider: Reflect on how movement vocabulary has extended across a unit — identify specific moments where encountering others' work opened new directions
Develop a personal artistic statement articulating the influences currently shaping own dance practice and how they are being engaged and adapted
Evaluate own choreographic or performance development against specific criteria — identify what has developed, what remains a goal, and what new directions have emerged

modes.reason: This node integrates influence investigation (Node 1) and feedback cycles (Node 2) into a sustained account of practice development. Students who can reflect on single moments but cannot demonstrate development over time have not met the descriptor's demand for reflection that informs ongoing practice.

descriptors.title: Investigate dance across cultures and contexts
descriptors.description: investigate ways that dance works, performers and/or choreographers across cultures, times, places and/or other contexts use the elements of dance, choreographic devices and/or production elements to communicate ideas, perspectives and/or meaning
descriptors.knowledge: Students can identify how elements of dance and choreographic devices are used to communicate ideas (AC9ADA6E01). They have not yet investigated how cultural, historical and contextual factors shape these choices across diverse dance traditions.
descriptors.endpoint: Students investigate how elements of dance, choreographic devices and production elements are used across cultures, times and contexts to communicate ideas, perspectives and meaning.

nodes.label: Identifying elements and devices in dance works
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify elements of dance and choreographic devices in a given work and describe how each contributes to the meaning communicated
criteria: Identifies at least two elements or devices in a given work
Describes how each contributes to meaning — not just names the element
Does not confuse describing what a dance looks like with explaining how it communicates

width.minimum: Identify at least two elements of dance or choreographic devices in a given work; describe how each contributes to the meaning or effect
width.typical: Analyse a range of dance works to identify elements and devices; explain how specific choices communicate intended ideas or perspectives
wider: Compare how the same element of dance (e.g. repetition, use of space) is used in two works from different genres or cultural contexts — analyse what the comparison reveals about how meaning is made differently

Use Viewpoints questions to investigate choreographic intention — 'What was the choreographer's intention?', 'What ideas did the dance express?' — and evaluate whether the choreographic choices achieve the intention
Analyse how a single realistic movement can be manipulated from representational to symbolic — investigate examples across different dance traditions

modes.reason: Students need to accumulate a repertoire of dance works and the elements/devices used within them before they can reason about how context shapes meaning-making choices. A single example gives too narrow a lens for genuine comparative analysis across cultures and times.

nodes.label: Investigating across cultures, times and contexts
nodes.checkpoint: Students can investigate how cultural, historical and contextual factors shape how elements of dance and choreographic devices are used to communicate ideas
criteria: Investigates at least one work whose choreographic choices are connected to cultural or historical context
Explains how context shapes specific element or device choices
Goes beyond surface description to explain the relationship between context and meaning

width.minimum: Investigate one dance work or choreographer whose practice is shaped by cultural or historical context; explain how context influences specific choreographic choices
width.typical: Investigate dance works across at least two different cultural or historical contexts; analyse how context shapes choreographic choices and what ideas each work communicates
wider: Investigate the development of a dance style across different social and historical contexts — analyse how social and environmental factors shaped the style's evolution
Investigate how digital tools and immersive technologies like VR are influencing contemporary choreography and performance — analyse what new expressive possibilities these technologies create
Investigate the reciprocal influence between dance traditions from different cultural contexts — analyse how cross-cultural exchange shapes dance practice

modes.reason: Students commonly describe what a dance work does without connecting it to cultural or historical context. Investigating works from multiple distinct cultural and historical contexts forces students to develop contextual reasoning as a habit — understanding that choreographic choices are shaped by social, historical and environmental factors, not just individual preference.

nodes.label: Connecting investigation to own choreographic practice
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use their investigation of dance works across contexts to inform specific decisions in their own choreography
criteria: Identifies at least one insight from investigating other works that influenced own choreography
Explains the connection — not just 'I was inspired by'
Distinguishes adaptation from imitation

width.minimum: Identify at least one specific insight from investigating other dance works that has influenced a decision in own choreography; explain the connection
width.typical: Analyse how investigating dance works across contexts informs own choreographic choices; document specific points of influence and how they are adapted rather than imitated
wider: Develop a journal documenting how investigation of diverse dance traditions has extended own choreographic vocabulary and opened new directions
Investigate how distinguishing stylistic features of specific dance genres can inform own choreography — develop a choreographic approach that is informed by but not derivative of those genres
Construct an argument about why investigating diverse dance traditions produces stronger and more distinctive choreography than drawing on a single tradition

modes.reason: This node requires students to bring together element/device analysis (Node 1) and contextual investigation (Node 2) and connect both to their own choreographic decisions. Students who can analyse other works but cannot use that analysis to inform own practice have not met the standard's full investigative demand.

Students commonly describe what they have investigated without articulating how it changes specific decisions in own work. Scaffolding the connection — what did I learn, what decision did it change, how is my adaptation different from imitation — builds the analytical-to-practical transfer.

descriptors.title: Diversity of First Nations dance
descriptors.description: investigate the diversity of dance choreographed and/or performed by First Nations Australians considering culturally responsive approaches to Indigenous Cultural and Intellectual Property rights
descriptors.knowledge: Students have some awareness that First Nations Australians have diverse dance traditions. They have not yet investigated this diversity systematically or engaged with ICIP rights frameworks in dance contexts.
descriptors.endpoint: Students investigate the diversity of First Nations Australian dance with genuine cultural responsiveness, understanding and applying ICIP rights frameworks.

nodes.label: Understanding ICIP rights in dance contexts
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain what ICIP rights mean in dance contexts and describe what culturally responsive engagement with First Nations dance looks like in practice
criteria: Explains what ICIP rights mean in a dance context
Gives at least one specific example of respectful engagement
Does not reduce ICIP to a checklist — explains the reasoning behind protocols

width.minimum: Explain what ICIP rights are in a dance context; give one example of what respectful engagement with First Nations dance looks like
width.typical: Investigate ICIP rights frameworks and explain how they apply to dance practice — using movement vocabulary, performing First Nations dances, referencing choreographic approaches
wider: Investigate a specific case of cultural appropriation in dance where ICIP rights were denied — explain what happened, who was harmed, and what a respectful alternative would have been
Research the questions practitioners should ask when engaging with First Nations dance material — 'Who created this dance?', 'Who owns these movements?' — and develop own practical guidelines
Explore how ICIP rights in dance differ from copyright in other arts — analyse why collective ownership of movement vocabulary requires different protocols

modes.reason: Students commonly understand ICIP rights in the abstract without being able to reason through specific dance scenarios — they know 'you need permission' without knowing who to ask, what counts as cultural movement vocabulary, or what respectful engagement looks like in practice. Scaffolding scenario-based reasoning builds actionable understanding.

nodes.label: Investigating diversity of First Nations Australian dance
nodes.checkpoint: Students can investigate the diversity of First Nations Australian dance practices across regions and contexts with cultural responsiveness
criteria: Investigates at least one First Nations Australian dance or practice in genuine depth
Explains cultural significance — not just describes what the dance looks like
Demonstrates cultural responsiveness throughout

width.minimum: Investigate at least one First Nations Australian dance work or choreographer in depth; explain what makes it culturally significant
width.typical: Investigate First Nations Australian dance from at least two different regional or cultural contexts; analyse what is distinctive about each and how ICIP responsibilities apply
wider: Use a map of First Nations Australian language groups to identify where choreographers and performers are working — investigate the geographic and cultural breadth of First Nations dance practice
Analyse how linear and non-linear narrative is used in specific First Nations Australian dance works to explore issues of identity, relationships or empathy
Investigate a contemporary First Nations Australian choreographer working in contemporary or cross-cultural contexts — analyse how they navigate cultural identity and ICIP responsibilities

modes.reason: Students commonly treat First Nations Australian dance as a single tradition rather than understanding the enormous diversity across hundreds of distinct cultural groups, regions, and contemporary/traditional contexts. Multiple distinct investigation contexts — different regions, contemporary vs traditional, cross-cultural — resolve this misconception through genuine breadth.

nodes.label: Applying culturally responsive approaches in dance
criteria: Applies at least one ICIP protocol question to a real or hypothetical dance practice scenario
Explains the ethical reasoning behind the protocol

width.minimum: Apply at least one ICIP protocol question to own dance practice; explain the reasoning behind the protocol.
width.typical: Apply multiple protocol questions to own practice; explain how the protocols guide ethical engagement with First Nations Australian dance in learning and performance contexts.
wider: Evaluate a specific case of cultural appropriation in dance — analyse who was harmed, what rights were denied, and what a respectful alternative would have been.
Develop personal guidelines for culturally responsive engagement with First Nations Australian dance, grounded in specific protocols.

modes.reason: Applying protocols requires reasoning through specific dance contexts — who created this movement, whose story is it, what permission is needed.

descriptors.title: Rehearse and perform dance
descriptors.description: rehearse and perform dance for audiences, using technical and expressive skills and, as appropriate genre- or style-specific techniques
descriptors.knowledge: Students can perform dance with basic technical and expressive skill for an audience (AC9ADA6P01). They have not yet used deliberate rehearsal strategies, production elements, or audience communication tools to enhance the performance experience.
descriptors.endpoint: Students rehearse and perform dance for audiences using deliberate rehearsal strategies, appropriate technical and expressive skills, and production elements to communicate choreographic intent.

nodes.label: Using rehearsal strategies to prepare for performance
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use deliberate rehearsal strategies to develop confidence, clarity and expressive quality in preparation for performance
criteria: Uses at least one deliberate rehearsal strategy with a specific goal
Explains what the strategy helped develop
Rehearsal strategy is targeted — not just 'run it again from the top'

width.minimum: Use at least one rehearsal strategy (e.g. spotting, spatial planning, repetition of key phrases) with a specific preparation goal; explain what the strategy helped develop
width.typical: Use a range of rehearsal strategies to develop confidence, clarity of movement, projection, focus and musicality; document how rehearsal strategies address specific performance challenges
wider: Use video review during rehearsal to identify and address spatial placement, articulation and expressive clarity — compare video observation with own sense of the performance
Plan effective use of available performance spaces during rehearsals — evaluate how spatial planning changes performer confidence and audience experience
Develop a personal rehearsal protocol for preparing a specific aspect of performance (e.g. projection, focus, musicality) — evaluate its effectiveness over multiple rehearsal sessions

modes.reason: Effective rehearsal — using targeted strategies repeatedly to address specific performance challenges — is a disciplined habit that develops through sustained practice cycles. Students who rehearse without strategy develop performance confidence more slowly and less deliberately. The skill is in the purposeful application of rehearsal strategies, which develops through iteration.

nodes.label: Using production elements to communicate intent
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use production elements to extend communication of choreographic intent to an audience beyond the movement alone
criteria: Identifies or uses at least one production element with a communicative purpose
Explains what the element adds to the communication of choreographic intent
Production choice is purposeful — connected to intent, not just visual interest

width.minimum: Identify at least one production element (projection, soundscape, voice-over, special effects) that could enhance the dance's communication; explain what it would add
width.typical: Use at least one production element to share key ideas or information about the creative intention of the dance with the audience; evaluate whether the production choice enhances the communication
wider: Develop a production design that uses multiple elements (sound, projection, spatial effects) in coordinated ways — evaluate how each element contributes to the total communicative experience
Investigate how production elements in contemporary professional dance works create meaning beyond the movement — use findings to inform own production decisions
Evaluate the difference between production elements that enhance and those that distract from choreographic intent — develop criteria for purposeful production choice

modes.reason: Students commonly add production elements for visual interest without reasoning through whether they enhance or distract from choreographic intent. Scaffolding the reasoning (what does this production choice add, does it serve the choreographic idea, what would the dance communicate without it?) builds purposeful production thinking rather than decoration.

nodes.label: Performing and communicating with audiences
nodes.checkpoint: Students can perform dance for an audience using technical and expressive skills appropriately, and communicate the choreographic intent through introduction and presentation
criteria: Performs dance with deliberate technical and expressive choices
Introduces the dance in a way that communicates choreographic intent to the audience
Performance is for the audience — not just an execution of choreography

width.minimum: Perform a dance for an audience with at least one deliberate technical and expressive choice; introduce the dance with basic contextual information
width.typical: Perform dance using technical and expressive skills that serve choreographic intent; introduce the dance using style-specific terminology that communicates the creative intention to the audience
wider: Develop a program note or voice-over introduction using style-specific dance terminology that communicates choreographic intent to an audience unfamiliar with the dance context
Evaluate the performance experience from the audience's perspective — use peer feedback to assess whether the technical and expressive application communicated the intended ideas
Perform the same dance in two different performance contexts (e.g. studio showing vs formal stage) — evaluate how context changes performance choices and audience experience

modes.reason: This node integrates rehearsal strategy (Node 1), production elements (Node 2), and technical and expressive skills from C02 into a complete performance event. The coordination of movement, production, and audience communication is the learning — students who can perform technically but cannot communicate with an audience have not met the standard's full demand.

descriptors.title: Improvise, devise and interpret drama
descriptors.description: improvise and devise drama and/or interpret scripted drama, manipulating elements of drama and applying conventions relevant to the style/form
descriptors.knowledge: Students can use elements of drama and simple conventions in own drama work (AC9ADR6C01). They have not yet selected and manipulated elements with clear rationale for how each serves the intended dramatic action, nor applied style-specific conventions with deliberate intent.
descriptors.endpoint: Students improvise, devise and interpret drama where manipulation of elements and application of conventions is deliberate and connected to intended dramatic action and meaning.

nodes.label: Identifying and developing dramatic potential
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify dramatic potential in a starting point and develop it into dramatic action using elements of drama
criteria: Identifies dramatic potential in a given starting point
Develops it into dramatic action using at least one element deliberately
Dramatic action has a clear direction — not just loosely connected scenes

width.minimum: Identify dramatic potential in a given starting point (stimulus, text, image, scenario); develop it into a short dramatic action using at least one element of drama deliberately
width.typical: Identify dramatic potential in diverse starting points; use improvisation to explore situations, characters and relationships; develop dramatic action using elements of drama with a clear purpose
wider: Use 'mantle of the expert' or play-building to develop dramatic action from an inquiry question — evaluate how the collaborative devising process constrains and enables dramatic choices
Respond to the dramatic potential of an image using the questions 'What's happening? What has happened? What's going to happen next?' — develop improvised scenes from each response
Identify dramatic potential in research or issues and use improvisation to develop situations and characters that represent multiple perspectives on the issue

modes.reason: Students need to build a repertoire of starting points — stimulus types, devising approaches, dramatic structures — before they can identify and develop dramatic potential reliably. Each approach (mantle of the expert, image response, play-building, inquiry question) produces different kinds of dramatic material and builds different generative skills.

nodes.label: Manipulating elements and applying conventions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can manipulate elements of drama and apply style-relevant conventions to shape and communicate dramatic action
criteria: Manipulates at least one element with a clear reason connected to dramatic action
Applies at least one relevant convention
Explains how each choice shapes the drama — not just describes what was done

width.minimum: Manipulate at least one element of drama (e.g. tension, symbol, space) and apply at least one convention with a clear reason; explain how each shapes the dramatic action
width.typical: Manipulate a range of elements and apply conventions relevant to the style or form; use voice, movement, space and time to heighten tension, focus action and shape meaning; document and justify choices
wider: Employ voice/vocalisation and movement to heighten tension and shape meaning — develop an extended sequence where multiple element manipulations build toward a dramatic climax
Apply conventions such as flashback, aside, slow motion or chorus — evaluate how each convention shapes what the audience understands about time, character and situation

Work collaboratively to interpret scripted drama — use improvisation to explore characters and relationships, apply conventions, block the performance space — evaluate how each decision changes the meaning

modes.reason: Students commonly apply elements and conventions by default — using the familiar rather than the purposeful. Working across multiple styles, forms and dramatic contexts — devised, scripted, collaborative, solo — forces students to develop the habit of purposeful element manipulation rather than defaulting to comfortable choices.

nodes.label: Using feedback to develop and refine drama
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use feedback, reflection and evaluation to develop and extend ideas when improvising, devising or interpreting drama
criteria: Uses at least one piece of feedback to make a specific documented change
Explains what the feedback revealed and what changed
Reflection is connected to dramatic intent — not just general improvement

width.minimum: Use at least one piece of feedback to make a specific change to own drama; explain what the feedback revealed and what changed
width.typical: Use feedback, reflection and evaluation throughout the devising or interpreting process; document how each round of feedback develops and extends the drama
wider: Use Viewpoints questions to evaluate own drama in progress — 'What are the intentions in the drama?', 'Is meaning clear?', 'How could elements be used differently?' — document how the questions direct development
Develop a devising journal that documents how feedback and reflection have shaped dramatic decisions across a unit
Evaluate own devising process against the intended dramatic purpose — identify moments where feedback changed the direction and evaluate whether the change improved the drama

modes.reason: Using feedback and reflection to genuinely develop drama — rather than just acknowledging it — requires sustained practice with the feedback cycle. Students who engage with one round of feedback without iterating haven't built the habit that makes reflection productive. The skill develops through iteration.

This node brings together dramatic potential identification (Node 1), element manipulation and convention application (Node 2), and reflective practice from D02 into a complete devising and evaluation cycle. Students who can make dramatic choices but cannot use feedback to develop them are missing the integration that makes the drama a sustained creative act.

descriptors.title: Evaluate and refine drama
descriptors.description: evaluate and refine use of elements of drama and/or conventions to shape and sustain dramatic action and/or communicate ideas, perspectives and/or meaning
descriptors.knowledge: Students can make basic evaluations of own drama work (AC9ADR6C02). They have not yet systematically evaluated element and convention choices against intended dramatic purpose, or used that evaluation to make and document specific refinements.
descriptors.endpoint: Students evaluate and refine use of elements and conventions through deliberate questioning, feedback and reflection to shape dramatic action and communicate intended meaning.

nodes.label: Evaluating element and convention choices
nodes.checkpoint: Students can evaluate their use of elements and conventions against intended dramatic purpose and identify specific refinements
criteria: Evaluates at least one element or convention against intended purpose
Identifies at least one specific refinement with a reason — not just 'make it better'
Evaluation is connected to dramatic intent, not just personal preference

width.minimum: Evaluate at least one element or convention in own drama against the intended purpose; identify at least one specific refinement and explain why it improves the drama
width.typical: Evaluate use of elements, conventions and design choices against dramatic intent; use Viewpoints questions to interrogate own choices; identify and document specific refinements with reasoning
wider: Use Viewpoints questions systematically to evaluate own drama — 'What are your intentions?', 'Is meaning clear?', 'How could elements be used differently?' — document what each question reveals about gaps between intention and execution
Evaluate how costume, props and setting contribute to dramatic meaning — assess whether design choices support or undermine the intended effect
Evaluate how empathy is built into the dramatic experience — assess whether character portrayal and dramatic choices treat subjects with the care they deserve

modes.reason: Students commonly evaluate drama as 'good' or 'needs work' without specifying what element or convention choice is at issue and why. Scaffolding the evaluation (what is the intention, which element or convention serves that intention, does the current choice achieve it, what specific change would improve it?) builds targeted evaluation rather than general impression.

nodes.label: Refining drama through rehearsal
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use the rehearsal process to refine dramatic action, adjusting element and convention choices based on evaluation and feedback
criteria: Makes at least one documented refinement during rehearsal
Explains what changed and why — not just 'I practised it more'
Refinement is targeted — connected to a specific element, convention or dramatic intention

width.minimum: Make at least one documented refinement to drama during rehearsal based on evaluation or feedback; explain what changed and why
width.typical: Use rehearsal as an iterative refinement process; plan, organise and rehearse dramatic action; document decisions about elements, conventions and design; evaluate progress toward intended effect
wider: Adjust performance based on audience response — evaluate how audience feedback reveals the gap between intention and reception
Plan and organise the use of available theatre technologies in rehearsal — evaluate how each production decision supports or changes the dramatic meaning
Develop a rehearsal structure that systematically addresses specific dramatic challenges — evaluate the effectiveness of the structure against the intended dramatic purpose

modes.reason: Productive rehearsal — making targeted refinements, iterating based on evaluation, building toward a sustained dramatic effect — is a disciplined practice that develops through repeated cycles. Students who rehearse once without targeted refinement don't develop the rehearsal habit that makes drama improve over time.

nodes.label: Sustaining dramatic action with coherent intent
nodes.checkpoint: Students can evaluate and refine drama to sustain dramatic action and communicate intended ideas, perspectives and meaning throughout a complete work
criteria: Evaluates whether intended meaning was communicated in a complete drama
Identifies at least one specific aspect that would change in a future version with reasoning
Evaluation addresses the whole work — not just isolated moments

width.minimum: Perform or present a drama and evaluate whether intended meaning was communicated; identify at least one aspect of element or convention use that would change in a future version
width.typical: Stage devised or scripted drama for a clear and intended purpose; evaluate whether the overall structure and use of elements and conventions sustained the dramatic action and communicated intended meaning throughout
wider: Consider how and why empathy should be built into the entire dramatic experience — evaluate whether empathy is maintained through all dramatic choices, not just in individual moments
Explore conventions for developing characters and stories from diverse cultures — evaluate how these conventions build empathy and cultural understanding for audiences
Reflect on whether the drama's overall structure and choices communicated intended ideas with clarity — evaluate both what worked and what the audience actually received

modes.reason: This node integrates evaluation of elements and conventions (Node 1), rehearsal refinement (Node 2), and performance skills from D01 into a coherent evaluation of a complete dramatic work. Students who can evaluate individual moments but cannot assess whether the whole drama sustained its intent have not met the standard's demand.

descriptors.title: Develop performance skills for drama
descriptors.description: develop performance skills relevant to selected drama styles and/or forms
descriptors.knowledge: Students can use voice and movement to communicate in drama (AC9ADR6D01). They have not yet developed skills systematically through deliberate practice, applied style-specific conventions, or used improvisation to extend technique.
descriptors.endpoint: Students develop vocal and physical performance skills relevant to selected drama styles and forms, using improvisation and deliberate practice to extend technique.

nodes.label: Developing vocal performance skills
nodes.checkpoint: Students can develop vocal skills — projection, clarity, pace, pitch, dynamics, pause — with deliberate intent to communicate in drama
criteria: Develops at least one vocal quality with a clear communicative purpose
Describes what changed and how the improvement affects the drama
Uses drama terminology to describe vocal development

width.minimum: Develop at least one vocal quality (e.g. projection, pace, dynamics) through deliberate practice; describe what changed and how the improvement changes the drama
width.typical: Develop a range of vocal qualities through sustained practice; use control of pace, pitch, dynamics, pause and silence to communicate mood, character and meaning; document development using drama terminology
wider: Develop vocal qualities of projection, clarity and contrast through deliberate work on all dimensions — pace, pitch, dynamics, pause and silence — document how each element changes what the voice communicates
Investigate how voice is used in a specific drama style/form (e.g. physical theatre, verbatim theatre) — experiment with those vocal conventions and evaluate what they add
Experiment with vocalisation beyond speech — silence, breath, sound — and evaluate how these communicate differently from language alone
