modes.reason: Vocal skill development — projection, clarity, dynamic range, controlled use of pause — is fundamentally a consolidation task. The skills develop through sustained deliberate practice with feedback, not through exposure to more dramatic contexts. Students who practise vocal control repeatedly across a unit build genuine vocal range; students who try different styles without sustained practice do not.

nodes.label: Developing physical performance skills
nodes.checkpoint: Students can develop physical skills — movement, stillness, gesture, use of space — to communicate relationships, status and meaning in drama
criteria: Develops at least one physical skill with a clear communicative purpose
Describes what the physical choice communicates about relationship, status or meaning
Physical choices are deliberate — not just habitual movement

width.minimum: Develop at least one physical skill (e.g. use of stillness, spatial relationship, gesture) with a clear communicative purpose; describe what the skill communicates
width.typical: Develop physical performance skills including movement, stillness, realistic and non-realistic movement; explore ways to transition between scenes; use physical skills to communicate status/power relationships
wider: Develop use of the body across realistic and non-realistic movement — evaluate how departing from realistic movement changes what can be communicated
Experiment with using physical skills to communicate status and power relationships — investigate how posture, proximity, eye contact and gesture convey social dynamics

Develop understanding of how respectful relationships and empathy are expressed physically — explore how body language can affirm or undermine the dignity of characters from diverse cultural backgrounds

modes.reason: Students commonly use physical skills by habit — making eye contact, standing upright — without reasoning through whether those choices serve the intended communication. Scaffolding the reasoning ('what am I trying to communicate about this relationship, what physical choices serve that, does the audience receive what I intend?') builds deliberate physical practice.

nodes.label: Applying style-specific conventions through improvisation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can experiment with conventions associated with specific drama styles/forms using improvisation to develop technique
criteria: Experiments with at least one style-specific convention through improvisation
Describes what the convention achieves — not just names it
Uses improvisation as a genuine discovery process, not just practice

width.minimum: Experiment with at least one style-specific convention (e.g. flashback, aside, slow motion, chorus) through improvisation; describe what the convention achieves and how it shapes dramatic action
width.typical: Experiment with a range of style-specific conventions using improvisation; use insights from improvisation to interpret scripted scenes in the style; document how conventions heighten tension, sustain dramatic action or communicate meaning
wider: Use improvisation to explore techniques for heightening and releasing tension in a specific style — then apply insights to scripted scene interpretation
Experiment with multiple conventions in sequence — evaluate how each shapes dramatic action differently and what combinations produce strongest effect
Investigate conventions from a drama style distinct from own familiar experience — develop enough command of the conventions to use them with intentional rather than approximate effect

modes.reason: Students who only practise conventions in one style cannot develop genuine understanding of what conventions do — they may apply them mechanically without understanding their function. Experimenting with conventions across multiple styles, using improvisation to discover their effects, builds genuine understanding of how conventions shape dramatic action.

descriptors.title: Reflect on drama to inform practice
descriptors.description: reflect on their own and others' drama to inform choices when manipulating elements of drama and/or conventions to shape dramatic action
descriptors.knowledge: Students can use teacher feedback to reflect on own drama practice (AC9ADR6D02). They have not yet systematically investigated others' drama as a source of influence, or used reflection to document and direct practice development over time.
descriptors.endpoint: Students reflect on own and others' drama to make and document informed choices about elements, conventions and dramatic action.

nodes.label: Reflecting on own dramatic action
nodes.checkpoint: Students can reflect on the effectiveness of own dramatic action and make specific decisions about what to do differently
criteria: Identifies at least one aspect that was effective and one that would be done differently
Reflection is specific — connected to elements and dramatic action, not just general impressions
Documentation uses drama terminology

width.minimum: Reflect on at least one aspect of own dramatic action; identify what was effective and what would be done differently; document the reflection
width.typical: Reflect independently and in class discussion on dramatic action created; evaluate what was effective, whether the purpose was achieved, whether elements could have been managed differently; document decisions
wider: Use Viewpoints questions to deepen reflection — 'Was meaning clear?', 'How could elements be used differently for better effect?', 'Which elements worked well to make meaning clear?' — evaluate how structured questions reveal things self-observation misses
Reflect on how performance skills communicate perspectives — investigate how drama can perpetuate or challenge unequal power relationships
Develop a sustained reflective journal across a unit — trace how reflection on own dramatic action has changed practice decisions over time

modes.reason: Productive self-reflection in drama — going beyond 'it went well/badly' to specific evaluation of what elements worked, what purpose was achieved, and what specific changes would improve the work — is a disciplined habit that develops through repeated cycles. Students need sustained practice with the reflection cycle, not more dramatic contexts.

nodes.label: Seeking and using feedback
nodes.checkpoint: Students can seek, accept and respond to feedback to inform choices about elements and conventions in own drama
criteria: Responds to at least one piece of feedback with a documented change
Explains what the feedback revealed about a specific dramatic choice
Change is specific — connected to elements or conventions, not just 'I tried harder'

width.minimum: Seek and respond to at least one piece of feedback; document how the feedback changes a specific choice in own drama
width.typical: Seek, accept and respond to feedback from peers and teachers; use Viewpoints questions to generate specific feedback about elements and conventions; document how feedback informs choices
wider: Use Viewpoints questions to generate feedback from observers — 'How did the performer use language/movement to make character believable?', 'What relationships did you observe between characters?' — evaluate how each question reveals different dimensions of the drama
Develop criteria for giving and receiving useful drama feedback — distinguish feedback that identifies specific dramatic choices from feedback that is merely evaluative
Compare feedback from multiple sources (self, peer, teacher, video) — evaluate what each source reveals that others miss

modes.reason: Students commonly receive feedback passively without reasoning through how it applies to specific dramatic choices. Scaffolding the process — what is the feedback pointing to, what specific choice is at stake, what would I change and why — builds the habit of productive feedback integration rather than vague acknowledgment.

nodes.label: Developing understanding of character and human behaviour
nodes.checkpoint: Students can develop understanding of human behaviours and emotions to inform authentic portrayal of characters and relationships in drama
criteria: Uses observation or recall to inform at least one aspect of character portrayal
Adapts at least one performance skill to portray character with authenticity
Portrayal demonstrates empathy and appropriate boundaries

width.minimum: Use observation and recall of human behaviour to inform at least one aspect of character portrayal; describe what the observation revealed about how to adapt performance skills
width.typical: Develop understanding of human behaviours and emotions through observation and recall; adapt facial expression, posture, gesture, movement and voice to portray age, power or attitude; apply this to character work with appropriate boundaries
wider: Investigate how to express character relationships through vocal dynamics, eye contact, distance and space — develop a vocabulary for physical and vocal relationship expression
Reflect on how performance skills can communicate perspectives about power relationships — evaluate how drama practitioners have used performance to challenge oppression
Develop understanding of how to portray characters from different cultural or historical contexts with empathy and respect — investigate what research and understanding is needed

modes.reason: This node integrates vocal skills (D01 Node 1), physical skills (D01 Node 2), and feedback-informed reflection (Nodes 1-2) into a coherent understanding of character and human behaviour. Students who can demonstrate individual performance skills but cannot use them to build an authentic and respectful character portrayal have not integrated the components.

descriptors.title: Investigate drama across cultures and contexts
descriptors.description: investigate ways the elements of drama and/or conventions are used to communicate ideas, perspectives and/or meaning in drama created and/or performed across cultures, times, places and/or other contexts
descriptors.knowledge: Students can identify how elements of drama and conventions communicate ideas (AC9ADR6E01). They have not yet investigated how cultural, historical and contextual factors shape these choices across diverse dramatic traditions.
descriptors.endpoint: Students investigate how elements of drama and conventions communicate ideas, perspectives and meaning across cultures, times and contexts.

nodes.label: Identifying elements and conventions in drama works
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify specific elements of drama and conventions in a given work and describe how each contributes to meaning
criteria: Identifies at least two elements or conventions in a given work
Describes how each contributes to meaning — not just names the element
Does not confuse describing what happens in a drama with explaining how it communicates

width.minimum: Identify at least two elements of drama or conventions in a given work; describe how each contributes to the meaning or effect
width.typical: Analyse a range of drama works to identify elements and conventions; explain how specific choices communicate intended ideas or perspectives
wider: Use Viewpoints questions to analyse a drama — 'What ideas did the drama express?', 'What conventions established time/place/context?', 'How was movement used?' — evaluate what each question reveals
Write or record a review of a drama focusing on specific elements and conventions — evaluate how each element choice communicates or fails to communicate intended ideas
Compare how the same element of drama (e.g. tension, symbol) is used in works from different genres or cultural contexts — analyse what the comparison reveals

modes.reason: Students need to accumulate experience with a range of drama works and the elements and conventions used within them before they can reason about how context shapes choices. A single example gives too narrow a lens for genuine comparative analysis across cultures and times.

nodes.label: Investigating context and meaning
nodes.checkpoint: Students can investigate how cultural, historical and contextual factors shape how elements and conventions communicate ideas and meaning in drama
criteria: Investigates at least one work whose choices are connected to cultural or historical context
Explains how context influences specific element or convention choices
Goes beyond surface description to explain the relationship between context and meaning

width.minimum: Investigate one drama work whose choices are shaped by cultural or historical context; explain how context influences specific element or convention choices
width.typical: Investigate drama works across at least two different cultural or historical contexts; analyse how context shapes choices and explain how the same conventions communicate differently across contexts
wider: Investigate how the impact of time and place shapes dramatic meaning — analyse how a drama from a historical period communicates differently to contemporary audiences
Analyse how linear and non-linear narrative is used in drama from diverse cultures — compare what each narrative structure produces for an audience
Investigate drama from a country or region in Asia — analyse how the cultural context shapes element and convention choices in ways that differ from Australian or European drama traditions

modes.reason: Students commonly describe what a drama does without connecting it to the cultural or historical context that shaped the choices. Investigating works from multiple distinct cultural and historical contexts — Asian drama traditions, historical periods, contemporary diverse contexts — forces students to develop the contextual reasoning habit rather than applying one familiar analytical frame.

nodes.label: Connecting investigation to own drama practice
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use investigation of drama across contexts to inform specific decisions in own devising, interpreting or performing
criteria: Identifies at least one insight from investigating other works that influenced own practice
Explains the connection — not just 'I was inspired by'
Distinguishes informed adaptation from imitation or appropriation

width.minimum: Identify at least one insight from investigating other drama works that has influenced a decision in own practice; explain the connection
width.typical: Analyse how investigating drama across contexts informs own choices about elements, conventions and dramatic action; document specific influences and how they are adapted rather than imitated
wider: Develop a journal documenting how investigation of diverse drama traditions has opened new possibilities in own practice
Investigate how drama from other cultural traditions uses specific conventions — experiment with how those conventions might inform own devising without cultural appropriation
Construct an argument about why investigating diverse drama traditions produces stronger and more distinctive own practice than drawing on a single tradition

modes.reason: This node requires students to bring together element/convention analysis (Node 1) and contextual investigation (Node 2) and connect both to own practice decisions. Students who can analyse other works but cannot use that analysis to inform own drama have not met the standard's full investigative demand.

Students commonly describe what they have investigated without articulating how it changes specific decisions in own work. Scaffolding the connection — what did I learn, what decision did it change, how is my adaptation different from imitation — builds the analytical-to-practical transfer.

descriptors.title: Diversity of First Nations drama
descriptors.description: investigate the diversity of drama created and/or performed by First Nations Australians, considering culturally responsive approaches to Indigenous Cultural and Intellectual Property rights
descriptors.knowledge: Students have some awareness that First Nations Australians have diverse storytelling and performance traditions. They have not yet investigated this diversity systematically or engaged with ICIP rights frameworks in drama contexts.
descriptors.endpoint: Students investigate the diversity of First Nations Australian drama with genuine cultural responsiveness, understanding and applying ICIP rights frameworks.

nodes.label: Understanding ICIP rights in drama
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain what ICIP rights mean in drama contexts and describe what culturally responsive engagement with First Nations drama looks like in practice
criteria: Explains what ICIP rights mean in a drama context
Gives at least one specific example of respectful engagement
Does not reduce ICIP to a checklist — explains the reasoning behind protocols

width.minimum: Explain what ICIP rights are in a drama context; give one example of what respectful engagement with First Nations drama looks like
width.typical: Investigate ICIP rights frameworks and explain how they apply to drama-making — using cultural stories, developing characters from First Nations contexts, representing historical events
wider: Investigate a specific case of cultural appropriation in drama where ICIP rights were denied — explain what happened, who was harmed, and what a respectful alternative would have been

Use ICIP protocols to reason through whether specific ideas from a cultural source can be used in new drama work — document the reasoning process including 'Whose story is it?' and 'Is this my story to share?'
Explore how drama practitioners can communicate First Nations Australian perspectives on resilience or colonisation respectfully — develop criteria for ethically engaging with this material

modes.reason: Students commonly understand ICIP rights abstractly without being able to reason through specific drama scenarios — they know permission is needed without being able to work out whose story it is, what counts as cultural expression, or what respectful engagement looks like in practice. Scenario-based scaffolding builds actionable understanding.

nodes.label: Investigating diversity of First Nations Australian drama
nodes.checkpoint: Students can investigate the diversity of First Nations Australian drama practices across contexts with cultural responsiveness
criteria: Investigates at least one First Nations Australian drama in genuine depth
Explains cultural significance — not just describes the content
Demonstrates cultural responsiveness throughout

width.minimum: Investigate at least one First Nations Australian drama work or practitioner in depth; explain what makes it culturally significant
width.typical: Investigate diverse examples of First Nations Australian drama; analyse how practitioners use historical and cultural material to create contemporary theatre; apply ICIP understanding to the investigation
wider: Investigate how contemporary First Nations Australian theatre practitioners use historical and cultural material — analyse how they communicate perspectives on resilience, identity and the impacts of colonisation

Investigate how First Nations Australian drama uses linear and non-linear narrative to explore issues of identity, relationships or empathy — compare with non-First Nations dramatic narrative approaches
Research how diverse First Nations Australian drama reflects the diversity of hundreds of distinct cultural groups — investigate the geographic and cultural breadth of practice

modes.reason: Students commonly treat First Nations Australian drama as a single tradition rather than understanding the enormous diversity across hundreds of distinct cultural groups, regions and contemporary contexts. Multiple distinct investigation contexts resolve this misconception through genuine breadth.

nodes.label: Applying culturally responsive approaches in drama
criteria: Applies at least one ICIP protocol question to a real or hypothetical drama practice scenario
Explains the ethical reasoning behind the protocol

width.minimum: Apply at least one ICIP protocol question to own drama practice; explain the reasoning behind the protocol.
width.typical: Apply multiple protocol questions to own practice as a devisor, interpreter and performer; explain how the protocols guide ethical engagement with First Nations Australian drama.
wider: Use ICIP protocols to reason through whether ideas from a cultural source can be used in new drama work — document the reasoning process.
Develop criteria for ethically engaging with First Nations Australian perspectives in drama — grounded in specific protocols and the principle of cultural responsiveness.

modes.reason: Applying ICIP protocols to drama requires reasoning through specific questions: whose story is it, is this my story to share, what permission is needed.

descriptors.title: Rehearse and perform drama
descriptors.description: rehearse and perform improvised, devised and/or scripted drama to audiences, using performance skills and conventions relevant to style and/or form
descriptors.knowledge: Students can perform drama for an audience with basic performance skills (AC9ADR6P01). They have not yet used deliberate rehearsal strategies, systematically collected audience feedback, or reflected on the relationship between intention and audience reception.
descriptors.endpoint: Students rehearse and perform drama for audiences using performance skills and conventions appropriate to style and form, reflecting on the relationship between intention and audience reception.

nodes.label: Rehearsing with performance intent
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use the rehearsal process to develop performance readiness — technical skills, conventions and expressive clarity — with a clear sense of intended audience experience
criteria: Rehearses with at least one clear performance goal
Explains what the rehearsal developed and how it affects audience experience
Rehearsal is targeted — not just running through material

width.minimum: Rehearse drama with at least one clear performance goal; explain what the rehearsal developed and how it affects the audience experience
width.typical: Plan and use rehearsal to develop performance readiness across technical skills, conventions and expressive clarity; use Viewpoints questions to evaluate rehearsal progress; document decisions
wider: Use Viewpoints questions to set and evaluate rehearsal goals — 'What are our intentions?', 'Is meaning clear?', 'Is it engaging?' — develop these as ongoing rehearsal tools rather than post-performance reflection
Use video to review own rehearsal performance — evaluate what the recording reveals that in-the-moment rehearsal misses
Develop rehearsal strategies that systematically address specific performance challenges — evaluate the strategies' effectiveness over multiple sessions

modes.reason: Purposeful rehearsal — using targeted strategies to address specific performance challenges — is a disciplined habit that develops through repeated cycles. Students who simply run through material repeatedly without targeted evaluation don't develop the rehearsal discipline that makes performance improve.

nodes.label: Performing with style-appropriate skills and conventions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can perform drama using performance skills and conventions relevant to the style or form with clear communicative intent
criteria: Uses at least one performance skill and one convention appropriate to the style
Choices are connected to communicative intent — not just demonstrations of ability
Performance demonstrates empathy and appropriate respect for material and audience

width.minimum: Perform drama using at least one performance skill and one convention relevant to the style or form; explain how each serves the intended dramatic communication
width.typical: Perform improvised, devised or scripted drama using performance skills and conventions appropriate to the style; suit choices to the underlying dramatic structure; demonstrate communicative intent throughout
wider: Perform using conventions that match the underlying dramatic structure — evaluate how structural choices constrain and enable performance decisions

Perform drama that explores First Nations Australian perspectives on identity, resilience or environmental practices — apply ICIP responsibilities and communicate with respectful and empathetic intent
Develop performance choices that demonstrate genuine empathy for the characters and situations portrayed — evaluate how empathy is expressed through performance skills rather than just described

modes.reason: Students commonly perform using familiar skills without reasoning through whether those choices serve the style or the intended communication. Scaffolding the reasoning — what does this style/form require, what performance skill or convention serves that, am I making choices that communicate to the audience or just demonstrating what I can do — builds purposeful performance thinking.

nodes.label: Evaluating performance and audience reception
nodes.checkpoint: Students can collect and evaluate audience feedback and reflect on whether performance communicated intended meaning
criteria: Reflects on whether intended meaning was communicated to the audience
Identifies at least one specific aspect that worked and one that would change
Evaluation addresses the gap between intention and audience reception

width.minimum: Reflect on whether the performance communicated the intended meaning; identify at least one thing that worked and one that would change
width.typical: Collect and evaluate audience feedback; use Viewpoints questions to reflect on intentions, clarity and engagement; evaluate the gap between intention and reception; document how the evaluation would inform future performance
wider: Collect audience feedback systematically — compare audience reception with own intentions and evaluate the gap between what was communicated and what was intended
Reflect on how respectful relationships and empathy were expressed in performance and interpreted by the audience — evaluate whether the audience received the intended empathetic portrayal

Use Viewpoints questions as reflective tools — 'What were your intentions?', 'Was meaning clear?', 'What audience response suggested it was engaging?' — evaluate what each question reveals about the performance

modes.reason: This node integrates rehearsal preparation (Node 1), purposeful performance (Node 2), and feedback-based reflection from D02 into a complete performance event and evaluation cycle. Students who can perform but cannot evaluate the relationship between intention and audience reception have not met the standard's full demand.

descriptors.title: Design and structure media arts works
descriptors.description: design and structure media arts works to communicate ideas, perspectives and meaning for an intended audience
descriptors.knowledge: Students can plan and structure media arts works with basic pre-production tools (AC9AMA6C01). They have not yet made deliberate design decisions about media languages and technical elements with a clear rationale for how each serves the intended representation for a specific audience.
descriptors.endpoint: Students design and structure media arts works where media language and technical element choices are deliberate and connected to intended ideas, perspectives and meaning for a specific audience.

nodes.label: Planning with pre-production tools
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use pre-production planning tools to design a media arts work with deliberate choices about structure, genre and representational intent
criteria: Uses at least one pre-production planning tool
Explains how at least two design choices communicate intended meaning for the audience
Planning is deliberate — choices are justified, not just listed

width.minimum: Use at least one pre-production planning tool (storyboard, shooting script, production schedule); explain how at least two design choices communicate intended meaning for the audience
width.typical: Use appropriate pre-production templates to plan a media arts work; make deliberate choices about structure, genre conventions and media languages; justify each choice in relation to intended meaning and audience
wider: Trial multiple structural approaches using storyboards — evaluate how different structures change what the work communicates and select the most effective
Plan a hybrid production by combining genre conventions — evaluate how the hybrid structure serves the intended meaning in ways single genres cannot
Develop a production schedule that considers responsible media practices throughout — plan how ICIP, copyright and ethical representation obligations will be met

modes.reason: Using pre-production tools productively — making deliberate choices and justifying them in relation to intended meaning — is a planning habit that develops through repeated cycles of planning and production. Students who complete planning tools as a formality without genuine deliberation don't develop the pre-production discipline that makes production more intentional.

nodes.label: Designing representations with media languages
nodes.checkpoint: Students can design representations using technical and symbolic elements — sound, lighting, framing, colour, font — that serve intended meaning for a specific audience
criteria: Designs at least two technical or symbolic elements with clear reasons
Explains how each choice constructs meaning for the audience
Design choices go beyond genre convention — connected to specific representational intent

width.minimum: Design at least two technical or symbolic elements in a media arts work with a clear reason for how each serves the intended meaning for the audience
width.typical: Design representations using a range of technical and symbolic elements; explain how each choice constructs intended meaning; consider how choices address issues such as bias, identity or stereotyping
wider: Design representations that deliberately challenge stereotyping, bias or unequal power relationships — evaluate whether the technical and symbolic choices achieve the intended challenge

Experiment with technical and symbolic elements to construct representations that address social issues (identity, sustainability, social justice) — evaluate the effectiveness for the intended audience
Design representations that are safe, legal, ethical and responsible — develop criteria for evaluating own representational choices before production

modes.reason: Students commonly design representations using familiar conventions without reasoning about whether those conventions serve the intended meaning or simply reproduce dominant representations. Designing across different representational challenges — identity, power, social issues — forces students to develop deliberate media language design rather than defaulting to genre norms.

nodes.label: Designing for specific audiences with empathy
nodes.checkpoint: Students can design media arts works that consider the intended audience relationship and approach representations of characters and cultural content with empathy and responsibility
criteria: Designs with at least one explicit consideration of the audience relationship
Explains how design choices create that relationship
Representations of cultural or social groups demonstrate empathy and responsibility

width.minimum: Design a media arts work with at least one explicit consideration of the audience relationship; explain how design choices create or shape that relationship
width.typical: Design media arts works with deliberate attention to audience relationships; apply empathy and respect when designing representations of cultural or social groups; document reasoning
wider: Design characters or representations that convey historical or cultural ideas with genuine empathy — evaluate whether design choices honour the people or cultures represented
Plan how to create relationships with audiences when developing characters — investigate how different design approaches create different emotional and cognitive responses
Design a work that explores how people are engaging in online social justice campaigns — evaluate how design choices can build solidarity or reinforce distance with the intended audience

modes.reason: Students commonly design for an abstract 'audience' without reasoning through who the specific audience is, what relationship the work should create with them, and how design choices build or undermine that relationship. Scaffolding the audience design reasoning — who are they, what do I want them to feel/think/do, which design choices serve that — builds audience-centred design thinking.

This node integrates pre-production planning (Node 1), deliberate media language design (Node 2), and investigative work from E01/E02 into a coherent design that serves a specific audience with appropriate ethical responsibility. Students who can design technically but cannot reason through the audience relationship and representational ethics have not met the standard's full demand.

descriptors.title: Apply production processes and concepts
descriptors.description: apply production processes and use media arts concepts to construct representations and produce media arts works that communicate ideas, perspectives and/or meaning for specific audiences using responsible media practice
descriptors.knowledge: Students can use production processes to create media arts works (AC9AMA6C02). They have not yet applied media arts concepts deliberately across the full production pipeline, nor maintained responsible media practice as a consistent production discipline.
descriptors.endpoint: Students apply production processes and media arts concepts to produce works that communicate intended meaning for specific audiences with responsible media practice throughout.

nodes.label: Applying production processes across the pipeline
nodes.checkpoint: Students can apply pre-production, production and post-production processes to produce a media arts work with deliberate intent at each stage
criteria: Applies at least two production stages with deliberate intent
Explains how each stage contributed to intended meaning
Production decisions are connected to representational intent — not just technical execution

width.minimum: Apply at least two stages of the production pipeline (pre-production, production, post-production); explain how each stage contributed to the intended meaning of the work
width.typical: Apply production processes across all three stages; document decisions made at each stage and how they contribute to the intended representation and audience relationship
wider: Produce a work that represents sustainable futures or social justice — evaluate how each production stage decision serves the communicative intent
Use Viewpoints questions at each production stage — 'What elements define this genre?', 'How am I creating mood?' — document how questioning drives production decisions

Transfer established technical codes across media types (framing in stills and moving image, sound in radio and audio-visual) — evaluate how the transfer changes meaning and what it reveals about how codes work

modes.reason: Students commonly move through production stages without reasoning about how each stage contributes to or detracts from the intended meaning. Scaffolding the stage-by-stage reasoning — what is the intended meaning, what does this stage produce, is it serving the intent — builds deliberate production practice rather than mechanical pipeline execution.

nodes.label: Applying media arts concepts to construct representations
nodes.checkpoint: Students can apply media arts concepts — genre conventions, technical codes, symbolic codes — to construct representations that communicate intended ideas for a specific audience
criteria: Applies at least one genre convention and one technical/symbolic code
Explains how each communicates to the intended audience
Choices are deliberate — connected to representational intent, not just convention

width.minimum: Apply at least one genre convention and one technical or symbolic code to construct a representation; explain how each communicates to the intended audience
width.typical: Combine genre conventions and technical/symbolic codes to construct representations; explain how each choice serves the intended meaning; evaluate whether the combination achieves the intended effect
wider: Combine established genre conventions to create a hybrid production — evaluate how hybridity serves representational purposes that single genres cannot
Produce a news story or social media campaign using media languages to construct perspective deliberately — evaluate how bias is constructed and how it could be challenged
Apply technical codes across media types in a single production — evaluate how transferring codes (e.g. low-angle framing) between contexts changes what they communicate

modes.reason: Students commonly apply familiar genre conventions without reasoning about whether those conventions serve the intended meaning. Working across different genre contexts — hybrid productions, news, social media campaigns — forces students to develop deliberate concept application rather than defaulting to single-genre conventions.

nodes.label: Applying responsible media practice throughout
nodes.checkpoint: Students can apply responsible media practice consistently throughout production — copyright, ICIP rights, ethical representation, safety and legality
criteria: Identifies and applies at least one responsible practice obligation
Explains how the obligation is met in specific production decisions
Responsible practice is built into the production — not just acknowledged at the end

width.minimum: Identify at least one responsible media practice obligation relevant to own production; explain how it is applied in the work
width.typical: Apply responsible media practice throughout the production process; explain how copyright, ICIP rights and ethical representation obligations are met in specific production decisions
wider: Produce a work that explores how people are engaging in social justice or sustainability issues — evaluate how responsible practice principles apply to sensitive social content
Construct representations that are safe, legal, ethical and responsible for cultural or social groups represented — develop and apply explicit criteria throughout production
Reflect on how responsible media practice has shaped production decisions — evaluate moments where responsible practice constrained or redirected creative choices

modes.reason: This node integrates production pipeline application (Node 1), concept application (Node 2), and ICIP/ethical understanding from E02 into a complete production that maintains responsible practice throughout. Students who can produce technically but treat responsible practice as an afterthought rather than a design principle have not met the standard's full demand.

descriptors.strand: Media arts: developing practices and skills
descriptors.title: Develop media production skills
descriptors.description: develop media production skills throughout the production process to construct representations using media languages and media technologies
descriptors.knowledge: Students can use media technologies and languages to construct representations (AC9AMA6D01). They have not yet developed production skills systematically across the full production process, or used digital tools to expand representational possibilities deliberately.
descriptors.endpoint: Students develop media production skills across pre-production, production and post-production, using media languages and technologies to construct increasingly sophisticated representations.

nodes.label: Developing technical media production skills
nodes.checkpoint: Students can develop specific technical skills in using media technologies — cameras, sound equipment, editing/animation software — through deliberate practice
criteria: Develops at least one technical skill with a clear production purpose
Describes what improved and how it affects the representation
Practice is deliberate — connected to a specific skill and improvement goal

width.minimum: Develop at least one technical skill (e.g. camera operation, sound recording, editing) through deliberate practice; describe what improved and how it affects the representation
width.typical: Develop technical skills across multiple media technologies through the production process; document skill development and its effect on the quality and intent of representations
wider: Experiment with digital tools including cameras, sound recording, editing, coding and animation software — evaluate how mastery of each tool expands representational possibilities
Experiment with audio effects (sound effects, music, Foley sounds) to construct ambient sound — evaluate how audio construction changes the meaning of a scene
Experiment with story principles (establishing setting, disrupting narrative structure) — evaluate how manipulation of time and structure changes what the work communicates

modes.reason: Technical media production skills — camera operation, audio recording, editing — develop through sustained deliberate practice with feedback, not through exposure to more representational contexts. Students who practise specific technical skills repeatedly build genuine technical competence; students who rotate through tools without sustained practice do not.

nodes.label: Using media languages to construct representations
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use media languages deliberately to construct representations of people, places or concepts with intended meaning
criteria: Uses at least one media language element with a clear representational purpose
Explains what meaning the choice produces — not just describes the choice
Representational choices are deliberate — not just genre conventions applied by default

width.minimum: Use at least one media language element (framing, lighting, sound, colour, font) to construct a representation; explain what meaning the choice produces
width.typical: Use a range of media language elements to construct representations across different genres or platforms; explain how each choice contributes to the intended meaning
wider: Explore how media languages can perpetuate or challenge stereotyping, bias or identity issues — develop representations that deliberately challenge rather than reproduce dominant representations
Construct representations that explore social relationships, power dynamics or sustainability issues — evaluate how media language choices carry ideological weight
Investigate how to create representations of cultural or social groups that are safe, legal, ethical and responsible — develop criteria for evaluating own representational choices

modes.reason: Students commonly use media language elements by convention — familiar framing choices, default sound design — without reasoning about what each choice communicates. Working across different representational challenges (identity, power, social issues) forces students to develop deliberate media language selection rather than defaulting to genre conventions.

nodes.label: Expanding representations through emerging technologies
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use emerging or extended technologies — AR, VR, green screen, hybrid genre forms — to construct representations that extend beyond conventional media forms
criteria: Experiments with at least one technology beyond conventional forms
Describes what representational possibilities it opens
Technology use is purposeful — connected to intended meaning, not just novelty

width.minimum: Experiment with at least one technology or technique beyond conventional media forms (AR/VR, green screen, hybrid genre); describe what representational possibilities it opens
width.typical: Construct representations using extended or emerging technologies; evaluate how these technologies create possibilities that conventional media cannot; document the production decisions and their effect
wider: Construct fictional versions of everyday spaces using AR/VR or green screen — evaluate how immersive technologies change the audience's relationship to the representation
Combine established genre conventions to create a hybrid production — evaluate how genre hybridity serves representational purposes that single genres cannot
Investigate how digital tools and emerging technologies are changing how representations are made and received — analyse the implications for responsible media practice

modes.reason: Students commonly use emerging technologies for novelty without reasoning through what representational purpose they serve. Scaffolding the reasoning — what does this technology allow that conventional media cannot, what representational problem does it solve, does the technology serve the intended meaning — builds purposeful technology use rather than technology for its own sake.

descriptors.strand: Media arts: developing practices and skills
descriptors.title: Reflect on media arts works to inform practice
descriptors.description: reflect on their own and others' media arts works and practices to inform choices they make during the production process
descriptors.knowledge: Students can use feedback to reflect on own media arts practice (AC9AMA6D02). They have not yet investigated others' media arts works and practices systematically as a source of influence, or used structured reflection to document and direct production decisions.
descriptors.endpoint: Students reflect on own and others' media arts works to make and document informed production choices throughout the production process.

nodes.label: Documenting and explaining creative choices
nodes.checkpoint: Students can document and explain their creative choices in relation to representations, genre codes and conventions with reference to intended meaning
criteria: Documents at least two creative choices with reasoning
Explains how each choice constructs a representation for the intended audience
Documentation goes beyond 'I decided to...' — explains why the choice serves the intended meaning

width.minimum: Document at least two creative choices in own media arts work; explain how each constructs a representation for the intended audience
width.typical: Document and explain creative choices throughout the production process in relation to representations, genre codes and conventions; use Viewpoints questions to interrogate own decisions
wider: Use Viewpoints questions to interrogate own representational choices — 'How can I represent a range of views?', 'What do I need to change to create stronger audience connection?' — document how each question drives production refinement
Use a storyboarding or editing template to annotate creative thinking — document the reasoning behind decisions, not just the decisions themselves
Develop a production journal that traces how creative choices have evolved across pre-production, production and post-production — evaluate what the documentation reveals about own decision-making

modes.reason: Documenting creative choices with genuine reasoning — explaining why a decision serves the intended representation rather than just recording what was decided — is a reflective practice habit that develops through sustained iteration. Students who document after the fact without reasoning through the decisions haven't built the habit of reflective production practice.

nodes.label: Reflecting on audience engagement
nodes.checkpoint: Students can reflect on potential audience engagement and use that reflection to refine production choices
criteria: Reflects on how at least one production choice affects audience engagement
Documents at least one refinement based on audience-centred reasoning
Reasoning is from audience perspective — not just own creative preference

width.minimum: Reflect on how at least one production choice affects potential audience engagement; document at least one refinement based on that reflection
width.typical: Consider potential audience engagement to inform refinements across the production process; use Viewpoints questions to evaluate how production choices create audience connection; document reasoning
wider: Justify decisions made by producers in the construction of representations — evaluate how technical and symbolic codes serve producer interests and audience positioning
Observe and consider how audience engagement would differ across different audience groups — evaluate how the same work could position different audiences differently
Investigate how media arts practitioners from other cultural contexts construct audience relationships — explore how cultural context shapes what 'engaging' means for different audiences

modes.reason: Students commonly make production choices without reasoning from the audience's perspective — they think about what they want to do rather than what the audience will receive. Scaffolding the audience perspective reasoning (who is my audience, how will they receive this choice, what does this choice communicate to them?) builds the habit of audience-centred production thinking.

nodes.label: Investigating others' practices to inform own
nodes.checkpoint: Students can investigate other media arts works and practices and use insights to inform deliberate choices in own production
criteria: Investigates at least one other work or practice with a specific analytical focus
Connects the investigation to a specific production decision
Distinguishes informed influence from uncritical imitation or cultural appropriation

width.minimum: Investigate at least one other media arts work or practice; identify one specific insight that has informed a choice in own production
width.typical: Document and explain how investigating other media arts works and practices informs own representational choices; connect specific analytical observations to specific production decisions
wider: Explore styles and representations from another cultural context (e.g. cartooning genres in Asia) — use the investigation to inform own practice and develop understanding of cultural appropriation vs cross-cultural influence
Investigate how media arts conventions from different cultural contexts use technical codes differently — analyse what each convention communicates and how cultural context shapes its meaning
Develop a reflective account of how investigation of others' practices has changed own production approach across a unit — trace specific moments of influence

modes.reason: This node integrates documentation practice (Node 1), audience-centred reflection (Node 2), and analytical skills from E01 into a coherent account of how investigation informs production. Students who can analyse other works but cannot connect that analysis to own production decisions have not met the standard's full demand.

descriptors.title: Investigate media arts concepts across contexts
descriptors.description: investigate the ways that media arts concepts are used in media arts works and practices across cultures, times, places and/or other contexts
descriptors.knowledge: Students can identify how media arts concepts are used in works (AC9AMA6E01). They have not yet investigated how cultural, historical and institutional contexts shape how media arts concepts construct representations and position audiences.
descriptors.endpoint: Students investigate how media arts concepts construct representations and position audiences across cultures, times and contexts.

nodes.label: Analysing media arts concepts in works
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and analyse how media arts concepts — cinematography, mise-en-scène, editing, sound — are used to construct representations
criteria: Identifies at least two media arts concepts in a given work
Explains how each constructs a representation — not just names the concept
Does not confuse describing what a work shows with explaining how it constructs meaning

width.minimum: Identify at least two media arts concepts in a given work; explain how each constructs a representation of a person, place, event or idea
width.typical: Analyse how media arts concepts are used across a range of works; explain how technical and symbolic codes construct representations and what meanings they produce
wider: Analyse how media languages are used to construct stereotypical representations in media products aimed at teenagers — evaluate how technical codes naturalise those stereotypes
Use Viewpoints questions to analyse cinematography, editing or sound — 'How does this element construct meaning?', 'What ideological position does this representation take?'
Compare how the same media arts concept (e.g. low-angle framing) is used across different genres and evaluate how context changes the meaning produced

modes.reason: Students need to build a repertoire of media arts concept examples across multiple works before they can reason about how context shapes representational choices. A single work gives too narrow a base for genuine comparative analysis of how technical codes construct meaning differently across cultures and contexts.

nodes.label: Investigating ideology and audience positioning
nodes.checkpoint: Students can investigate how media arts works position audiences to respond to representations and what ideological positions those representations carry
criteria: Explains how a work positions audiences to respond to a representation
Identifies which technical or symbolic codes produce the positioning
Connects representational choices to ideological position or institutional context

width.minimum: Investigate how a given media work positions audiences to respond to a representation; explain which technical or symbolic codes produce that positioning
width.typical: Analyse how audiences are positioned across multiple media works; investigate the ideological or philosophical viewpoints constructed; explain how institutional contexts shape those positions
wider: Investigate the ideology of a media work including what institutions were involved in its distribution and its potential audience impact — evaluate how institutional context shapes representational choices
Analyse how depictions of cultural or social groups in Australian film and television construct meaning for diverse audiences — evaluate how representations serve or challenge dominant ideologies
Investigate how technical and symbolic codes are used to challenge as well as perpetuate unequal power relationships — compare examples that challenge vs reinforce

modes.reason: Students commonly analyse media texts as if meaning is fixed in the text, without reasoning about how different audiences in different contexts receive representations differently. Investigating works across cultures, times and institutional contexts — including how the same codes position different audiences differently — forces students to develop audience positioning as an analytical concept rather than assuming universal reception.

nodes.label: Connecting investigation to own production practice
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use investigation of how media arts concepts construct representations to inform deliberate choices in own media arts production
criteria: Identifies at least one analytical insight that influenced a production decision
Explains the connection between analysis and decision
Distinguishes informed production choice from uncritical imitation

width.minimum: Identify at least one insight from investigating other works that has influenced a specific decision in own production; explain the connection
width.typical: Analyse how investigating media arts concepts in existing works informs own choices about technical codes, representations and audience positioning; document specific influences and adaptations
wider: Develop analysis that connects how media arts concepts are used in investigated works to specific production decisions — document the chain from analysis to practice
Investigate how media conventions from another cultural context (e.g. cartooning in Asia) can inform own practice — develop understanding of both influence and cultural appropriation
Construct an argument about why critical investigation of media works produces more deliberate and effective production choices than making without analytical grounding

modes.reason: This node requires students to connect concept analysis (Node 1) and ideological investigation (Node 2) to own production decisions. Students who can analyse other works analytically but cannot use that analysis to inform deliberate production choices have not met the standard's full investigative demand.

Students commonly describe what they found in analysed works without articulating how it changes specific production decisions. Scaffolding the connection — what did I learn about how this concept works, what decision does that change in my own work, how is my adaptation different from copying — builds the analytical-to-practical transfer.

descriptors.title: Diversity of First Nations media arts
descriptors.description: investigate the diversity of First Nations Australians' media arts works and practices, considering culturally responsive approaches to Indigenous Cultural and Intellectual Property rights
descriptors.knowledge: Students have some awareness that First Nations Australians have media arts practices. They have not yet investigated this diversity systematically or engaged with ICIP rights frameworks in media arts contexts.
descriptors.endpoint: Students investigate the diversity of First Nations Australian media arts with genuine cultural responsiveness, understanding and applying ICIP rights frameworks.

nodes.label: Understanding ICIP rights in media arts
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain what ICIP rights mean in media arts contexts and describe what culturally responsive engagement looks like in practice
criteria: Explains what ICIP rights mean in a media arts context
Gives at least one specific example of respectful engagement
Does not reduce ICIP to a checklist — explains the reasoning behind protocols

width.minimum: Explain what ICIP rights are in a media arts context; give one example of what respectful engagement with First Nations media arts looks like
width.typical: Investigate ICIP rights frameworks and explain how they apply to media arts practice — using cultural images, sounds or stories in works, distributing works that feature cultural content
wider: Investigate a specific case of cultural appropriation in media arts where ICIP rights were denied — explain what happened and what a respectful alternative would have looked like
Collaboratively construct guidelines for safe, ethical, legal and responsible media use — develop criteria for deciding whether ideas from existing cultural expressions can be used in new work
Investigate issues relating to use of First Nations languages or stories in screen-based works — analyse specific case studies illustrating ICIP protocols

modes.reason: Students commonly understand ICIP rights abstractly without being able to reason through specific media arts scenarios — knowing permission is needed without working out who to ask, what counts as cultural expression in media, or what responsible practice looks like. Scenario-based scaffolding builds actionable understanding rather than declarative awareness.

nodes.label: Investigating First Nations Australian media arts
nodes.checkpoint: Students can investigate the diversity of First Nations Australian media arts works and practices with cultural responsiveness
criteria: Investigates at least one First Nations Australian media work in genuine depth
Explains cultural significance — not just describes content
Demonstrates cultural responsiveness throughout

width.minimum: Investigate at least one First Nations Australian media arts work or practitioner in depth; explain what makes it culturally significant and how ICIP principles are evident
width.typical: Investigate diverse First Nations Australian media arts works and practices; analyse choices artists make about technical elements, story principles and audience relationships; explain how ICIP principles shape those choices
wider: Investigate how First Nations Australian media artists construct representations of resilience in response to colonisation — analyse how technical and symbolic choices serve that communicative purpose
Investigate how First Nations Australian media arts works use story principles that may differ from dominant Western narrative structures — analyse what those differences communicate
Research how to select and use historical materials that accurately communicate First Nations perspectives — develop own criteria for responsible use in media arts practice

modes.reason: Students commonly treat First Nations Australian media arts as a single tradition rather than understanding the diversity across hundreds of distinct cultural groups and a wide range of contemporary media forms. Multiple distinct investigation contexts — different practitioners, forms, and thematic focuses — resolve this misconception through genuine breadth.

nodes.label: Applying culturally responsive approaches in media arts
criteria: Applies at least one ICIP protocol question to a real or hypothetical media arts practice scenario
Explains the ethical reasoning behind the protocol

width.minimum: Apply at least one ICIP protocol question to own media arts practice; explain the reasoning behind the protocol.
width.typical: Apply multiple protocol questions to own practice across production and distribution; explain how the protocols guide ethical engagement with First Nations Australian cultural material in media arts.
wider: Collaboratively construct guidelines for safe, ethical, legal and responsible use of First Nations Australian cultural material in media arts — develop criteria for deciding whether ideas from existing cultural expressions can be used.
Evaluate a specific case where ICIP rights were denied in media arts — analyse what happened and what a respectful alternative would have looked like.

modes.reason: Applying ICIP protocols in media arts requires reasoning through specific production decisions — what content is being used, who owns it, what permission is needed.

descriptors.title: Present media arts works
descriptors.description: present media arts works, using responsible media practices and considering potential relationships the work could create with audiences
descriptors.knowledge: Students can present media arts works to an audience (AC9AMA6P01). They have not yet made deliberate presentation decisions about distribution context, audience relationships, copyright/ICIP obligations, or evaluated how different presentation contexts change audience reception.
descriptors.endpoint: Students present media arts works using responsible media practices and with deliberate consideration of how presentation choices shape audience relationships.

nodes.label: Applying responsible media practices in presentation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can apply copyright, ICIP and ethical obligations when presenting media arts works
criteria: Identifies and applies at least one responsible practice obligation in presentation
Explains why the obligation exists and how it applies
Responsible practice is genuinely applied — not just acknowledged

width.minimum: Identify at least one responsible media practice obligation relevant to presenting own work; explain how it is applied in the presentation
width.typical: Apply copyright, ICIP and ethical obligations when presenting media arts works; explain specific decisions made to comply with responsible practice requirements
wider: Research copyright laws and ICIP rights relevant to specific content in own work — document how permission was obtained or why specific material was not included
Develop a presentation plan that explicitly addresses all responsible practice obligations before distribution — evaluate how responsible practice shaped presentation decisions
Investigate how media arts makers navigate copyright and ICIP obligations in professional distribution contexts — apply those practices to own work

modes.reason: Students commonly treat copyright and ICIP obligations as administrative hurdles rather than reasoned professional practice. Scaffolding the reasoning — what is the obligation, why does it exist, how does it apply to this specific content in this specific context — builds genuine understanding of responsible practice rather than compliance-as-checklist.

nodes.label: Considering audience relationships in presentation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can make deliberate presentation decisions that consider the potential relationship the work creates with the intended audience
criteria: Makes at least one presentation decision with explicit audience relationship reasoning
Explains how the presentation context shapes the audience relationship
Presentation is audience-centred — not just platform selection

width.minimum: Make at least one deliberate presentation decision (platform, timing, context) with an explicit consideration of the audience relationship it creates; explain the reasoning
width.typical: Plan presentation with deliberate consideration of audience relationships; reflect on how different presentation contexts affect interpretation and engagement; document reasoning
wider: Distribute a media arts work to a specific audience using appropriate platforms — evaluate how the distribution context shapes audience engagement and relationship
Present media arts works in multiple contexts (online platform, school exhibition, community screening) — evaluate how each context changes audience interpretation and response
Reflect on how relationships develop between media arts makers and audiences across a cohort — evaluate how shared or differentiated audience experiences change reception

modes.reason: Thinking deliberately about audience relationships in presentation — not just choosing a platform but reasoning through what relationship the presentation creates — is a production practice habit that develops through repeated consideration cycles. Students who present without this reasoning don't develop the audience-centred presentation thinking the descriptor requires.

nodes.label: Evaluating presentation and audience reception
nodes.checkpoint: Students can evaluate how presentation choices affected audience reception and what this reveals about the relationship between presentation context and meaning
criteria: Reflects on how presentation context affected audience reception
Identifies at least one specific aspect that worked and one that would change
Evaluation addresses the relationship between presentation choice and audience reception

width.minimum: Reflect on how the chosen presentation context affected how audiences received the work; identify at least one thing that worked and one that would change
width.typical: Evaluate the effectiveness of presentation choices across different audience contexts; reflect on the relationship between presentation decisions and audience reception; document how evaluation would inform future presentation
wider: Present the same work in different contexts and compare audience responses — evaluate how context changes what the work communicates and what relationship it creates
Collect audience feedback and evaluate the gap between intended and received meaning — develop criteria for evaluating presentation effectiveness
Evaluate how different audiences within the same cohort interpreted the work differently — analyse what the differences reveal about how media works create meaning

modes.reason: This node integrates responsible practice application (Node 1), audience relationship consideration (Node 2), and production work from C01/C02 into a complete evaluation of how a media arts work reached its audience. Students who can present but cannot evaluate the relationship between presentation choices and audience reception have not met the standard's full demand.

descriptors.title: Interpret music
descriptors.description: interpret music in a variety of forms and/or styles, manipulating elements of music and employing relevant vocal/instrumental techniques
descriptors.knowledge: Students can manipulate elements of music and use compositional devices to communicate ideas when composing and practising music for performance (AC9AMU6C01). They can notate, document and/or record music they compose. They have not yet focused on interpretation of existing works across a variety of forms and styles, nor on deliberately employing style-specific vocal/instrumental techniques to realise stylistic features.
descriptors.endpoint: Students interpret music in a variety of forms and/or styles by manipulating elements of music and employing relevant vocal/instrumental techniques to realise stylistic features and achieve intended expressive effects.

nodes.label: Identifying stylistic features
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify the stylistic features of a piece of music that need to be realised in performance, including relevant elements of music and technical demands
criteria: Identifies at least two stylistic features of a piece
Describes what each feature requires from a performer (technical or expressive demand)

width.minimum: Identify at least two stylistic features of a given piece and describe what they require from a performer
width.typical: Identify stylistic features across a range of forms/styles; describe what each requires technically and expressively from the performer
wider: Analyse recordings of expert performers to identify how specific stylistic features are realised differently across interpretations of the same work
Compare stylistic features across two contrasting genres (e.g. jazz and classical) to identify what changes technically and what remains common

modes.reason: Students need to accumulate a range of stylistic feature examples before they can reliably identify and target them in their own interpretation. Exposure to multiple styles and forms builds the reference bank that makes identification purposeful rather than guesswork.

nodes.label: Trialling techniques for stylistic effect
nodes.checkpoint: Students can trial and select vocal/instrumental techniques that realise identified stylistic features, including manipulation of dynamics, timbre, articulation and accent/stress
criteria: Trials at least one vocal/instrumental technique with a clear stylistic rationale
Can explain how the technique contributes to the intended stylistic effect

width.minimum: Trial at least one technique (e.g. accent placement, dynamic shaping, timbre manipulation) and explain how it contributes to the stylistic effect
width.typical: Trial multiple techniques across elements of music; compare approaches and select those that best realise the intended style; document choices as a reference
wider: Experiment with effects such as distortion, decay or delay to achieve stylistic feel in digital or amplified performance contexts; evaluate how these change the expressive character of the music

Investigate how the same melodic or rhythmic pattern sounds and feels differently when accent/stress placement is changed — connect this to genre-specific performance conventions (e.g. swing feel, syncopation in funk)

modes.reason: Students frequently apply techniques mechanically without understanding their stylistic purpose. Trialling the same technique across multiple contexts (acoustic vs digital, different genres) helps students hear what the technique does and why it matters — shifting from execution to interpretation.

nodes.label: Rehearsing toward interpretation goals
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use student and teacher set goals to focus rehearsal, tracking progress toward an intended interpretation
criteria: Identifies at least one explicit rehearsal goal
Can describe whether and how the goal was met

width.minimum: Use at least one explicit goal to focus rehearsal; identify whether the goal was met and what still needs work
width.typical: Set and use multiple rehearsal goals across technical and expressive dimensions; adjust goals as rehearsal progresses; document decisions
wider: Record alternative approaches to interpreting a phrase or melody and evaluate each against the intended stylistic effect — use the recording to identify what the ear notices that playing alone doesn't reveal
Limited width — rehearsal goal-setting is a process skill; breadth comes from the variety of repertoire and styles rehearsed, not from multiplying goal-setting procedures.

modes.reason: Goal-directed rehearsal is a precision and persistence skill — students need sustained practice with the feedback loop (set goal → rehearse → evaluate → adjust) rather than exposure to more contexts. The cognitive work is in the iteration, not the variety.

nodes.label: Working from notation and documentation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can interpret music notated or documented in a range of formats, using the notation as a basis for developing their interpretation
criteria: Uses at least one notation format to inform an interpretation
Makes at least one deliberate interpretive decision not fully specified by the notation

width.minimum: Use at least one notation format (staff notation, tablature, chord chart, graphic score, or recording) to inform an interpretation
width.typical: Use multiple notation formats to develop an interpretation; identify what each format communicates and what it leaves open for interpretive decision-making
wider: Use a recording and a chart (melody, form, harmony/chords) to develop an arrangement of a song — make deliberate interpretive decisions about elements the chart leaves unspecified
Compare how the same piece looks and sounds when documented in two different formats (e.g. staff notation vs chord chart) and explain what each format prioritises for the performer

modes.reason: Students need familiarity with a range of notation formats to work fluently across genres and performance contexts. Accumulating experience with different formats — what each captures and what each leaves open — builds the practical literacy that interpretation depends on.

nodes.label: Integrated interpretation across a piece
nodes.checkpoint: Students can produce an interpretation of a piece in a chosen style that integrates stylistic feature decisions, technique choices, notation reading and rehearsal goals into a coherent expressive whole
criteria: Produces an interpretation that realises at least two stylistic features
Technique choices are appropriate to the style and support expressive intent

width.minimum: Perform or record an interpretation that realises at least two identified stylistic features using appropriate technique
width.typical: Perform or record an interpretation that demonstrates consistent stylistic understanding across the piece, with technique choices that support expressive intent throughout; reflect on what worked and what would change
wider: Compare two contrasting interpretations of the same piece (own and a recording) to evaluate how different technique choices realise the same stylistic features differently
Perform music in a variety of forms or styles across the unit, demonstrating that stylistic interpretation choices are style-specific rather than universal defaults

modes.reason: This is where stylistic identification, technique selection, notation reading and rehearsal goal-setting come together in a single performance. The coordination of these components is the learning — students discover that interpretation is not a sequence of separate decisions but a unified expressive act.

descriptors.title: Compose and notate music
descriptors.description: compose using the elements of music and compositional devices to communicate ideas, perspectives and/or meaning, and notate, document and/or record the music
descriptors.knowledge: Students can manipulate elements of music and use compositional devices to communicate ideas when composing and practising music for performance (AC9AMU6C01). They can notate, document and/or record their compositions. They have not yet focused on communicating specific ideas, perspectives or meaning as a compositional intent, nor on arranging or re-imagining existing works.
descriptors.endpoint: Students compose music using elements of music and compositional devices to communicate specific ideas, perspectives or meaning, and notate, document or record the composition in a format appropriate to the genre, style or intended performers.

nodes.label: Establishing compositional intent
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify an idea, perspective or meaning they want to communicate through music and describe how musical choices might serve that intent
criteria: States a compositional intent beyond general mood description
Identifies at least one musical element or device connected to the intent

width.minimum: State a compositional intent (idea, perspective, theme or purpose) and identify at least one musical element or device that could help communicate it
width.typical: Articulate a compositional intent with enough specificity to guide musical decisions; identify multiple elements or devices that could serve the intent and explain the connection
wider: Investigate how composers have used music to communicate perspectives on social issues (e.g. protest songs, nationalistic music) — analyse the musical choices made and connect them to the intended message
Compare how the same broad intent (e.g. 'friendship' or 'belonging') could be communicated differently depending on genre — what changes and what stays the same?

modes.reason: Students often default to vague or generic compositional intents ('I want it to sound happy') that don't drive meaningful musical decisions. Encountering a range of real compositional purposes — protest, ceremony, film scoring, community — helps students understand that intent shapes musical choices, not just mood.

nodes.label: Using patterns and devices as compositional material
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use harmonic, rhythmic or melodic patterns and compositional devices as the basis for a composition or improvisation
criteria: Uses at least one pattern or device as compositional material
Composes or improvises additional material that relates to the pattern

width.minimum: Use at least one pattern (e.g. ostinato, riff, chord progression) as compositional material; compose or improvise additional material over or around it
width.typical: Use multiple patterns or devices (e.g. loops, harmonic progressions, melodic motifs) in combination; make deliberate choices about how patterns are combined, varied or contrasted
wider: Create a composition built entirely from loops or layered ostinati, then compose or improvise additional melodic lines that interact with the looped material — evaluate how the layers interact
Develop an arrangement or re-imagining of an existing melody by improvising over or around given material (melody, riff or chord progression) and documenting the choices made

modes.reason: Students need to accumulate a working vocabulary of patterns and devices before they can combine them purposefully. Experiencing loops, ostinati, chord progressions and melodic motifs as distinct compositional tools — with their own affordances — builds the palette that compositional decision-making draws on.

nodes.label: Shaping music for purpose and context
nodes.checkpoint: Students can compose music shaped by a specific purpose or context, making decisions about form, style and instrumentation appropriate to that context
criteria: Composes music for an identified purpose or context
