Makes at least one deliberate musical decision based on the context

width.minimum: Compose music for a specific purpose or context (e.g. ensemble repertoire, theatrical work, event); make at least one deliberate decision about form or instrumentation based on the context
width.typical: Compose music whose form, style and instrumentation are clearly shaped by the purpose — explain how the context drove specific musical decisions
wider: Compose music for a theatrical, site-specific or media work context — consider how the non-musical context (narrative, space, visual elements) constrains and enriches the musical choices
Write a song or instrumental piece that communicates a perspective on a local issue (sustainable living, relationships, identity) — evaluate whether the musical choices support the message

modes.reason: Students often compose in a vacuum without considering how purpose and audience shape musical decisions. Encountering a range of real compositional contexts — fanfares, ensemble repertoire, media music, songs with social purpose — helps students understand that context is not an external constraint but a compositional driver.

nodes.label: Notating, documenting and recording
nodes.checkpoint: Students can notate, document or record their composition in a format appropriate to the genre, style or intended performers
criteria: Documents the composition in at least one format
The format is appropriate for the genre or style

width.minimum: Document a composition in at least one format (staff notation, chord chart, lead sheet, percussion notation, recording, or digital file); the format is appropriate for the style
width.typical: Choose a documentation format appropriate to the genre and intended performers; explain why the chosen format suits the work better than alternatives
wider: Use software to notate or record a composition in a format appropriate to the genre — evaluate how the software shapes or constrains compositional decisions
Document an arrangement in a format appropriate for the musicians performing it, considering both their reading abilities and the conventions of the style

modes.reason: Students need familiarity with multiple documentation formats to make genre-appropriate choices. Encountering staff notation, chord charts, lead sheets, percussion notation and digital recording as distinct tools — each suited to different genres and performers — builds the practical literacy that appropriate documentation requires.

nodes.label: Integrated composition communicating intent
nodes.checkpoint: Students can produce a complete composition that integrates compositional intent, use of patterns/devices, contextual shaping and appropriate documentation into a unified work
criteria: Produces a documented composition
At least one musical choice is traceable to the stated compositional intent

width.minimum: Produce a documented composition in which at least one musical choice can be traced back to the stated compositional intent
width.typical: Produce a documented composition in which musical choices (elements, devices, form, instrumentation) consistently serve the compositional intent; reflect on how successfully the intent is communicated
wider: Arrange a familiar piece into a different style by manipulating elements of music to convey meaning — document the arrangement in a form appropriate for the musicians performing it, explaining the interpretive choices made
Produce a composition that will be performed or shared, then evaluate audience or peer response against the intended communication — what was received as intended, what wasn't, and why?

modes.reason: This node is where intent, pattern use, contextual shaping and documentation come together as a single compositional act. Students discover that these are not separate steps but simultaneous considerations — a composition communicates intent through every choice, from material to documentation format.

descriptors.title: Develop listening and performance skills
descriptors.description: develop and practise listening/aural skills and vocal and/or instrumental skills/techniques for manipulating elements of music to achieve expressive effects
descriptors.knowledge: Students can develop listening/aural skills and skills for manipulating elements of music to achieve expressive effects when composing, singing and playing instruments (AC9AMU6D01). They have not yet focused on documenting their developing skills, experimenting with digital tools for arranging, or extending and varying harmonic, rhythmic and melodic patterns systematically.
descriptors.endpoint: Students develop and practise listening/aural skills and vocal/instrumental techniques for manipulating elements of music to achieve expressive effects, documenting their ideas and progress as a reference for performance and composition.

nodes.label: Listening with intent — aural skill development
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use focused listening to identify how elements of music are being manipulated and how this creates expressive effects
criteria: Identifies at least one expressive effect in a listening example
Connects the effect to a specific manipulation of a musical element

width.minimum: Listen to a piece and identify at least one expressive effect achieved through manipulation of an element of music (e.g. how dynamic shaping creates tension, how rhythmic articulation creates drive)
width.typical: Identify multiple expressive effects across a listening example; use music terminology accurately; connect what is heard to specific performance choices
wider: Use a listening diary/journal format to document aural observations across multiple pieces over time — identify patterns in how expressive effects are achieved across different styles
Listen to and compare multiple recordings of the same piece to evaluate how different performers manipulate elements differently to achieve expressive effects

modes.reason: Aural identification is a precision skill built through repeated attentive listening. Students need sustained practice connecting what they hear to musical terminology and cause-effect reasoning — breadth of listening material helps, but the cognitive work is the focused listening habit itself.

nodes.label: Technical and expressive performance skills
nodes.checkpoint: Students can practise technical and expressive performance skills including intonation, pitch/rhythmic accuracy, phrasing, dynamics and articulation to communicate expressive intent
criteria: Practises at least one technical or expressive skill with an identified intent
Can describe what changed through practice and what remains to work on

width.minimum: Practise at least one technical or expressive skill (e.g. intonation, phrasing, dynamic control) with a focus on communicating expressive intent; identify what improved and what remains to work on
width.typical: Practise multiple technical and expressive skills in combination; use deliberate practice strategies to address specific weaknesses; evaluate progress against intended expressive outcomes
wider: Record alternative approaches to interpreting a phrase or melody and evaluate each to identify which best communicates the intended expressive effect — explain what the ear notices that playing alone doesn't reveal
Experiment with different ways to control tone and volume in solo and ensemble contexts — evaluate how balance and blend affect the expressive character of the music

modes.reason: Technical and expressive performance skills require deliberate, sustained practice with feedback — this is where the cognitive work is repetitive and iterative by design. Breadth of skills matters, but the learning mechanism is practice-and-evaluate, not exposure to more contexts.

nodes.label: Extending and varying patterns
nodes.checkpoint: Students can extend and vary harmonic, rhythmic or melodic patterns, including developing chord progressions and improvising over them
criteria: Varies or extends at least one pattern in a deliberate way
Can describe the musical effect of the variation

width.minimum: Take an existing pattern (chord, rhythmic or melodic) and vary or extend it in at least one way; explain the musical effect of the variation
width.typical: Experiment with multiple ways to vary a pattern (e.g. vary chord ordering to create a progression, vary rhythmic pattern for feel, vary melodic pattern for development); evaluate which variations serve a musical purpose
wider: Identify the qualities of chords in isolation, experiment with different orderings to create chord progressions, then improvise a melody over the progression — evaluate how the progression shapes the melodic possibilities
Investigate how repeating patterns (ostinati) create different effects when layered — compose or improvise additional parts that interact with an established ostinato

modes.reason: Students often vary patterns randomly without understanding the musical logic. Encountering pattern variation across harmonic, rhythmic and melodic domains — and hearing what each type of variation does expressively — helps students build a vocabulary of deliberate variation strategies rather than trial-and-error.

nodes.label: Using digital tools in practice
nodes.checkpoint: Students can experiment with digital tools to arrange musical ideas or create effects, using digitally produced parts alone or in combination with voice or acoustic instruments
criteria: Uses at least one digital tool to arrange or create a musical effect
Can describe at least one thing the digital tool makes possible or easier

width.minimum: Use at least one digital tool to arrange a musical idea or create an effect; describe what the digital tool makes possible that acoustic means alone would not
width.typical: Experiment with multiple digital tools or approaches; evaluate how digital production choices affect the expressive character of the music; integrate digital and acoustic elements
wider: Use digital tools to create effects (e.g. loops, layering, processing) that combine with acoustic performance — evaluate how the blend affects the stylistic and expressive outcome
Use software to write additional parts (e.g. a bassline to accompany a melody) and evaluate how the added parts change the musical texture and expressive effect

modes.reason: Students need hands-on experience with a range of digital tools to understand what each affords — DAWs, notation software, loop-based production and effects processing are distinct tools with different creative possibilities. Accumulating experience across these builds a working digital toolkit.

nodes.label: Documenting practice and intentions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can document their musical ideas, practice progress and performance or compositional intentions in a format useful for future reference
criteria: Produces at least one piece of documentation (written, notation, or recording) that captures a musical idea or decision
The documentation is in a format usable for future reference

width.minimum: Document musical ideas, rehearsal decisions or expressive intentions in at least one format (written, notation, recording, or digital); the documentation is usable as a reference
width.typical: Use documentation consistently across practice — notation charts, listening diary entries, transcriptions, recordings — as a working reference that informs and develops their practice
wider: Use a listening diary/journal to document ideas for compositions, interpretations or re-imaginings over time — review entries to identify patterns in their musical thinking and preferences
Write or notate a chart or lead sheet from a songwriting workshop, or transcribe a bassline or additional part — evaluate how the act of documenting clarifies musical thinking

modes.reason: Documentation as a practice habit requires repeated reinforcement — students need to experience the feedback loop of documenting → returning to → building on their notes before the habit becomes automatic. Variety of documentation formats matters less than consistency of the practice.

descriptors.title: Reflect to inform practice
descriptors.description: reflect on their own and others' music to inform choices they make as composers and performers about how they will manipulate elements of music and/or compositional devices
descriptors.knowledge: Students can develop listening/aural skills and skills for manipulating elements of music to achieve expressive effects when composing, singing and playing instruments (AC9AMU6D01). They have not yet focused explicitly on evaluative reflection — using aural analysis of self and others to drive deliberate choices as a composer or performer.
descriptors.endpoint: Students reflect on their own and others' music using aural skills and music terminology to evaluate how elements of music and compositional devices are used, and use this reflection to inform deliberate choices in their own composing and performing.

nodes.label: Describing music using terminology
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and describe technical and expressive elements of music in their own and others' work using music terminology
criteria: Uses at least two music terminology terms accurately to describe a piece
Connects the described element to its expressive effect

width.minimum: Describe at least two technical or expressive elements heard in a piece of music using appropriate terminology (e.g. chord progression, phrasing, dynamics, articulation)
width.typical: Describe multiple technical and expressive elements accurately; use terminology consistently; connect observed elements to their expressive effect
wider: Analyse how a performer interprets or shapes melodies, phrasing or dynamics in a recording — use specific terminology to describe the choices made and evaluate their effect
Compare descriptions of the same piece written by different listeners — identify where terminology is shared and where subjective interpretation diverges

modes.reason: Accurate use of music terminology is a precision skill requiring repeated practice. Students need to build fluency with terminology through frequent description tasks across a variety of music before the language becomes a reliable tool for reflection.

nodes.label: Evaluating using focused listening
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use focused listening and selected aural skills to evaluate how elements of music are used, with the purpose of informing their own interpretive decisions
criteria: Evaluates at least one element or device in a recording with a stated purpose
Connects the evaluation to at least one decision about their own work

width.minimum: Listen to a recording with a specific evaluative focus; identify at least one element or device and explain how the performer or composer has used it; connect the observation to a decision about their own work
width.typical: Apply multiple focused listening strategies to evaluate a recording; use the evaluation to identify specific choices to apply or adapt in their own composing or performing
wider: Use focused listening to evaluate alternative interpretations of a piece (two different recordings) — identify which interpretive choices are more effective for the intended stylistic effect and explain why
Evaluate a recording of their own performance using the same criteria applied to others — identify at least one choice they would change and explain the musical reasoning

modes.reason: Evaluation without a clear purpose easily becomes description — students listen and notice things but don't connect observations to decisions. Scaffolding the evaluative reasoning explicitly (what am I listening for → what do I observe → what does this suggest I should do in my own work) keeps reflection purposeful and productive.

nodes.label: Using ensemble cues in performance
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use aural and visual cues when playing or singing in an ensemble to maintain ensemble cohesion and respond to musical signals
criteria: Identifies at least one aural and one visual cue relevant to ensemble performance
Can describe how each cue supports ensemble coordination

width.minimum: Identify at least one aural cue (e.g. a chord or phrase indicating place in structure) and one visual cue (e.g. a gesture indicating tempo or an entry) used in ensemble performance
width.typical: Use both aural and visual cues in ensemble performance to maintain place in the structure and respond to other musicians; explain how cue-reading contributes to ensemble cohesion
wider: Reflect on an ensemble rehearsal or performance to identify moments where ensemble cohesion broke down — diagnose whether the cause was missing an aural cue, a visual cue, or a misunderstanding of structure
Limited width — ensemble cue-reading is fundamentally a practised perceptual skill; breadth of ensemble contexts matters more than analytical extension.

modes.reason: Ensemble cue-reading is a real-time perceptual skill that improves through practice, not through conceptual variety. Students need repeated ensemble experience to develop the ear-body-response loop that makes cue-reading automatic.

nodes.label: Reflection informing compositional and performance choices
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use reflection on their own and others' music to make deliberate, informed choices as a composer or performer about how to manipulate elements of music or use compositional devices
criteria: Identifies at least one deliberate compositional or performance choice that was informed by reflection
Can explain the connection between the reflection and the decision

width.minimum: Identify at least one choice made in their own composing or performing that was directly informed by reflection on music (own or others'); explain the connection between what they heard and what they decided
width.typical: Demonstrate a consistent reflective practice in which observations about music (own and others') lead to deliberate compositional or performance choices; document the reflection-to-decision chain
wider: Develop a structured reflection process used across both composition and performance work — compare how reflection functions differently in each context (retrospective in composition, anticipatory and real-time in performance)

Use aural reflection to identify a pattern in their own musical tendencies (e.g. always choosing the same dynamic range, defaulting to similar rhythmic patterns) and deliberately experiment with alternatives

modes.reason: This node integrates terminology, focused listening, and ensemble awareness into a deliberate reflective practice that feeds back into making. The coordination of reflection and decision-making as a unified practice — rather than separate activities — is the learning.

The reflection-to-decision chain needs explicit scaffolding — students often reflect and then make their next choice without connecting the two. Structuring the reasoning (what I heard → what it tells me → what I will do differently) makes the feedback loop visible and habitual.

descriptors.title: Investigate composers and performers across contexts
descriptors.description: investigate the ways that composers and/or performers use the elements of music and/or compositional devices in music composed across cultures, times, places and/or other contexts
descriptors.knowledge: Students can explore ways that the elements of music are combined in music across cultures, times, places and/or other contexts (AC9AMU6E01). They have explored rather than investigated — they have not yet analysed how elements and devices are used with the specific purpose of informing their own performance or composition decisions.
descriptors.endpoint: Students investigate how composers and/or performers use elements of music and compositional devices in music across cultures, times, places and/or other contexts, using this investigation to describe stylistic features and inform their own practice.

nodes.label: Accessing and analysing music across contexts
nodes.checkpoint: Students can access and analyse music from a range of cultural, historical or contextual sources, identifying how elements of music are manipulated and how compositional devices are used
criteria: Identifies at least two ways elements of music are manipulated or devices are used in a piece
Connects the analysis to the cultural, historical or contextual background

width.minimum: Analyse at least one piece of music from a specified context (culture, time or place); identify at least two ways elements of music are manipulated or compositional devices are used
width.typical: Analyse music across multiple contexts; identify stylistic characteristics through listening; connect analytical observations to the cultural, historical or contextual background
wider: Access multiple live or recorded performances and analyse how performers interpret the same stylistic conventions differently — identify which elements are fixed by style and which are open to interpretive choice

Analyse how elements of music are manipulated in music composed with social intent (protest songs, nationalistic music, music about identity or belonging) — connect specific musical choices to the intended message

modes.reason: Students need to accumulate experience with a range of musical contexts before they can identify what is style-specific versus universal. Analysis of multiple pieces — across cultures, times and places — builds the comparative reference base that stylistic description depends on.

nodes.label: Describing stylistic features of genres and styles
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe the stylistic features of a musical style or genre using music terminology, based on analytical listening
criteria: Describes at least two stylistic features of a genre or style using music terminology
The description is specific enough to distinguish the style from at least one other

width.minimum: Describe at least two stylistic features of one genre or style using music terminology; the description is specific enough to distinguish this style from others
width.typical: Describe the stylistic features of multiple genres or styles; use terminology consistently and accurately; identify what makes each style distinctive
wider: Compare the stylistic features of two genres that share historical roots (e.g. blues and rock, folk and country, Western classical and film scores) — identify what was inherited and what diverged

Research the social, cultural and historical developments that shaped a specific style or tradition (e.g. 32-bar song form, chamber music, singer-songwriter) — explain how these developments are reflected in the music's stylistic features

modes.reason: Students frequently describe stylistic features in generic terms ('it sounds old-fashioned', 'it has a strong beat') that don't distinguish between styles. Encountering multiple styles and practising comparative description — what this style does that others don't — builds the specificity that useful stylistic description requires.

nodes.label: Analysing performer interpretation of composer intentions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can analyse how performers interpret composers' intentions, identifying specific choices about tempo, instrumentation, feel or articulation and evaluating their effect
criteria: Identifies at least one interpretive choice made by a performer
Explains how the choice relates to the composer's apparent or documented intentions

width.minimum: Use a recording and available score, chart or other information (interview, review) to identify at least one way a performer has interpreted a composer's intention; explain the effect of that interpretive choice
width.typical: Analyse multiple interpretive choices (tempo, instrumentation, feel, articulation) in a performance; evaluate how the choices relate to the composer's apparent intentions
wider: Compare two recordings of the same work to identify where interpretive choices diverge — evaluate which interpretation is more aligned with the composer's apparent intentions and justify the judgement
Access an interview or review alongside a recording and score to triangulate performer intentions with composer intentions — identify where they align and where they diverge

modes.reason: Analysing interpretation requires students to hold two perspectives simultaneously — composer intention and performer choice — and reason about the relationship between them. Scaffolding this reasoning (what does the score/chart show → what did the performer do → how do these relate) prevents students from simply describing what they hear without engaging the interpretive layer.

nodes.label: Using investigation to inform own practice
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use their investigation of composers' and performers' use of elements and devices to inform specific choices in their own performance or composition
criteria: Identifies at least one practice decision informed by investigation
Can explain the connection between what they found and what they decided

width.minimum: Identify at least one choice in their own performance or composition that was informed by their investigation; explain the connection
width.typical: Demonstrate multiple connections between investigative findings and practice decisions; explain how understanding a style or tradition informed how they approached their own work in that style
wider: Research a style or tradition in depth, then use that research to develop a set of rehearsal or composition aims — evaluate how well the resulting work reflects the stylistic understanding gained
Incorporate findings from research into social, cultural and historical developments into a performance or composition — reflect on how the research changed or deepened their musical choices

modes.reason: This node connects investigation (analysis, description, interpretation) to practice (composing, performing). The integration of analytical understanding into creative and technical decision-making is the learning — students discover that research about music informs what they do as musicians.

descriptors.title: First Nations music and ICIP rights
descriptors.description: investigate the diversity of music composed and/or performed by First Nations Australians, considering culturally responsive approaches to Indigenous Cultural and Intellectual Property rights
descriptors.knowledge: Students can explore ways First Nations Australians use music to continue and revitalise culture (AC9AMU6E02). They have explored rather than investigated — they have not yet engaged with the specific question of Indigenous Cultural and Intellectual Property (ICIP) rights or considered the ethical responsibilities of listeners, performers and composers when engaging with First Nations music.
descriptors.endpoint: Students investigate the diversity of music composed and/or performed by First Nations Australians and engage with culturally responsive approaches to Indigenous Cultural and Intellectual Property rights as they are relevant to their practice as listeners, composers and performers.

nodes.label: Diversity of First Nations Australian music
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe the diversity of music composed and/or performed by First Nations Australians, including the range of styles, genres and cultural contexts represented
criteria: Describes the work of at least one First Nations Australian composer or performer
Identifies at least one style or genre the musician draws on and how they use it to communicate

width.minimum: Investigate at least one First Nations Australian composer or performer; describe the styles or genres they draw on and how they communicate ideas or messages
width.typical: Investigate multiple First Nations Australian composers and/or performers across different styles and contexts; describe how each communicates ideas across communities and cultures
wider: Investigate the impacts of a First Nations Australian musician's or musicians' work — consider what communities or audiences they reach, how their music has been received, and what ideas or messages travel across cultural contexts
Explore how First Nations Australian musicians draw on multiple styles or genres in creating their own music — identify both traditional and contemporary musical influences in their work

modes.reason: Students need to encounter genuine diversity in First Nations Australian music before they can understand what 'diversity' means in this context. A narrow sample produces stereotyped understandings — breadth of artists, styles, regions and purposes builds the knowledge base for respectful, informed engagement.

nodes.label: Understanding ICIP rights
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain what Indigenous Cultural and Intellectual Property rights are and why they exist, including when and how they might be relevant to music
criteria: Explains what ICIP rights are
Identifies at least one context in which ICIP rights are relevant to music practice

width.minimum: Explain what ICIP rights are and give at least one example of when they might be relevant to music — as a listener, songwriter, composer or performer
width.typical: Explain why ICIP rights exist and how copyright and ICIP rights interact; identify scenarios relevant to music where ICIP rights are relevant and explain what they require
wider: Investigate a case study that illustrates protocols relating to ICIP rights in music — consider how the case clarifies when permission is required and what respectful engagement looks like

Investigate issues relating to the use of First Nations Australian languages or stories in lyrics, songs or screen-based music — identify the ethical questions these raise and the protocols that apply

modes.reason: Students often understand ICIP rights in the abstract but don't know how to apply them in practice. Encountering multiple specific contexts — listening, sampling, songwriting, performing — where the rights question arises helps students move from abstract understanding to practical ethical reasoning.

nodes.label: Applying culturally responsive approaches
nodes.checkpoint: Students can make ethical choices about how they engage with First Nations Australian music, using protocols for ICIP rights as a guide
criteria: Applies at least one protocol question to a real or hypothetical music practice scenario
Explains the ethical reasoning behind the protocol

width.minimum: Apply at least one protocol question to their own practice (e.g. 'Who wrote this music?', 'May I use ideas from this, and do I need permission?'); explain the reasoning behind the protocol
width.typical: Apply multiple protocol questions to their own practice as listeners, composers and/or performers; explain how the protocols guide ethical engagement with First Nations Australian music
wider: Evaluate a scenario in which a creator used First Nations Australian music without following ICIP protocols — analyse the ethical issues raised and consider what the creator should have done differently

Develop a set of personal guidelines for culturally responsive engagement with First Nations Australian music — based on the protocols investigated, articulate what they will do as a listener, composer and performer

modes.reason: Applying protocols requires students to reason through specific situations — the ethical logic doesn't transfer automatically from principle to practice. Scaffolding the reasoning (who created this → what rights apply → what does that mean for what I want to do) makes the protocol application purposeful rather than checklist-driven.

descriptors.title: Perform music
descriptors.description: perform music using relevant vocal and/or instrumental techniques and performance skills
descriptors.knowledge: Students can perform music in a range of forms they have learnt and/or composed in informal and/or formal settings (AC9AMU6P01). They have not yet focused on the full range of performance skills — posture, technical control, tonal balance, real-time problem-solving — or on planning and presenting performances that demonstrate stylistic understanding.
descriptors.endpoint: Students perform music using relevant vocal and/or instrumental techniques and performance skills, demonstrating technical control and expressive understanding appropriate to the style and context.

nodes.label: Technique for solo and ensemble performance
nodes.checkpoint: Students can apply relevant vocal/instrumental techniques in solo and ensemble performance contexts, maintaining posture and technical control throughout
criteria: Demonstrates appropriate posture for the instrument/voice and context
Maintains technical control across at least part of a performance

width.minimum: Perform a piece with attention to at least two technical aspects (e.g. posture, tone production, intonation, rhythmic accuracy); identify what is working and what needs further development
width.typical: Maintain technical control across a performance, applying appropriate posture and technique for the instrument/voice and context (solo, ensemble, amplified); identify and address technical issues in rehearsal
wider: Analyse the performance practices of musicians identified as experts in specific styles — identify strategies for authentic stylistic interpretation and apply at least one strategy to their own rehearsal

Compare performance posture and technique requirements across different instruments or voice types used in the same ensemble — evaluate how technical choices in each part contribute to the ensemble's overall sound

modes.reason: Technical performance skills are built through deliberate, sustained practice — repetition with feedback is the learning mechanism. Students need repeated opportunities to practise technique with specific feedback rather than exposure to more performance contexts.

nodes.label: Tonal balance and blend in ensemble
nodes.checkpoint: Students can control tone and volume in ensemble performance to create a balanced sound, identifying and responding to imbalances in real time
criteria: Identifies at least one instance of tonal imbalance in ensemble performance
Describes an adjustment that was or could be made to address it

width.minimum: In an ensemble performance, identify at least one instance where tonal balance or blend needed adjustment; describe what adjustment was or could be made
width.typical: Monitor and adjust tone and volume in ensemble performance to maintain balance; reflect on how balance affects the expressive quality of the ensemble sound
wider: Problem-solve a real-time tonal imbalance during rehearsal — diagnose the cause and apply a correction; evaluate whether the correction worked and why
Seek and use feedback from an audience or recording to evaluate ensemble balance — identify at least one aspect of balance that the feedback revealed that was not apparent during performance

modes.reason: Real-time ensemble listening and adjustment is a perceptual and motor skill requiring sustained practice. Students develop the ear-to-response feedback loop through repeated ensemble experience — breadth of ensemble contexts matters, but the mechanism is practice, not new information.

nodes.label: Planning and rehearsing for performance
nodes.checkpoint: Students can plan a performance, identifying expressive skills and stylistic understanding to communicate, and rehearse with attention to those goals
criteria: Identifies at least one expressive or stylistic goal before rehearsal
Demonstrates that rehearsal was shaped by that goal

width.minimum: Identify at least one expressive or stylistic goal for a performance before rehearsal; use that goal to focus at least one rehearsal session
width.typical: Plan a performance with multiple expressive and stylistic goals; rehearse with deliberate attention to those goals; adjust the plan based on rehearsal findings
wider: Plan and present an in-school performance — attend to how elements of music and vocal/instrumental techniques will convey stylistic understanding; evaluate the performance against the stated plan
Use rehearsal recordings to evaluate progress toward performance goals over time — identify turning points in the rehearsal process where goals were achieved or needed revision

modes.reason: Performance planning requires students to work backwards from an intended expressive outcome to specific rehearsal decisions. Scaffolding this reasoning (what do I want to communicate → what technical and expressive choices serve that → what do I need to practise) makes planning purposeful rather than procedural.

nodes.label: Integrated performance with stylistic understanding
nodes.checkpoint: Students can perform music that demonstrates technical control and expressive understanding appropriate to the style, in solo and/or ensemble contexts, for a range of audiences
criteria: Performs a piece in which at least two expressive or stylistic features are evident
Reflects on the performance with at least one specific observation about what worked and what would change

width.minimum: Perform a piece for an audience in which at least two expressive or stylistic features are evident; reflect on what worked and what would change in a future performance
width.typical: Perform music in solo and/or ensemble contexts that demonstrates consistent technical control and stylistic understanding throughout; seek and use feedback to reflect on the performance
wider: Perform a range of music across different styles or forms, demonstrating that technique and expressive choices are adapted to each style rather than applied uniformly
Plan and present a performance that includes their own composed or arranged music alongside other repertoire — evaluate how performing their own work differs from performing existing repertoire

modes.reason: This is where technique, tonal balance, rehearsal planning and stylistic understanding come together in a single live performance for an audience. The coordination of these components under performance conditions — where real-time adjustment is required — is the learning that only performance itself can provide.

descriptors.title: Generate and develop ideas
descriptors.description: generate, document and develop ideas for artworks
descriptors.knowledge: Students can generate and document ideas for artworks using planning strategies (AC9AVA6C01). They have not yet developed sustained visual inquiry, moved through multiple development stages, or justified compositional decisions in relation to intended meaning.
descriptors.endpoint: Students generate, document and develop ideas for artworks through sustained visual inquiry, making and justifying compositional decisions that connect to intended meaning.

nodes.label: Generating ideas through visual brainstorming
nodes.checkpoint: Students can generate ideas for artworks through visual brainstorming that explores multiple approaches before committing to a direction
criteria: Completes at least two planning stages
Explains what each stage contributed to the developing idea
Shows evidence of exploring multiple directions before committing

width.minimum: Complete at least two planning stages for an artwork (e.g. visual brainstorm, compositional sketch); explain what each stage contributed to the developing idea
width.typical: Generate ideas through sustained visual brainstorming across a range of approaches (images, forms, processes, materials); annotate the process using visual arts terminology; explain which directions were pursued and which were set aside and why
wider: Use Viewpoints to generate questions that push brainstorming beyond familiar territory — document how generative questions open unexpected directions
Explore how combining materials or processes that don't obviously belong together produces surprising possibilities — document the combinations and evaluate which are worth developing
Research how artists use visual brainstorming differently across traditions (e.g. studio sketchbooks, mood boards, material exploration) and experiment with unfamiliar approaches

modes.reason: Productive visual brainstorming — staying open, exploring multiple directions, resisting premature commitment — is a studio practice habit developed through sustained repetition. Students who brainstorm once and move to execution haven't built the generative patience that makes ideation genuinely productive. The skill develops through disciplined practice, not through broader contexts.

nodes.label: Developing ideas through research and investigation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can develop ideas through investigation of subject matter, artists and contexts, using research to deepen and refine the artistic concept
criteria: Researches at least one relevant source
Explains how the research changed or deepened the idea — not just describes what was found
Documentation shows research as a generative step, not just background information

width.minimum: Research at least one source relevant to the artwork idea (an artist, a context, a subject matter angle); explain how the research changed or deepened the idea
width.typical: Research subject matter, artists and contexts to develop the artwork idea; document how research opens up the concept; make decisions about which directions to pursue based on research findings
wider: Develop an idea through research into subject matter from multiple perspectives — document how shifting perspective changes what the artwork might communicate

Investigate how artists from different cultural contexts have approached the same subject — use findings to develop a distinctively personal approach that is informed by but not derivative of those artists
Explore ideas about significant subjects or concepts through a particular perspective or range of perspectives — document how perspective shifts the artistic problem

modes.reason: Students commonly use research to confirm an already-formed idea rather than to genuinely develop it. Investigating subject matter from multiple perspectives, and artists from multiple cultural contexts, forces students to let research change the idea rather than just illustrate it. Multiple research contexts are what builds this as a genuine practice rather than a box-ticking step.

nodes.label: Making and justifying compositional decisions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can develop a series of compositional decisions for an artwork and justify each in relation to intended meaning
criteria: Develops at least one compositional sketch that documents visual convention choices
Justifies at least two specific compositional choices in relation to intended meaning
Justification goes beyond 'I liked it' — uses visual arts reasoning

width.minimum: Develop at least one compositional sketch that documents how visual conventions will communicate the intended meaning; justify at least two specific compositional choices
width.typical: Develop a series of compositional sketches as planning for a final artwork; make and justify decisions about visual conventions and planned processes; document decisions using visual arts terminology
wider: Develop multiple alternative compositional approaches to the same idea and evaluate each against the intended meaning — document why the chosen approach is strongest
Use Viewpoints questions ('What combinations are surprising?', 'What would happen if I...?', 'How can I push these ideas further?') to generate compositional decisions that go beyond the obvious
Evaluate how other artists' compositional decisions communicate their intended meaning — use the analysis to sharpen own compositional justifications

modes.reason: Students commonly make compositional decisions intuitively without being able to articulate a justification connected to intended meaning. Scaffolding the reasoning (what is this composition trying to communicate, what convention serves that purpose, why this rather than the alternative?) builds the reflective practice that makes planning documents genuinely useful rather than perfunctory.

descriptors.title: Select and manipulate for meaning
descriptors.description: select and manipulate visual conventions, visual arts processes and/or materials to create artworks that represent ideas, perspectives and/or meaning
descriptors.knowledge: Students can use visual conventions and materials to make artworks that communicate ideas (AC9AVA6C02). They have not yet deliberately selected and manipulated conventions with a clear rationale for how each choice serves the intended meaning.
descriptors.endpoint: Students select and manipulate visual conventions, processes and materials to create artworks where choices are deliberate and connected to intended ideas, perspectives and meaning.

nodes.label: Making deliberate choices with visual conventions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can make deliberate choices about visual conventions and explain how each choice serves the intended meaning or effect
criteria: Makes at least two convention choices that are deliberate and documented
Explains how each choice serves the intended meaning — not just describes the choice
Does not explain choices as 'I like how it looks' without connecting to intended meaning

width.minimum: Make at least two deliberate convention choices in an artwork; explain how each contributes to the intended meaning or effect
width.typical: Create an artwork where convention choices are deliberate and documented; explain the reasoning behind each significant choice using visual arts terminology
wider: Experiment with using modulated and directional lines to create a sense of movement — evaluate whether the convention achieves the intended effect and what adjustments are needed
Explore how breaking a rhythmic pattern creates discord — deliberately deploy this in own work and evaluate its expressive impact
Develop an artwork where every major convention choice is documented and justified — use the documentation as a reflective text about own decision-making

modes.reason: Students commonly make convention choices by intuition or habit without connecting them to intended meaning — they use familiar conventions because they're comfortable, not because they're the best choice. Working across different convention types and intended effects forces students to develop the habit of purposeful selection rather than defaulting to familiarity.

nodes.label: Working across media and processes
nodes.checkpoint: Students can select processes and materials appropriate to their intended meaning and explain why those choices serve the artistic concept better than alternatives
criteria: Selects process or material with a documented rationale connected to intended meaning
Explains what the choice enables that an alternative would not
Material/process choice is connected to concept, not just to familiarity or convenience

width.minimum: Select at least one process or material with a clear rationale for why it suits the intended meaning; explain what this choice enables that an alternative would not
width.typical: Create artworks using selected processes and materials that are connected to intended meaning; evaluate whether material and process choices are serving the concept; document decision-making
wider: Create a work using digital tools (AR assets, photographic manipulation, digital drawing) and evaluate how digital processes extend or constrain expressive possibilities compared to analog approaches
Transform an analog artwork into digital versions and evaluate which transformation best serves the intended meaning — document the decision using visual arts terminology
Consider sustainable design practices as a material constraint — explore sustainable fabrics or recycled materials and evaluate how constraints generate creative possibilities

modes.reason: Students commonly select materials and processes based on what they know how to use rather than what serves the intended meaning. Scaffolding the selection reasoning (what does this material allow, what does it prevent, how does that connect to what I'm trying to communicate?) builds the habit of purposeful material thinking rather than defaulting to the familiar.

nodes.label: Creating artworks that communicate ideas and meaning
nodes.checkpoint: Students can create an artwork where visual convention, process and material choices work together to communicate ideas, perspectives or meaning to an audience
criteria: Creates an artwork that realises at least two intended ideas or meanings
Convention, process and material choices are deliberate and connected to intended meaning
Can explain what the artwork communicates and how specific choices serve that communication

width.minimum: Create an artwork that realises at least two intended ideas or meanings through deliberate convention, process or material choices
width.typical: Create an artwork demonstrating consistent and considered selection and manipulation of conventions, processes and materials; reflect on whether the artwork communicates the intended meaning effectively
wider: Create an artwork that explores personal feelings or emotions — evaluate whether the visual choices successfully externalise an internal experience
Create a work (independently or collaboratively) that tells a story or creates awareness about a significant issue — evaluate how visual choices support the communicative intent
Develop an extended artistic practice across a unit using a visual diary — reflect on how convention, process and material choices have evolved as the concept has deepened

modes.reason: This node integrates deliberate convention selection (Node 1), purposeful process and material choice (Node 2), and planning/development work from AC9AVA8C01 into a completed artwork. The coordination of all these elements into a coherent communicative whole is the learning — students who can make individual deliberate choices but cannot sustain those choices across a complete work have not reached this node.

descriptors.strand: Visual arts: developing practices and skills
descriptors.title: Experiment to develop skills
descriptors.description: experiment with visual conventions, visual arts processes and materials to develop skills
descriptors.knowledge: Students can use visual conventions, processes and materials with increasing control (AC9AVA6D01). They have not yet systematically experimented to develop skills through deliberate practice, nor documented and evaluated that process using visual arts terminology.
descriptors.endpoint: Students experiment with visual conventions, processes and materials to develop skills, documenting and evaluating their practice using visual arts terminology.

nodes.label: Purposeful experimentation with materials and processes
nodes.checkpoint: Students can experiment with a visual convention, process or material with a clear purpose — to discover what it can do — and document what the experimentation reveals
criteria: Experiments with at least one convention, process or material with a clear purpose
Documents at least two outcomes using visual arts terminology
Describes what the experimentation reveals — not just what was tried

width.minimum: Experiment with at least one visual convention, process or material; document at least two outcomes and describe what each reveals about what the material or process can do
width.typical: Experiment with a range of materials, processes or conventions across the unit; approach each experiment with a question or purpose; document outcomes using visual arts terminology
wider: Investigate how artists use encryption, layering or symbolic content and experiment with these approaches — document what the technique adds to meaning-making in own work
Experiment with sustainable materials (natural dyes, recycled materials) and document how material constraints generate rather than limit creative possibilities
Study how a specific artist uses a particular material or process and experiment with replicating and then diverging from that approach — document what is learned through the divergence

modes.reason: Purposeful experimentation — setting a question, trying approaches, documenting outcomes using correct terminology — is a studio practice habit that develops through repeated cycles, not through exposure to more material types. The skill is in the discipline of the process itself: students need to practise the documentation cycle until it becomes habitual.

nodes.label: Learning from other artists to inform own experimentation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can investigate how other artists use materials and processes and use these insights to direct their own experimentation
criteria: Investigates at least one artist's use of a material or process
Uses the investigation to set a specific experimentation direction — not just 'I was inspired'
Documents the connection between the investigation and own experimentation outcomes

width.minimum: Investigate how at least one artist uses a specific material or process; use this as a starting point for own experimentation; document the connection
width.typical: Investigate multiple artists' approaches to materials and processes; use the investigation to set specific experimentation goals; document how the investigation informed the direction of own experimentation
wider: Explore how artists respond to sensory qualities of materials as inspiration — experiment with allowing material properties to direct the work rather than imposing a plan
Compare how artists working in different cultural traditions respond to the same material — use the comparison to develop own informed approach
Investigate how an artist's choice of material carries meaning beyond technical function — experiment with making material choice a deliberate expressive decision in own work

modes.reason: Students commonly look at other artists' work and describe what they see without reasoning through how it informs their own decisions — the investigation stays at appreciation rather than becoming analytical. Scaffolding the connection (what specific technique or choice am I investigating, what does it do, how would I try it, what would I change?) builds the transfer from investigation to practice.

nodes.label: Evaluating experimentation with feedback
nodes.checkpoint: Students can evaluate their own experimentation using teacher and peer feedback, and use evaluation to set future practice directions
criteria: Responds to at least one piece of feedback with a documented change in practice direction
Evaluation uses visual arts terminology — not just 'I liked it' or 'it didn't work'
Documents the feedback-evaluation-decision cycle

width.minimum: Respond to at least one piece of teacher or peer feedback on own experimentation; document how the feedback changes subsequent practice direction
width.typical: Use teacher and peer feedback to evaluate own experimentation outcomes; set future goals based on evaluation; document the feedback-evaluation-decision cycle using visual arts terminology
wider: Develop a systematic evaluation process for own studio practice — use Viewpoints to generate questions that push reflection beyond surface assessment
Evaluate own experimentation against the work of artists investigated — identify specific points of comparison and what they reveal about own skill development
Develop criteria for evaluating own experimentation that go beyond 'it worked/didn't work' — use visual arts vocabulary to articulate what success looks like at multiple levels

modes.reason: Using feedback productively — receiving it, interpreting it in relation to visual arts criteria, and translating it into changed practice — is a reflective habit that develops through repeated cycles. Students need sustained practice with the feedback loop rather than exposure to more experimentation contexts.

descriptors.strand: Visual arts: developing practices and skills
descriptors.title: Reflect on influences to inform practice
descriptors.description: reflect on the ways that they and other artists respond to influences to inform choices they make in their own visual arts practice
descriptors.knowledge: Students can use teacher feedback to reflect on their practice (AC9AVA6D02). They have not yet investigated how other artists respond to influences and used that investigation to articulate and inform their own practice choices.
descriptors.endpoint: Students reflect on how they and other artists respond to influences — materials, emotions, cultural context, other artworks — to make informed and documented choices in own visual arts practice.

nodes.label: Identifying influences on artistic choices
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify the influences on an artist's choices — including material properties, emotional responses, cultural context and investigation of other artists — and explain how these shape the work
criteria: Identifies at least two influence types on an artist's choices
Explains how each influence shaped a specific decision — not just lists influences
Does not reduce 'influence' to 'inspiration' without explanation

width.minimum: Identify at least two influences on an artist's choices in a given work; explain how each influence shaped a specific decision in the work
width.typical: Investigate a range of influences on an artist's practice (material, emotional, cultural, contextual); explain how these converge in specific works and choices
wider: Investigate how an artist responds to sensory qualities of materials as a generative influence — analyse how material properties direct the work's development
Compare how two artists from different cultural contexts respond to similar influences — analyse what differs and why
Investigate how an artist's emotional or personal experience becomes a generative influence rather than just a theme — analyse how this shapes visual convention choices

modes.reason: Students need to build a repertoire of influence types — material properties, emotional experience, cultural context, investigation of other artists, sensory stimuli — before they can meaningfully reflect on which influences are shaping their own practice. A single influence type gives too narrow a lens for genuine reflection.

nodes.label: Reflecting on own influences and practice choices
nodes.checkpoint: Students can reflect on the influences on their own practice choices and document how those influences are shaping specific decisions
criteria: Identifies at least one specific influence on a practice decision
Explains the connection between influence and decision — not just 'I decided to...'
Documentation uses visual arts terminology and goes beyond surface description

width.minimum: Identify at least one influence on a specific choice in own practice; explain the connection between the influence and the decision made
width.typical: Use teacher and student set goals to reflect on and practise skills over time; document how specific influences (investigation of other artists, material properties, personal experience) are shaping practice choices; evaluate outcomes
wider: Develop an extended reflection documenting how multiple influences converge and sometimes conflict in own practice decisions
Explore colour theory in depth (harmonious/contrasting palettes, emotional associations, cultural meanings) and apply systematically — document the reasoning at each compositional decision
Investigate sustainable material practices and reflect on how sustainability constraints become productive influences rather than limitations

modes.reason: Sustained reflective practice — setting goals, practising, evaluating against criteria, adjusting — requires disciplined iteration rather than broader contexts. The skill is in the reflection cycle itself: students who practise the cycle repeatedly develop genuine self-awareness as artists. More influence types don't help; more rounds of the reflection cycle do.

Students commonly describe what they did without reasoning through why they made specific choices or how influences shaped them. Scaffolding the reasoning (what influenced this decision, how did I respond to it, what alternative did I reject and why?) builds the reflective vocabulary that makes documentation meaningful rather than descriptive.

nodes.label: Using reflection to develop visual arts practice over time
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use reflection on influences — their own and other artists' — as a sustained practice that develops over time and produces increasingly informed and distinctive artistic choices
criteria: Shows at least one example where reflection led to a changed practice direction
Documentation demonstrates development over time — not a single reflection moment
Reflection on influences is connected to increasingly distinctive and informed choices

width.minimum: Show at least one example where reflection on an influence led to a changed practice direction; document the before/after and explain what changed and why
width.typical: Document how practice has developed over a unit as a result of sustained reflection on influences; show how reflection has produced increasingly informed and distinctive choices
wider: Build on understanding of composition to explore multiple approaches to representing space and depth — document how each investigation changes subsequent compositional decisions
Develop a personal artistic statement that articulates the influences currently shaping own practice and how those influences are being engaged and adapted
Reflect on the work of multiple artists alongside own explorations — document convergences and divergences and explain what they reveal about own developing practice identity

modes.reason: This node integrates influence identification (Node 1), reflective practice cycles (Node 2), and evidence of development over time into a coherent account of own practice development. Students who can reflect on single influences but cannot demonstrate sustained development over a unit have not met the descriptor's demand for reflection that informs practice.

descriptors.title: Investigate conventions and meaning
descriptors.description: investigate ways that visual conventions, visual arts processes and materials are manipulated to represent ideas, perspectives and/or meaning in artworks created across cultures, times, places and/or other contexts
descriptors.knowledge: Students can identify how artists use visual conventions and materials to communicate ideas (AC9AVA6E01). They have not yet investigated how cultural, historical and contextual factors shape these choices or analysed how the same subject is represented differently across cultures and times.
descriptors.endpoint: Students investigate how visual conventions, processes and materials are manipulated to represent ideas, perspectives and meaning across cultures, times, places and contexts.

nodes.label: Identifying visual conventions and their purpose
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify specific visual conventions used in an artwork and describe what role they play in communicating ideas or meaning
criteria: Identifies at least two visual conventions in a given artwork
Describes what role each convention plays in communicating meaning — not just names the convention
Does not confuse describing what an artwork looks like with explaining how it makes meaning

width.minimum: Identify at least two visual conventions in a given artwork and describe what each contributes to the meaning or effect
width.typical: Analyse a range of artworks to identify visual conventions and explain how each has been manipulated to communicate specific ideas or perspectives
wider: Compare how two artists working in different media use the same visual convention (e.g. line, colour, composition) to achieve different expressive effects
Investigate how a visual convention carries different meanings in different cultural contexts — e.g. how white is used in Western vs East Asian funerary traditions
Analyse how a First Nations Australian artist uses visual conventions that carry cultural knowledge — investigate what those conventions mean within their cultural context

modes.reason: Students need to accumulate a range of visual convention examples before they can analyse how manipulation of conventions produces meaning. Exposure to multiple artworks, media and cultural contexts builds the visual literacy needed for genuine analysis rather than surface description.

nodes.label: Investigating across cultures and contexts
nodes.checkpoint: Students can investigate how visual conventions and processes are shaped by cultural, historical and contextual factors and explain how these factors influence meaning-making
criteria: Investigates at least one artist whose practice is shaped by cultural or historical context
Explains how the context influences specific visual convention or process choices
Goes beyond surface description to explain the relationship between context and meaning

width.minimum: Investigate one artist whose practice is shaped by cultural or historical context; explain how that context influences their use of visual conventions
width.typical: Investigate artists from at least two different cultural or historical contexts who represent a similar subject or theme; explain how context shapes their approach to visual conventions and meaning
wider: Investigate First Nations Australian artworks that cross multiple artforms — analyse how visual, performative and musical elements combine to produce layered meaning
Research the reciprocal influence between Australian and Asian artists; analyse how cross-cultural exchange shapes visual conventions and practice
Investigate how artists across different times have represented the same subject (e.g. portraiture, the natural world) — analyse what changes and what persists across cultural conventions

modes.reason: Students commonly describe what an artist does without connecting it to cultural or historical context — the analysis stays at the surface of visual features. Investigating artists from multiple cultural and historical contexts forces students to develop the contextual reasoning habit rather than applying one familiar analytical frame.

nodes.label: Connecting investigation to own practice
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use their investigation of other artists' use of visual conventions to inform decisions in their own visual arts practice
criteria: Identifies at least one specific insight from investigating other artists that influenced own work
Explains the connection between the investigation and the decision — not just 'I was inspired by'
Distinguishes adaptation (informed influence) from imitation (copying)

width.minimum: Identify at least one specific insight from investigating other artists' use of visual conventions that has influenced a decision in own work; explain the connection
width.typical: Analyse how investigating artists' choices informs own approach to visual conventions and processes; document specific points of influence and how they are adapted, not just imitated
wider: Develop written accounts (catalogue entries, reviews or discussions) that connect the investigation of other artists to own artistic decisions
Investigate how artists are inspired by practitioners from other countries or cultures and use this as a model for own cross-cultural investigation
Construct an argument about why investigating diverse artistic traditions produces stronger and more distinctive own practice than studying a single tradition

modes.reason: This node requires students to bring together visual convention analysis (Node 1) and cultural/contextual investigation (Node 2) and connect both to their own practice decisions. The integration is the learning — students who can analyse other artists but cannot use that analysis to inform their own work have not reached this standard's demand.

Students commonly describe what they have investigated without articulating the connection to own practice — 'I liked how Mondrian used primary colours' without reasoning through how that insight changes a specific decision in own work. Scaffolding the connection explicitly (what did I learn, what decision did it change, how is my adaptation different from imitation?) builds the analytical-to-practical transfer.

descriptors.title: Diversity of First Nations visual arts
descriptors.description: investigate the diversity of First Nations Australians' artworks and arts practices, considering culturally responsive approaches to Indigenous Cultural and Intellectual Property rights
descriptors.knowledge: Students have some awareness that First Nations Australians have rich artistic traditions. They have not yet investigated the diversity of these practices in depth, nor engaged systematically with ICIP rights frameworks.
descriptors.endpoint: Students investigate the diversity of First Nations Australians' artworks and arts practices with genuine cultural responsiveness, understanding and applying ICIP rights frameworks.

nodes.label: Understanding ICIP rights and protocols
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain what ICIP rights are, why they exist, and what culturally responsive engagement with First Nations artworks looks like in practice
criteria: Explains what ICIP rights are and why they exist
Gives at least one specific example of what respectful engagement looks like in practice
Does not reduce ICIP to a checklist — explains the reasoning behind the protocols

width.minimum: Explain what ICIP rights are and give one example of what respectful engagement with First Nations cultural material looks like in a visual arts context
width.typical: Investigate ICIP rights frameworks and explain how they apply to different scenarios — using cultural material in own work, selecting source material for collage, referencing traditional imagery
wider: Investigate a specific case of cultural appropriation in visual arts — explain what ICIP rights were denied, who was harmed, and what a respectful alternative would have looked like
Research how professional artists and design companies obtain permission to use cultural material belonging to a collective rather than an individual
Develop own practical guidelines for engaging with First Nations cultural material in visual arts practice — ground them in specific protocol sources endorsed by First Nations organisations

modes.reason: Students commonly understand ICIP rights in the abstract without being able to reason through specific scenarios — they know 'you need permission' without being able to work out who to ask, what counts as cultural material, or what respectful engagement looks like in practice. Scaffolding the scenario-based reasoning (who created this, whose story is it, what permission is needed, how do I obtain it?) builds actionable understanding rather than declarative awareness.

nodes.label: Investigating diversity of First Nations visual arts
nodes.checkpoint: Students can investigate the diversity of First Nations Australian artworks and arts practices — across regions, styles, media and contexts — with cultural responsiveness
criteria: Investigates at least one First Nations Australian artwork or practice in genuine depth
Explains what makes it culturally significant — not just describes what it looks like
Demonstrates cultural responsiveness throughout — not just awareness of protocols

width.minimum: Investigate at least one First Nations Australian artwork or arts practice in depth; explain what makes it distinctive and culturally significant
width.typical: Investigate First Nations Australian artworks and practices from at least two different regional or cultural contexts; analyse what is distinctive about each and what connects them; approach the investigation with genuine cultural responsiveness
wider: Investigate how First Nations Australian artists work across multiple artforms — analyse how visual elements interact with performance, music or storytelling to produce layered cultural meaning

Investigate contemporary First Nations Australian artists who are engaging with digital media or international art contexts — analyse how they navigate cultural identity and ICIP responsibilities in these spaces
Research how First Nations Australian visual arts practices have changed and adapted over time while maintaining cultural continuity

modes.reason: Students commonly treat First Nations Australian visual arts as a monolithic tradition rather than understanding the enormous diversity across hundreds of distinct cultural groups, regions, media and contexts. Investigating multiple distinct practices — from different regions, media, and contemporary/traditional contexts — resolves this misconception through genuine breadth rather than a single example.

nodes.label: Applying culturally responsive approaches in visual arts
criteria: Applies at least one ICIP protocol question to a real or hypothetical visual arts practice scenario
Explains the ethical reasoning behind the protocol

width.minimum: Apply at least one ICIP protocol question to own practice; explain the reasoning behind the protocol.
width.typical: Apply multiple protocol questions to own practice as a viewer, researcher and maker; explain how the protocols guide ethical engagement with First Nations Australian visual arts.
wider: Evaluate a scenario in which a creator used First Nations Australian visual arts without following ICIP protocols — analyse the ethical issues and what should have been done differently.
Develop a set of personal guidelines for culturally responsive engagement with First Nations Australian visual arts, grounded in specific protocols.

modes.reason: Applying protocols requires reasoning through specific situations — the ethical logic does not transfer automatically from principle to practice.

descriptors.title: Curate and present visual arts practice
descriptors.description: curate and present examples of their visual arts practice to accompany exhibits of their artworks to communicate ideas, perspectives and/or meaning to audiences
descriptors.knowledge: Students can present artworks with basic accompanying documentation (AC9AVA6P01). They have not yet made deliberate curation decisions about which works to present, how to organise them, or how documentation can connect artworks to ideas and meaning for an audience.
descriptors.endpoint: Students curate and present examples of their visual arts practice with documentation that connects artworks to ideas, perspectives and meaning for a specific audience.

nodes.label: Understanding curation and audience
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain what curation involves and how curation choices affect what an audience understands about the artworks and the artist's ideas
criteria: Explains what curation involves
Identifies at least two curation decisions and explains how each affects audience experience
Does not treat presentation as merely displaying artworks — understands it as a communicative act

width.minimum: Explain what curation involves; describe at least two decisions a curator makes and how each affects audience experience
width.typical: Investigate examples of curated exhibitions; analyse the curation decisions made (selection, arrangement, labelling, space) and explain how each shapes audience experience and understanding
wider: Visit and critically evaluate an exhibition in a gallery, museum or community site — analyse specific curation decisions and evaluate their effectiveness for the intended audience
Investigate how digital curation (webpage, walkthrough, online showcase) makes different choices than physical curation — analyse what each enables and constrains
Research how artists describe their artistic vision in exhibition contexts — analyse how language choices in labels and statements shape audience understanding

modes.reason: Students need exposure to multiple curation contexts — physical and digital, school and professional, different audience types — to understand that curation is a design practice with genuine decisions and consequences. A single example of a school display doesn't build the conceptual understanding needed for deliberate curation choices.

nodes.label: Creating documentation for artworks
nodes.checkpoint: Students can create documentation (labels, statements, explanations) that connects their artworks to intended ideas, perspectives and meaning for an audience
criteria: Creates documentation that connects artworks to intended ideas or meaning
Documentation goes beyond description — communicates meaning and artistic vision
Uses visual arts terminology appropriately

width.minimum: Create at least one piece of documentation (label, statement or explanation) for an artwork; documentation should connect the work to its intended ideas or meaning
width.typical: Create documentation for multiple artworks that communicates the ideas, perspectives and meaning behind each work to a specific audience; use visual arts terminology appropriately
wider: Research a variety of gallery label formats and develop own label that goes beyond basic identification to communicate artistic vision
Create an extended artist statement that articulates the ideas, processes and decisions behind a body of work
Develop documentation that uses different formats for different audience types — e.g. a technical statement for peers and an accessible explanation for younger students

modes.reason: Writing documentation that genuinely connects artworks to ideas — rather than just describing what they look like or how they were made — is a precision writing skill that develops through repeated practice with feedback. Students need to practise the specific move of articulating meaning rather than process, and this habit develops through iteration, not through broader documentation contexts.

Students commonly write documentation that describes the artwork ('I used blue because I like blue') rather than explaining the meaning ('I used blue to communicate the coldness and distance in the relationship depicted'). Scaffolding the reasoning distinction — what does this work communicate vs how was it made — builds the writing habit that makes documentation genuinely useful for audiences.

nodes.label: Curating and presenting a coherent exhibition
nodes.checkpoint: Students can make deliberate curation decisions about which works to present, how to arrange them, and how documentation supports the exhibition's communicative intent
criteria: Presents artworks with documentation in a chosen context
Makes and explains at least two deliberate curation decisions
Curation choices are connected to communicative intent — not just aesthetic preference

width.minimum: Present at least one artwork with documentation in a chosen context; explain at least two curation decisions made and why
width.typical: Curate a selection of works for presentation; make deliberate decisions about selection, arrangement and documentation; explain how curation choices support the exhibition's communicative intent
wider: Create a themed series of artworks curated for display — use Viewpoints questions to guide decisions about visual narrative, spatial relationships and audience experience

Create a digital presentation (webpage, walkthrough) to connect geographically distanced audiences with a visual arts showcase — evaluate the specific curation decisions needed for digital presentation
Develop an exhibition that tells a story through the arrangement and relationships between works — document the curatorial thinking behind the visual narrative

modes.reason: This node integrates understanding of curation principles (Node 1), documentation writing skills (Node 2), and artwork creation from AC9AVA8C02 into a coherent presented exhibition.
