The coordination of selection, arrangement, documentation and communicative intent is the learning — students who can create artworks and write labels but cannot make the curation decisions that connect them into a coherent whole have not reached this node.

descriptors.title: Choreograph to communicate and challenge
descriptors.description: choreograph dance that communicates ideas, perspectives and/or meaning by selecting and manipulating elements of dance, choreographic devices and/or structure
descriptors.knowledge: Students can choreograph dance by selecting and manipulating elements of dance and choreographic devices to communicate ideas, perspectives and/or meaning (Y7-8, AC9ADA8C01). They have worked with binary, ternary and narrative structures, transitions, variation and contrast, and can document their process.
descriptors.endpoint: Students choreograph dance that communicates ideas, perspectives and/or meaning by selecting and manipulating elements of dance, choreographic devices and/or structure.

nodes.label: Developing motifs and innovative manipulation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can develop movement motifs and manipulate elements and choreographic devices in innovative ways to communicate a clear choreographic intent.
criteria: Student can develop a movement motif and generate at least three variations using named manipulation techniques
Student can explain how the manipulation choices serve the choreographic intent
nodes.hinge_reason: Motif development and innovative manipulation are the compositional engine of senior dance. Without this, students produce choreography that is movement arrangement rather than genuine compositional craft — which limits expressive range and structural sophistication in the final work.

width.minimum: Developing at least one movement motif; applying at least two forms of manipulation (e.g. addition, diminution, force, tempo) to generate material from the motif.
width.typical: Developing movement motifs and using choreographic devices or manipulating elements in innovative ways; experimenting with addition and diminution, force and tempo, different body parts; developing motifs from dances shared via social media or other sources; using style-specific forms to structure work.
wider: Develop motifs that synthesise influences from dances of different cultures, times and places — using respectful dance practice to adapt rather than appropriate
Use digital tools or social media-inspired movement (e.g. viral movement motifs) as starting points — manipulating these into original work that communicates a personal perspective

modes.reason: Innovative manipulation requires students to move beyond familiar devices — scaffold with explicit manipulation menus (addition, diminution, inversion, retrograde, fragmentation) and encourage systematic exploration before selection.
Students who develop motifs from diverse cultural influences and contemporary movement sources build wider compositional range and more personal choreographic voice.

nodes.label: Structuring and communicating intent
nodes.checkpoint: Students can structure a dance using elements, devices and/or choreographic forms — communicating ideas, perspectives or meaning with intentional structural choices.
criteria: Student produces a complete dance with identifiable structural choices connected to communicative intent
Student can explain how at least two structural decisions serve the ideas, perspectives or meaning they intend to communicate

width.minimum: A structured dance using at least one choreographic form or structural principle; clear communicative intent connected to structural choices.
width.typical: Choreographing dance that communicates ideas about identity, belonging or social justice; using and combining choreographic devices (addition, diminution, force, tempo); using style-specific forms; using Viewpoints to interrogate spatial and dynamic choices; adapting dance ideas from different cultural influences respectfully.
wider: Choreograph a dance that uses a culturally specific form (e.g. form associated with a specific cultural genre/style) — researching and applying it with appropriate cultural respect
Create a dance that takes a political position or advocates for a community — using structural choices to build argument or narrative

modes.reason: Structural communication integrates motif work (N1) with choreographic intent and audience relationship. Encourage students to test structural choices against their stated intent — 'Does this structure serve what you want to say?'

nodes.label: Documenting and reflecting on process
nodes.checkpoint: Students can document their choreographic process — including analysis and evaluation of choices — and use this reflection to refine their work.
criteria: Student produces a process document recording at least two choreographic decisions with reasoning
Student can evaluate the effectiveness of at least one structural or element choice in communicating their intent

width.minimum: A brief documented record of choreographic process — at least two decision points noted with reasoning.
width.typical: Documenting creative process in journals, blogs, video or audio recordings (with permissions); using Viewpoints to reflect on space, dynamics, intent; improvising and analysing movement choices to clarify choreographic intent; considering how emotion, political positions, critical theories shape their approach.
wider: Create a reflective portfolio documenting the full choreographic journey — including blind alleys, pivots and key insights
Use documented process to evaluate the relationship between intent and realised work — identifying the gap between what was planned and what was communicated

modes.reason: Choreographic documentation requires reflective writing and evaluation skills alongside artistic ones. Scaffold with specific reflection prompts — 'What decision did you make here?', 'What alternatives did you consider?', 'What influenced this choice?'

descriptors.title: Apply skills to enhance communication
descriptors.description: apply technical and expressive skills and genre- or style-specific techniques to enhance communication of ideas, perspectives and/or meaning
descriptors.knowledge: Students can apply technical and expressive skills and genre- or style-specific techniques to communicate ideas, perspectives and/or meaning (Y7-8, AC9ADA8C02). They have worked with strength, balance, coordination, and have used feedback to refine technical and expressive quality.
descriptors.endpoint: Students apply technical and expressive skills and genre- or style-specific techniques to enhance communication of ideas, perspectives and/or meaning.

nodes.label: Genre/style-specific technique application
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify characteristic techniques in a selected genre or style and apply them to enhance performance of dances in that style.
criteria: Student can identify at least three characteristic techniques of their selected genre/style
Student demonstrates these techniques in performance with safe execution

width.minimum: Identifying at least three characteristic techniques of a selected genre/style and demonstrating them in performance — with attention to safe execution.
width.typical: Using observations/analysis of a dance in a selected genre/style to identify characteristic techniques; building ability to execute techniques using safe dance practice over time; applying techniques to enhance performance; seeking feedback on choreography and performance using Viewpoints questions.
wider: Study a genre or style from a culture students identify with — using cultural knowledge to inform authentic technique application rather than imitation
Compare how the same technique functions differently in two related genres/styles — developing nuanced style-literacy

modes.reason: Style-specific technique develops through sustained engagement with the genre's movement vocabulary. Identify the characteristic techniques explicitly, then build repetition across sessions.

nodes.label: Applying musculoskeletal knowledge to safe technique
nodes.checkpoint: Students can apply knowledge of the musculoskeletal system to execute movement techniques safely and prevent injury.
criteria: Student can explain how at least one musculoskeletal principle applies to the safe execution of a specific technique
Student consistently applies safe practice principles when executing demanding techniques
nodes.hinge_reason: At Y9-10, technical demands increase significantly and students work with genre-specific technique that carries real injury risk if executed without anatomical awareness. Students who lack this knowledge cannot safely pursue the level of technical challenge expected.

width.minimum: Explaining at least one musculoskeletal principle relevant to a technique they are practising; applying it to modify or refine execution.
width.typical: Applying knowledge of the structure and function of the musculoskeletal system to execute movements safely; preventing injury to self and others; connecting anatomical understanding to technique decisions in a specific genre/style.
wider: Analyse a physically demanding technique in their chosen style through an anatomical lens — identifying injury risks and safe practice modifications
Research how professional dance practitioners in their chosen style approach injury prevention and recovery — applying this knowledge to their own practice

modes.reason: Anatomical knowledge requires explicit instruction — it does not arise naturally from movement practice alone. Teach relevant musculoskeletal concepts in direct connection to the techniques being practised, not as standalone science content.

nodes.label: Seeking feedback and refining
nodes.checkpoint: Students can seek and use feedback on choreography and performance to refine technical and expressive skill application.
criteria: Student seeks specific feedback on performance using at least one Viewpoints question
Student makes an identifiable refinement to technical or expressive skill application in response to feedback received

width.minimum: Seeking feedback on at least one aspect of performance using a Viewpoints question; making at least one identifiable refinement in response.
width.typical: Seeking feedback on choreography and performance using Viewpoints questions ('What emotion did you feel most strongly?'); using feedback to refine technical and expressive skills; evaluating the success of skill application in communicating intent.
wider: Seek feedback from multiple sources (peer, teacher, video self-review) on the same performance — synthesising across feedback sources to prioritise development areas
Document a feedback-revision cycle — recording the feedback received, the decision made in response, and the effect on the work

modes.reason: Using feedback to refine integrates technical skill, expressive skill, and reflective capacity. Frame feedback-seeking as a professional practice — dancers in all genres use this cycle throughout their careers.

descriptors.title: Refine safe dance and genre techniques
descriptors.description: develop and refine safe dance practice, expressive and technical skills and genre- or style-specific techniques
descriptors.knowledge: Students have developed safe dance practice and technical/expressive skills (Y7-8, AC9ADA8D01). They can extend their movement vocabulary through improvisation and work with genre/style-specific techniques.
descriptors.endpoint: Students develop and refine safe dance practice, expressive and technical skills and genre- or style-specific techniques.

nodes.label: Refining technical precision
nodes.checkpoint: Students can refine technical skills — control, accuracy, strength, balance, alignment, flexibility, endurance, coordination, articulation — through self-reflection and targeted practice.
criteria: Student identifies a specific technical skill development goal and can articulate what improvement looks like
Student demonstrates measurable improvement in a target technical skill following focused practice

width.minimum: Setting a specific technical skill development goal; practising with targeted self-reflection; demonstrating improvement in one technical quality.
width.typical: Refining technical skills in response to self-reflection: developing safe dance practice and control, accuracy, strength, balance, alignment, flexibility, endurance, coordination, articulation; using experimentation and improvisation to develop techniques for executing expressive skills in a range of genres/styles.
wider: Develop a sustained personal technical development plan — setting measurable targets across two or three skills over an extended period
Explore how technical training approaches differ across dance genres — comparing the physical demands and preparation methods of two different styles

modes.reason: Technical precision at senior level requires deliberate, focused practice — not just exposure. Set specific quality targets for each session and create conditions for productive repetition.

nodes.label: Genre/style proficiency
nodes.checkpoint: Students can practise and refine genre- and style-specific techniques toward developing proficiency.
criteria: Student demonstrates proficiency in at least two genre- or style-specific techniques — evidencing both technical quality and stylistic awareness
Student applies safe dance practice consistently as technical demands increase
nodes.hinge_reason: Genre/style proficiency is the technical foundation of the senior Presenting strand — students performing in formal contexts must have sufficient genre-specific technique to communicate authentically, not just approximately.

width.minimum: Demonstrating proficiency in at least two characteristic techniques of a selected genre/style — with attention to both technical quality and stylistic authenticity.
width.typical: Practising and refining technical skills to develop proficiency in genre- and style-specific techniques; using experimentation and improvisation to develop expressive technique execution; applying safe dance practice as complexity and demand increase.
wider: Pursue proficiency in techniques from a genre/style associated with a cultural identity or tradition — engaging with community knowledge where possible
Compare how proficiency is understood and assessed across two genres — exploring what counts as excellence in each context

modes.reason: Proficiency requires accumulated repetition across extended time. Frame genre/style technique development as a long arc — not a unit. Identify technique benchmarks and return to them across the year.

descriptors.title: Reflect to inform choreographic choices
descriptors.description: reflect on own and others' use of the elements of dance, choreographic devices, structure, genre- or style-specific techniques and/or technical and expressive skills to inform their choreographic or performance choices
descriptors.knowledge: Students can reflect on own and others' dance works and/or practices to inform choreographic choices and use of technical and expressive skills (Y7-8, AC9ADA8D02). They can use journals and peer feedback as reflective tools.
descriptors.endpoint: Students reflect on own and others' use of elements, choreographic devices, structure, genre- or style-specific techniques and/or technical and expressive skills to inform their choreographic or performance choices.

nodes.label: Analytical reflection using Viewpoints
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use Viewpoints-based evaluation to analyse element and device use in their own and others' work — connecting analysis to specific choreographic or performance choices.
criteria: Student uses at least two Viewpoints questions to analyse specific element or device use in a dance work
Student connects the analysis to a specific choreographic or performance decision

width.minimum: Using at least two Viewpoints questions to reflect analytically on a specific aspect of own or another's work — connecting analysis to at least one decision.
width.typical: Using Viewpoints to reflect on and evaluate forms and elements: 'How can I use space and dynamics to convey my ideas?'; evaluating choreographic and performance choices ('How successful were the dancers in conveying the stated intent?', 'What was the impact of choosing gesture to communicate emotion?'); documenting in reflective records.
wider: Maintain a systematic reflective journal across an extended choreographic project — analysing key decision points and their outcomes
Analyse a professional dance work for element and device use — applying the same analytical frame to their own choreographic process

modes.reason: Analytical reflection — not just impressionistic response — requires a consistent evaluative framework. Viewpoints questions provide this frame; students need practice using them analytically before using them generatively.

nodes.label: Reflecting on personal identity and influence
nodes.checkpoint: Students can reflect on how personal identity, emotions, political positions and critical theories influence and shape their approach to dance.
criteria: Student identifies at least one personal influence that shapes their choreographic approach — connecting it to a specific decision
Student can explain how a specific element of their identity or perspective is expressed through their choreographic or movement choices
nodes.hinge_reason: Personal voice and reflective identity awareness are what distinguish creative work at senior level from technical reproduction. Students who cannot yet connect personal influence to choreographic choice produce work that is stylistically competent but personally unmotivated.

width.minimum: Identifying at least one personal influence (cultural identity, emotion, interest) that shapes their choreographic choices — connecting it to a specific decision.
width.typical: Improvising using elements of dance and analysing movement choices to reflect individuality and clarify choreographic intent; considering how emotion, political statements, critical theories or lived experiences influence approach to dance; documenting creative process including analysis and evaluation.
wider: Explore how their cultural background or identity influences their choreographic choices — comparing this with how other choreographers' identities shape their work
Investigate a choreographer whose political or social identity is central to their practice — analysing how personal position is translated into choreographic choices

modes.reason: Personal reflection integrates analytical skill (N1) with self-knowledge and creative ownership. Frame as: 'Your choreographic choices reveal something about you — what do you want them to reveal?'

descriptors.title: Investigate choreographers and meaning
descriptors.description: investigate performers' and/or choreographers' use of elements of dance, choreographic devices, genre- or style-specific techniques, conventions and/or production elements to communicate and/or challenge ideas, perspectives and/or meaning in dance across cultures, times, places and/or other contexts
descriptors.knowledge: Students can investigate dance works, performers and/or choreographers across cultures, times, places and contexts (Y7-8, AC9ADA8E01). They can analyse element and device use, investigate digital tool influence, and evaluate choreographic intent.
descriptors.endpoint: Students investigate performers' and/or choreographers' use of elements, devices, genre/style-specific techniques, conventions and/or production elements to communicate and/or challenge ideas, perspectives and/or meaning across cultures, times, places and/or other contexts.

nodes.label: Investigating choreographic practice in context
nodes.checkpoint: Students can investigate how and why choreographers and performers work within specific cultural, social, historical and environmental contexts — analysing how context shapes practice.
criteria: Student connects at least two choreographic choices to the practitioner's contextual position (cultural, social, historical)
Student can articulate how context shapes the way a dance communicates or challenges ideas
nodes.hinge_reason: Context-driven analysis — understanding why a choreographer made specific choices given their position — is the analytical depth that distinguishes investigating from describing. Students without this move cannot engage critically with cultural diversity or social justice in dance.

width.minimum: Investigating one choreographer or dance practitioner — connecting their contextual position (cultural, historical, social) to at least two identifiable choices in their work.
width.typical: Investigating how and why choreographers work with communities to advocate for social justice or sustainable living; exploring specific examples of practitioners working with communities in Australia with cultural links to Asia; analysing how traditions, styles and contexts affect experience and interpretation; extending own movement vocabulary through analysis of others' stylistic preferences.
wider: Investigate a choreographer whose practice is grounded in a specific cultural community — analysing how community context shapes every aspect of the work
Compare how two choreographers from different cultural or historical contexts address the same theme — analysing how context determines approach, form and reception

modes.reason: Contextual analysis requires an explicit methodology — teach students to move from 'what I see' to 'why this choice, given this context'. Use a structured inquiry model: context → choice → effect → interpretation.
Investigating practitioners across genuinely diverse cultural, temporal and geographic contexts builds analytical range and prevents single-tradition dominance of the student's interpretive frame.

nodes.label: Personal identity and stylistic development
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use investigation of diverse dance styles and genres to inform and develop their own stylistic preferences and personal choreographic identity.
criteria: Student analyses element use in at least one unfamiliar genre/style
Student can explain how this analysis informs or challenges their own choreographic or performance practice

width.minimum: Analysing element use in at least one genre/style they have not previously worked in — identifying one way it could inform their own practice.
width.typical: Extending movement vocabulary as they explore own stylistic preferences and personal identity; using analysis of dance styles from cultures they identify with or from different times to inform choreographic practice; analysing element use in popular culture styles or styles from Asia as stimulus.
wider: Develop a personal style statement — articulating the choreographic influences, cultural references and aesthetic preferences that shape their dance identity
Investigate how a dance style from a country or region in Asia has been adopted, adapted or appropriated in Western contexts — using this analysis to inform respectful practice

modes.reason: Style development integrates contextual investigation (N1) with personal identity and creative practice. The key move is from 'I analysed this style' to 'and here is what it does for my work'.

descriptors.title: First Nations identity and challenge
descriptors.description: investigate the ways First Nations Australian choreographers and/or performers celebrate and challenge multiple perspectives of Australian identity through dance
descriptors.knowledge: Students can investigate the diversity of dance choreographed and/or performed by First Nations Australians, considering ICIP rights (Y7-8, AC9ADA8E02). They understand cultural appropriation and can apply culturally responsive approaches to First Nations dance.
descriptors.endpoint: Students investigate the ways First Nations Australian choreographers and/or performers celebrate and challenge multiple perspectives of Australian identity through dance.

nodes.label: Celebrating and challenging Australian identity
nodes.checkpoint: Students can investigate how First Nations Australian choreographers and/or performers use dance to celebrate and challenge perspectives of Australian identity.
criteria: Student can describe how a specific First Nations Australian dance work celebrates or challenges a perspective of Australian identity
Student connects the choreographer's community position and lived experience to specific choices in the work
nodes.hinge_reason: Understanding dance as a site of cultural celebration and political challenge — not merely cultural expression — is the conceptual shift that enables genuine critical engagement with First Nations Australian art. Without it, students remain in appreciation mode rather than critical analysis.

width.minimum: Investigating at least one example of a First Nations Australian dance work that either celebrates or challenges a perspective of Australian identity — describing the choreographer's approach.
width.typical: Evaluating ways that First Nations Australian performers and/or choreographers work respectfully and collaboratively with communities to explore local histories, cultures and identities; investigating dance works that challenge understandings about 'first contacts' between First Nations Peoples and colonisers; exploring how choreographers and performers communicate ideas, messages and lived experiences to the broader community.
wider: Investigate a First Nations Australian choreographer's sustained practice — examining how their work has evolved in response to historical and contemporary events
Compare how two different First Nations Australian dance practitioners address Australian identity — analysing what different community positions produce in terms of choreographic choices

modes.reason: The concept of challenging identity requires students to understand that art can be a form of advocacy, resistance and reframing — not just representation. Explore specific examples where the work explicitly challenges dominant narratives. Use resources that centre First Nations voices.
First Nations Australian choreographic practices are diverse — no single example represents the whole. Investigate multiple practitioners from different communities and contexts.

nodes.label: Communicating lived experience through dance
nodes.checkpoint: Students can analyse how First Nations Australian choreographers and/or performers communicate lived experiences and ideas to the broader community through dance.
criteria: Student identifies at least two choreographic choices in a First Nations Australian work that communicate lived experience to a broad audience
Student can explain what the work communicates and to whom — recognising that different audiences may read the work differently

width.minimum: Identifying how at least two specific choreographic choices in a First Nations Australian work communicate a lived experience or idea to a broad audience.
width.typical: Exploring the ways that First Nations Australian choreographers and/or performers use their practice to communicate ideas, messages and lived experiences to the broader community; considering how the work addresses audiences who may have no prior relationship to First Nations Australian cultures.
wider: Investigate how a First Nations Australian dance work was received by different audiences — comparing how community audiences and broader Australian audiences read the same work
Explore how a First Nations Australian choreographer's relationship to both First Nations and broader Australian cultural contexts shapes their communicative choices

modes.reason: Communicating lived experience is both a choreographic and a political act. Help students understand the layers of address in First Nations Australian dance — to community, to country, and to a broader national audience — and how each layer produces different interpretive demands.

descriptors.title: Rehearse and perform with genre skills
descriptors.description: rehearse and perform dance for audiences, using technical and expressive skills and genre- or style-specific techniques
descriptors.knowledge: Students can rehearse and perform dance for audiences using technical and expressive skills and genre/style-specific techniques (Y7-8, AC9ADA8P01). They have worked with production elements, rehearsal strategies and performed in formal and informal contexts.
descriptors.endpoint: Students rehearse and perform dance for audiences, using technical and expressive skills and genre- or style-specific techniques.

nodes.label: Performance entry/exit and spatial fluency
nodes.checkpoint: Students can plan and execute performance entry and exit in ways consistent with genre/style, mood or the ideas conveyed in the dance.
criteria: Student enters and exits the performance space in a way that is consistent with the genre/style and communicative intent
Student maintains accurate spatial placement throughout performance

width.minimum: Planning and executing a performance entry and exit that is consistent with the genre/style and communicative intent of the dance.
width.typical: Planning how to enter and leave the performance space consistently with genre/style, mood or ideas conveyed; building confidence in accurate and fluent spatial placement maintenance throughout performance; using rehearsal to develop fluency and consistency.
wider: Choreograph the entry and exit as deliberate compositional elements — using them to establish and resolve the performance's communicative arc
Rehearse spatial placement and entry/exit in a range of performance space configurations — developing adaptable performance spatial awareness

modes.reason: Spatial fluency in performance requires repetition in realistic performance conditions — not just rehearsal room practice. Simulate performance conditions (including entry/exit) in rehearsals.

nodes.label: Genre/style technique in performance
nodes.checkpoint: Students can apply genre- or style-specific techniques with technical and expressive skill in formal performance — communicating ideas, perspectives or meaning authentically within the style.
criteria: Student applies at least two genre- or style-specific techniques recognisably in performance
Student uses at least one production element purposefully — enhancing rather than distracting from the communicative intent
Student's performance communicates the intended ideas, perspectives or meaning — evidenced through audience response or reflection
nodes.hinge_reason: Genre/style-authentic performance — not just technically competent movement — is the standard for this band. Students who cannot yet apply style-specific technique in performance context have not met the descriptor's demand and are not prepared for post-school performance or arts industry pathways.

width.minimum: Performing in a selected genre/style with at least two identifiable style-specific techniques — demonstrating both technical quality and expressive communication.
width.typical: Applying technical and expressive skills and genre- or style-specific techniques when performing learned and/or choreographed dances; using available production elements (music, costume, props) to enhance communication of ideas, perspectives or meaning.
wider: Perform in a culturally specific genre/style with input or guidance from community representatives — demonstrating authentic engagement beyond surface imitation
Perform in more than one genre/style context during the year — comparing the performance demands and audience relationships each context creates

modes.reason: Genre-authentic performance integrates technical skill, expressive skill, style-specific technique, and production element use into a communicative event. The audience relationship is the test: does this read as this style/genre to an informed observer?

descriptors.title: Improvise, devise and interpret
descriptors.description: improvise and devise drama, and interpret scripted drama, using elements of drama and conventions to shape and manipulate dramatic action and convey intended ideas, perspectives and/or meaning
descriptors.knowledge: Students can improvise, devise and interpret scripted drama, manipulating elements and applying conventions relevant to style/form (Y7-8). They can evaluate and refine dramatic work and develop performance skills for specific styles.
descriptors.endpoint: Students improvise and devise drama, and interpret scripted drama, using elements of drama and conventions to shape and manipulate dramatic action and convey intended ideas, perspectives and/or meaning.

nodes.label: Working within a framework to develop dramatic intention
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use a teacher-provided or self-generated framework to develop a clear dramatic intention — specifying audience, viewpoint, purpose, style and form before devising.
criteria: Student articulates a dramatic intention addressing audience, purpose and style/form
Student can explain how their devising decisions are driven by that intention
nodes.hinge_reason: At Y9-10, devising and interpretation without a clear intentional framework produces technically competent but purposeless work; the aesthetic-choice refinement in the second strand (AC9ADR10C02) depends entirely on having a clear unified intention to refine toward.

width.minimum: Student articulates a clear dramatic intention that addresses at least audience, purpose and style/form before beginning devising or interpretation work.
width.typical: Students use frameworks (stimulus material, imagery, character lists, narrative outlines) to develop drama; they consider contexts such as audiences, viewpoints, intentions, purpose and style/form when planning interpretations; they work collaboratively to devise and develop dramatic action.
wider: Students script scenes initially developed through improvisation, applying play-building techniques to refine them into coherent dramatic work

Students develop devised drama that presents a range of perspectives on an event — using non-linear structures, narrator/chorus conventions, or disruptive characters to challenge 'agreed' understandings
Students devise drama responding to an issue identified from another learning area, building purposeful interdisciplinary dramatic work

modes.reason: Require an explicit 'intention statement' before devising work begins — audience, purpose, style, key message. This is not bureaucracy; it is the analytical foundation for all subsequent refining decisions.

nodes.label: Manipulating elements and conventions to convey meaning
nodes.checkpoint: Students can select and manipulate elements of drama and conventions to shape dramatic action that conveys intended meaning — including tension, character relationships and symbolic communication.
criteria: Student makes at least three deliberate element or convention choices that serve their dramatic intention
Student can explain what each choice is doing in the drama and how it affects audience experience
Student demonstrates use of at least one convention beyond basic improvisation (e.g. symbol, subtext, non-linear structure, chorus)

width.minimum: Student makes at least three deliberate convention or element manipulation choices that serve their dramatic intention, and can explain each.
width.typical: Students convey tensions in stories, ideas, characters and relationships through manipulation of language, movement and symbol; they shape dramatic action using props, set items or digital tools; they employ multiple conventions (flashback/flash-forward, chorus, symbol, subtext) to shape meaning and audience experience.
wider: Students explore how non-linear narrative structures — presenting the same story from multiple character perspectives — affect audience experience and meaning
Students use design elements (costume, lighting, set, sound) as integral meaning-making tools, not just support materials
Students investigate conventions from Asian or other cultural dramatic traditions and apply them in their own devising, reflecting on what the conventions carry culturally

modes.reason: Students at Y9-10 need a broad repertoire of conventions to draw on; deliberately introduce and practise specific conventions (subtext, beats, chorus, mediatisation) so students can make informed rather than default choices.

descriptors.title: Rehearse and refine aesthetic choices
descriptors.description: rehearse and refine drama making deliberate aesthetic choices to unify dramatic meaning
descriptors.knowledge: Students can evaluate and refine use of elements and conventions to shape dramatic action (Y7-8). They can plan, organise and rehearse, and adjust performance based on feedback and audience response.
descriptors.endpoint: Students rehearse and refine drama, making deliberate aesthetic choices to unify dramatic meaning.

nodes.label: Deliberate aesthetic choice-making
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify the aesthetic choices operating in their drama — and articulate why each choice serves the unified dramatic meaning.
criteria: Student identifies at least three aesthetic choices in their drama
Student explains how each choice contributes to the unified dramatic meaning — not just what it does technically, but why it belongs in this work
nodes.hinge_reason: The concept of aesthetic unity — all choices serving a single coherent meaning — is what distinguishes sophisticated drama-making at this band from technically competent but unfocused work; without this frame, refining is just fixing individual problems rather than shaping a unified work.

width.minimum: Student identifies at least three aesthetic choices (elements, conventions, design) in their drama and explains how each contributes to unified meaning.
width.typical: Students evaluate how ideas, emotions and audience response can be used to refine the drama; they consider the impact of design elements (costume, prop, set, lighting, sound) on meaning and aesthetic effect; they manipulate elements and use conventions to create and manipulate actor-audience relationships.
wider: Students take on specific production roles (director, designer, stage manager) and articulate aesthetic decisions from within that role
Students evaluate how actor-audience relationship conventions (fourth wall, direct address, immersive staging) change the nature of audience experience and adjust their choices accordingly

modes.reason: Introduce 'aesthetic unity' as an explicit concept before the refinement phase; use analysis of existing works to model what it looks like, before applying the lens to students' own drama.

nodes.label: Refining through rehearsal toward unified meaning
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use the rehearsal process to strengthen and unify dramatic action — adjusting pace, staging, vocal delivery, transitions and design toward a coherent intended effect.
criteria: Student makes at least two documented refinements during rehearsal in response to evaluation
Student can explain how each refinement strengthens the unified dramatic meaning
Student evaluates how successfully the final work achieves its intention and draws at least one lesson for future practice

width.minimum: Student makes at least two documented refinements during rehearsal in response to evaluation of how well the drama achieves its intention.
width.typical: Students focus and strengthen dramatic action by manipulating pace, cues, vocal tone, physical proximity and transitions; they collaborate as directors and performers — blocking staging, directing action; they reflect and evaluate how successfully intentions and effects were achieved, and draw lessons for future practice.
wider: Students collaborate with community members or external performers in a shared production process, managing ownership, protocol and collective decision-making about aesthetic choices
Students document and analyse their refinement process — using annotated scripts, rehearsal notes or video review — to develop metacognitive awareness of their own practice

modes.reason: Refinement is the integration of all prior skills and knowledge into a cohesive artistic work. Structured post-rehearsal evaluation ('Was the intention achieved? What broke the unity?') is the essential teaching scaffold.

Refining drama across different performance contexts — class showing, external audience, community collaboration — builds richer understanding of what 'unified meaning' looks like for different audiences.

descriptors.title: Performance skills for characters
descriptors.description: develop performance skills and/or techniques to manipulate elements of drama and/or use conventions to communicate the physical and psychological aspects of roles and characters consistent with intentions
descriptors.knowledge: Students can develop performance skills relevant to selected drama styles and forms (Y7-8). They can develop vocal quality, movement skills, and use improvisation to explore character.
descriptors.endpoint: Students develop performance skills and techniques to communicate the physical and psychological aspects of roles and characters consistent with their dramatic intentions.

nodes.label: Physical and psychological character preparation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can analyse character to identify both physical and psychological dimensions, and use that analysis to ground performance choices.
criteria: Student identifies at least two physical and two psychological dimensions of a character through analysis
Student demonstrates at least one performance choice grounded in psychological analysis (not just physical imitation)
nodes.hinge_reason: The move from externally-imposed role-playing to internally-grounded character work is the key development at Y9-10; without psychological grounding, physical performance choices are decorative rather than expressive — the character lacks coherence across the full range of dramatic action.

width.minimum: Student uses text analysis or improvisation to identify at least two physical and two psychological dimensions of a character, and applies these in a short scene.
width.typical: Students use analysis of examined text and performances to provide information for exploring the implied and underlying aspects of character; they refine understanding of human behaviours and emotions using appropriate boundaries; they use character analysis to ground voice, physicality and relationship choices.
wider: Students explore how contemporary performance styles and non-realistic conventions can reshape meaning for a character from a classic text
Students investigate how comedy forms (physical comedy, satire, irony) require specific physical and psychological approaches distinct from dramatic character work

modes.reason: Use character analysis frameworks (Stanislavski objectives, given circumstances, subtext) or equivalent structured approaches before performance work; make the interior life explicit before asking students to express it physically.

nodes.label: Refining skills for style-specific and convention-based performance
nodes.checkpoint: Students can refine and adapt their performance skills for specific styles and conventions, achieving coherence between character intention and physical/vocal execution.
criteria: Student applies at least two style-specific techniques with consistency across a rehearsed piece
Student can articulate the connection between their technique choices and the character's physical and psychological dimensions

width.minimum: Student applies and refines at least two style-specific techniques across multiple rehearsal iterations, demonstrating measurable improvement in consistency.
width.typical: Students experiment with, reflect on and refine styles and conventions explored in class; they workshop comedy forms, physical theatre, non-realistic conventions or others; they refine voice through warm-ups focusing on character and delivery; they shape action using analysed conventions.
wider: Students perform the same character through two different stylistic conventions (realism and physical theatre, or naturalism and Brechtian), reflecting on how style shapes character expression

Students develop a character who must communicate both individual psychology and cultural or collective identity simultaneously — as in many First Nations, Asian or community-based dramatic traditions

modes.reason: Style-specific refinement requires iterative practice with focused feedback; each rehearsal session should target a specific technical dimension rather than running the full work.
Developing performance skills across multiple styles and conventions — including non-Western or contemporary forms — builds substantially richer expressive range.

descriptors.title: Reflect to refine dramatic practice
descriptors.description: reflect on their own and others' drama or practices to refine and inform their use of elements of drama, conventions and/or approaches to shape and sustain dramatic action
descriptors.knowledge: Students can reflect on their own and others' drama to inform choices when manipulating elements and conventions (Y7-8). They can seek, accept and respond to feedback, and develop understanding of human behaviours and emotions in performance contexts.
descriptors.endpoint: Students reflect on their own and others' drama or practices to refine and inform their use of elements of drama, conventions and approaches to shape and sustain dramatic action.

nodes.label: Analytical reflection on elements, conventions and approaches
nodes.checkpoint: Students can analyse their own and others' drama at the level of specific element, convention and approach choices — identifying what is working, what is not, and why.
criteria: Student analyses at least two specific dramatic choices with reasoning — not just description
Student's reflection distinguishes intention from effect and addresses the gap between them
nodes.hinge_reason: Reflective practice at the analytical level — not just 'what happened' but 'why this choice and what was its effect' — is the mechanism through which Y9-10 students develop independent dramatic judgment; without it, refining is reactive rather than intentional.

width.minimum: Student produces a reflection that analyses at least two specific choices (element, convention, or approach) in their own or a peer's drama, with reasoning for each assessment.
width.typical: Students compare use of conventions to explore and challenge power and oppression across performance styles; they analyse and make choices about manipulating elements and experimenting with conventions (subtext, beats) to affect meaning; they shape their use of elements and conventions to achieve intended meaning.
wider: Students write, pod-cast or video-cast a critical analysis of their own rehearsal process — documenting decisions, testing alternatives, and evaluating outcomes
Students analyse how their own dramatic practice responds to (or resists) cultural influences, naming specific choices as culturally shaped

modes.reason: Provide analytical frameworks — 'What was the intention? What choice was made? What was the effect? What would you change and why?' — to scaffold the move from descriptive to analytical reflection.

nodes.label: Using reflection to shape and refine practice
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use reflective analysis to make informed, documented refinements to their dramatic practice — demonstrating that reflection has changed specific choices.
criteria: Student documents at least one change to dramatic practice explicitly motivated by reflective analysis
Student evaluates the effect of that change on the drama's meaning or effectiveness
Student draws at least one lesson for future practice

width.minimum: Student documents at least one change to their dramatic practice that is explicitly motivated by reflective analysis.
width.typical: Students shape their use of elements, conventions and styles to achieve intended meaning or effect; they reflect on and evaluate how successfully intentions, meaning and effects were achieved; they draw lessons for future dramatic practice.
wider: Students maintain a reflective practice journal or portfolio across a substantial drama project, analysing how their thinking evolved across multiple iterations
Students engage in peer-critique sessions using a shared analytical framework, developing capacity to give and receive high-quality developmental feedback

modes.reason: Reflection-into-practice is the integration move at Y9-10: analysis informs choice, choice produces work, work is analysed again. Structured cycles of make-reflect-revise are the key pedagogical scaffold.
Building a repertoire of reflective approaches — personal journal, peer critique, video review, critical writing — gives students multiple lenses for examining their own practice.

descriptors.title: Investigate drama to challenge meaning
descriptors.description: investigate use of elements of drama, performance skills and/or conventions to communicate and/or challenge ideas, perspectives and/or meaning in drama across cultures, times, places and/or other contexts
descriptors.knowledge: Students can investigate how elements and conventions communicate meaning in drama across cultures, times and places (Y7-8). They can analyse and evaluate use of elements and conventions in drama they experience or participate in.
descriptors.endpoint: Students investigate how elements of drama, performance skills and conventions are used to communicate and/or challenge ideas, perspectives and/or meaning in drama across cultures, times, places and other contexts.

nodes.label: Drama that challenges — identifying the 'challenge' move
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify when and how drama is being used to challenge — not just communicate — ideas, perspectives or meaning, and describe the specific dramatic devices doing that work.
criteria: Student identifies at least one drama that challenges a perspective or meaning
Student names at least one specific dramatic device used to create that challenge and explains how it works
nodes.hinge_reason: The 'challenge' dimension — drama as a site of contestation, not just communication — is new at Y9-10; without students grasping how dramatic form can be used to disrupt rather than confirm, their analysis stays at the level of communication and misses the critical dimension of the descriptor.

width.minimum: Student identifies at least one example of drama that challenges a dominant perspective or meaning, and names at least one dramatic device used to create the challenge.
width.typical: Students view examples of drama from diverse styles or forms — historical, modern, from Australia and Asia — to identify how conventions are used to communicate and challenge; they identify how contemporary performance styles (mediatisation, intertextuality, physical theatre) affect meaning; they consider actor-audience relationships in different dramatic contexts.
wider: Students investigate how drama that uses satire, irony or Brechtian distancing to challenge ideas operates differently from drama that seeks to create identification and empathy
Students investigate drama from a country or region in Asia considering the social, cultural and historical context in which it challenges or affirms dominant meanings

modes.reason: Use comparative analysis: show two dramas treating the same theme, one that communicates a perspective and one that challenges it; make the distinction explicit before asking students to analyse independently.

nodes.label: Investigating conventions, context and cultural challenge across drama
nodes.checkpoint: Students can investigate how performance conventions, context and cultural position shape whether and how drama communicates or challenges — across diverse cultural, historical and contemporary examples.
criteria: Student analyses at least two drama examples from different contexts, explaining how each uses conventions to communicate or challenge
Student identifies how social, cultural or historical context shapes the drama's meaning or challenge

width.minimum: Student investigates at least two drama examples from different cultural, historical or contextual positions and analyses how each uses conventions to communicate or challenge.
width.typical: Students view examples of varied styles/forms to understand how conventions are shared and differ across styles; they consider questions of social context, cultural movement, historical influence and actor-audience relationships; they use Viewpoints-style analysis to frame their investigation.
wider: Students investigate how First Nations Australian drama that challenges colonial narratives operates — identifying the specific conventions and structural choices that make the challenge culturally and dramatically effective

Students investigate a contemporary global drama phenomenon (mediatisation, site-specific performance, immersive theatre) and analyse how it reframes the audience relationship and challenges traditional dramatic conventions

modes.reason: The depth of understanding available through wide exposure to diverse drama traditions — including contemporary, non-Western and challenging forms — is the substance of this standard.

descriptors.title: First Nations drama and identity
descriptors.description: investigate the ways that drama created and/or performed by First Nations Australians celebrates and challenges multiple perspectives of Australian identity
descriptors.knowledge: Students have investigated the diversity of drama created by First Nations Australians, considering culturally responsive approaches and ICIP rights (Y7-8). They understand that First Nations drama is diverse and requires culturally responsive engagement.
descriptors.endpoint: Students investigate the ways that drama created and/or performed by First Nations Australians celebrates and challenges multiple perspectives of Australian identity.

nodes.label: Australian identity as contested — and drama as a site of that contest
nodes.checkpoint: Students can articulate that Australian identity is multiple and contested, and identify how drama becomes a site for celebrating and challenging specific versions of that identity.
criteria: Student articulates that Australian identity is multiple and contested
Student identifies both a celebration and a challenge in a specific First Nations drama work, naming the dramatic elements involved
nodes.hinge_reason: The concept of Australian identity as plural and contested — not a settled shared story — is foundational for the critical analysis this standard demands; without it, students treat First Nations drama as 'different perspective' rather than as a challenge to the dominant frame.

width.minimum: Student identifies at least one version of Australian identity that a First Nations drama celebrates and one that it challenges, and names specific dramatic elements doing that work.
width.typical: Students investigate how and why drama practitioners work collaboratively with communities to develop and present contemporary First Nations Australian theatre; they consider how global trends in drama are influencing First Nations drama; they investigate how contemporary First Nations theatre explores and challenges histories of Australia and Australian identity.
wider: Students compare and critique how contemporary drama from different First Nations communities and non-Indigenous Australian dramatists treat the same historical or contemporary issues — examining whose version of Australian identity is being presented
Students investigate how a specific First Nations drama work has changed in reception over time — what it celebrated or challenged at first performance vs. how it is read now

modes.reason: Explicitly establish the concept of contested national identity before analysing drama; use comparative examples of how different communities tell the story of Australian identity before analysing how First Nations drama intervenes.

nodes.label: Investigating how drama celebrates and challenges — global, collaborative, contemporary
nodes.checkpoint: Students can investigate specific examples of contemporary First Nations drama, analysing how global trends, community collaboration and historical engagement shape celebration and challenge.
criteria: Student analyses at least one contemporary First Nations drama work in depth — addressing global trends, community context, or historical engagement
Student explains both what the work celebrates and what it challenges in relation to Australian identity
Student engages with cultural authority and appropriateness in their investigation

width.minimum: Student investigates at least one contemporary First Nations drama work in depth, analysing how it engages with global trends or community collaboration to celebrate or challenge Australian identity.
width.typical: Students investigate how global trends influence First Nations drama; they examine how collaborative community development processes produce drama with particular political and cultural dimensions; they compare and critique ways contemporary drama celebrates and challenges influences on Australian identity.
wider: Students investigate how a First Nations drama work navigates the tension between international festival audiences (who may consume cultural difference) and local community audiences (for whom the drama is an act of cultural assertion)

Students investigate the relationship between First Nations drama and legal or political history — land rights, sovereignty, recognition — and how specific dramatic works have been shaped by or have shaped those histories

modes.reason: The diversity of contemporary First Nations drama — in form, purpose, community context and global reach — is extensive; engagement with multiple works prevents students from treating any single work as representative.

descriptors.title: Perform to audiences with intention
descriptors.description: perform improvised, devised and/or scripted drama to audiences, using performance skills and conventions to shape the drama
descriptors.knowledge: Students can rehearse and perform drama to audiences using performance skills and conventions relevant to style and form (Y7-8). They can collect and evaluate audience feedback and reflect on how respectful relationships and empathy were applied and interpreted.
descriptors.endpoint: Students perform improvised, devised and/or scripted drama to audiences, using performance skills and conventions to shape the drama.

nodes.label: Performing with sustained intentionality
nodes.checkpoint: Students can sustain a coherent performance throughout — maintaining intentional character, vocal delivery and physical presence in alignment with unified dramatic meaning.
criteria: Student sustains performance intention — character, voice, physicality — across a complete scene or piece
Student's performance is consistent with the drama's unified meaning (does not have isolated technically good moments that contradict the whole)
nodes.hinge_reason: Sustained intentionality — performance in alignment with a unified intention across the whole work — is what distinguishes Y9-10 performance from earlier bands; without it, students can produce technically competent moments that don't cohere into a purposeful whole.

width.minimum: Student sustains performance — character, voice, physicality — across a full scene or piece with consistent intentionality.
width.typical: Students convey tensions in stories, characters, relationships and dialogue through voice, movement and symbol; they engage audiences and elicit responses; they sustain presentation in a class or stage context; they adhere to protocols when performing material connected to community ownership.
wider: Students perform in a sustained, extended context (multi-scene work, community presentation, festival showing) where stamina and consistency across a longer arc is required
Students perform devised drama created in a shared process with community members, observing protocols for collective ownership and cultural authority

modes.reason: Sustained performance coherence develops through run-through rehearsals of the whole work, not just scene-by-scene work; students need experience of performing through, not just in, a drama.

nodes.label: Evaluating performance and drawing forward
nodes.checkpoint: Students can evaluate how successfully their performance achieved its intentions and draw specific lessons for future dramatic practice.
criteria: Student evaluates their performance across at least three dimensions: intention, execution, audience effect
Student draws at least one specific lesson for future practice
Student demonstrates appropriate cultural protocols when performing material connected to community ownership or cultural knowledge

width.minimum: Student produces a performance evaluation that addresses at least three dimensions (intention, execution, audience effect) and draws at least one lesson for future practice.
width.typical: Students reflect on and evaluate how successfully intentions, meaning and effects were achieved in context; they consider use of elements, conventions, performance skills and design; they identify what can be learnt from this for future dramatic practice.
wider: Students compare their own evaluation of the performance with collected audience feedback, analysing the gap between intended and experienced meaning
Students use a structured performance review framework consistently across multiple performances, tracking their development across the year

modes.reason: Post-performance evaluation is the culminating integration of performance skills, reflective practice and dramatic intention; it closes the make-perform-reflect cycle and generates the foundation for continued development.

descriptors.title: Design to examine and communicate
descriptors.description: design and structure media arts works that examine and communicate ideas, perspectives and/or meaning
descriptors.knowledge: Students can design and structure media arts works using pre-production processes and apply media arts concepts to construct representations for specific audiences. They have applied genre codes and conventions and reflected on communicative intent. They have not yet designed works that specifically examine and communicate ideas — applying critical analysis of existing conventions to produce works that confirm or challenge them.
descriptors.endpoint: Students design and structure media arts works that examine and communicate ideas, perspectives and/or meaning using pre-production processes and deliberate application of technical and symbolic codes.

nodes.label: Critical analysis of genre conventions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can analyse how technical and symbolic codes in a specific genre, auteur or film movement communicate values, themes or ideas — and identify how those codes could be used, confirmed or challenged in original work.
criteria: Student can analyse how at least two technical and symbolic codes in a genre communicate values, themes or ideas
Student can identify how those codes could be used or challenged in original design work
nodes.hinge_reason: Critical analysis of genre conventions is the conceptual prerequisite for designing works that examine ideas — without it, production is replication rather than examination, and the 'examine' command term is not met.

width.minimum: Analyse how technical and symbolic codes in one genre communicate at least two specific values, themes or ideas, and identify how those codes could be replicated or challenged in an original work.
width.typical: Examine technical and symbolic codes in specific film, television or radio genres; analyse how codes construct stereotypical or alternative representations; identify conventions that confirm or challenge audience expectations; use pre-production processes (shot list, treatment, storyboard) to trial ideas before designing.
wider: Analyse how a specific auteur's use of technical and symbolic codes constructs a recognisable visual/audio language — and design an original work that either pays homage to or deliberately subverts that style, documenting the design decisions

Examine how the same genre conventions have been used differently in film works from different decades or cultural contexts — identifying how social forces shaped the conventions, and designing a response that positions itself in relation to that history

modes.reason: Students need a structured analytical framework: 'What values does this code communicate? Who benefits from this representation? What alternative representation would challenge it?' This reasoning chain grounds design decisions in critical analysis.

nodes.label: Pre-production design
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use pre-production tools to design and structure a media arts work — making deliberate decisions about how technical and symbolic codes will examine and communicate ideas for an intended audience.
criteria: Student produces a pre-production document for a planned media arts work
Student can explain at least three design decisions in terms of the ideas, perspectives or meaning to be examined

width.minimum: Produce a pre-production document (shot list, storyboard, shooting script, treatment or screenplay) for a planned media arts work — including at least three design decisions explicitly linked to the ideas, perspectives or meaning to be examined.
width.typical: Use pre-production processes to design and structure media arts works across two or more forms — documenting how camera work, sound, editing, mise-en-scène or media technologies will construct representations; trial ideas for different production approaches before committing; design alternative representations of the same subject.
wider: Design a media arts work using a storyboard and shooting script — then design an alternative version of the same work that challenges the representations constructed in the first version, comparing how each communicates differently to audiences

Design a social media campaign or community service announcement using detailed pre-production documentation — including target audience analysis, platform selection reasoning, and representation design rationale

modes.reason: Pre-production design discipline at Y9-10 requires sustained investment — students who use pre-production tools superficially produce works that are not designed but assembled. Thorough pre-production is the difference between examination and illustration.

descriptors.title: Produce works for/challenging audiences
descriptors.description: apply production processes and use media arts concepts to construct representations and produce media arts works that communicate ideas, perspectives and/or meaning, and confirm or challenge the expectations of specific audiences
descriptors.knowledge: Students can design media arts works using pre-production processes. They can apply genre conventions deliberately. They have not yet produced works that specifically confirm or challenge audience expectations — applying full production processes with critical awareness of how representations position audiences.
descriptors.endpoint: Students apply production processes and media arts concepts to produce media arts works that communicate ideas, perspectives and/or meaning, and confirm or challenge the expectations of specific audiences.

nodes.label: Production to confirm or challenge expectations
nodes.checkpoint: Students can apply production processes to produce a media arts work — making deliberate choices about whether to confirm or challenge genre conventions and audience expectations, and explaining how each choice serves this intent.
criteria: Student produces a media arts work making deliberate choices about genre conventions and audience expectations
Student can explain how at least two production choices confirm or challenge those expectations
nodes.hinge_reason: The ability to consciously position production choices in relation to audience expectations is the core capability of this standard — without it, production is competent craft but not critical media practice.

width.minimum: Produce one media arts work that either confirms or challenges at least two audience expectations — documenting the production choices made and explaining how each serves the intended relationship with the audience.
width.typical: Produce media arts works across forms (silent film, music video, stop motion, animation, genre film) using full production processes; use mise-en-scène, camera work, sound, editing and media technologies in genre-typical or genre-disrupting ways; apply ethical, legal and cultural safety considerations; evaluate how production choices position audiences.
wider: Produce a genre film that either conforms to or deliberately challenges the conventions of its genre — documenting the production decisions made and evaluating how each positions the audience, then producing an alternative opening or sequence that takes the opposite approach

Create multiple representations of the same person, place or concept in different media forms and for different intentions — evaluating how each medium, genre choice and audience relationship shapes the representation produced

modes.reason: Use Viewpoints questions to make the confirmation/challenge decision explicit: 'How does this camera choice confirm what the audience expects? What would happen if I did the opposite?' The reasoning behind each choice is as important as the choice.

nodes.label: Ethical and collaborative production
nodes.checkpoint: Students can apply ethical, legal and culturally safe production practices — including community collaboration approaches — throughout the production process.
criteria: Student applies at least two ethical, legal or culturally safe production practices and documents them
Student can explain how each practice shaped production decisions

width.minimum: Apply at least two ethical, legal or culturally safe production practices during a production (e.g. copyright compliance, ICIP protocol, community consultation) and document these applications.
width.typical: Apply ethical, legal and culturally safe practices throughout production; use Viewpoints questions to evaluate communicative intent during post-production; consider community collaboration protocols when representing local histories or identities; evaluate how production intentions are being communicated at each stage.
wider: Collaborate with a community (using school protocols to contact First Nations Australian or other community groups) to produce a media arts work that explores, challenges or celebrates local histories, cultures or identities — documenting the collaboration process and reflecting on how it shaped the production

Produce a media arts work on a social or cultural issue — applying full ethical, legal and cultural safety review at each production stage, and reflecting on how the issue's sensitivity shaped production decisions

modes.reason: Ethical production practice is integrated throughout the production cycle, not a separate compliance step — ensure students treat ethical decisions (community consultation, copyright, ICIP) as production decisions, not administrative requirements.

descriptors.strand: Media arts: developing practices and skills
descriptors.title: Construct representations with intention
descriptors.description: experiment with ways to construct representations that reflect ideas, perspectives and/or meaning, and/or use of media conventions, media languages and media technologies
descriptors.knowledge: Students can manipulate media languages to change meaning and develop production skills across multiple forms. They can apply genre conventions deliberately. They have not yet experimented systematically with how an auteur, genre or film movement shapes a distinctive representational language — or used target audience research to inform production.
descriptors.endpoint: Students experiment with ways to construct representations that reflect ideas, perspectives and/or meaning using media conventions, languages and technologies — informed by analysis of practitioners and target audience research.

nodes.label: Auteur, genre and representational language
nodes.checkpoint: Students can analyse how a specific media artist (auteur, social media influencer, game designer, music video director) uses technical and symbolic codes to construct a recognisable representational language — and apply this analysis to inform their own construction experiments.
criteria: Student can analyse how a media artist uses at least three technical and symbolic elements to construct a distinctive representational language
Student can apply at least one observed technique in original production work with a documented rationale
nodes.hinge_reason: Auteur/practitioner analysis is the conceptual foundation for informed experimentation — without it, production experiments are undirected, and the connection between technical choices and representational intent cannot be articulated.

width.minimum: Analyse how one media artist uses at least three technical and symbolic elements to construct a distinctive representational language, and apply one observed technique in an original production experiment.
width.typical: Examine how auteurs, genre directors, social media influencers and game designers use technical and symbolic codes to construct representations; apply findings to design and production experiments; investigate multiple practitioners and identify common and divergent approaches.
wider: Investigate a specific auteur or film movement's use of mise-en-scène, camera work, sound and editing to construct a recognisable visual language — produce an original work that pays homage to or responds to that language, documenting the design decisions

Research how a social media influencer or game designer uses technical and symbolic elements to construct audience relationships — apply findings to produce an original media arts work that builds a specific audience relationship using the same strategies

modes.reason: Use Viewpoints questions to build the analysis-to-production reasoning chain: 'How does this director's use of sound construct the audience relationship? How could I apply or subvert this in my own work?'

nodes.label: Audience research and production experimentation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can research a target audience and use findings to design and produce a media arts work — experimenting with multiple production approaches and selecting the most effective for the intended audience relationship.
criteria: Student researches a target audience and identifies at least two media conventions specific to that audience
Student uses those findings to make and document at least two production decisions

width.minimum: Research a target audience for a planned media arts work (identifying genre, platform, and representative media conventions for that audience) and use at least two findings to shape production decisions.
width.typical: Research target audiences and conventions in successful online media arts works; use research to inform design, production and post-production decisions; manipulate technical and symbolic codes to produce works for identified target audiences; experiment with multiple production approaches and select the most effective.
wider: Research target audiences and conventions in successful online media arts works — use findings to design and produce a work that deliberately constructs audience relationships, documenting at each production stage how research findings shaped decisions

Manipulate technical and symbolic codes across multiple production drafts for the same target audience — comparing how different approaches position the audience differently, and selecting the final approach with a documented justification

modes.reason: Build students' repertoire of production experimentation strategies — multiple drafts, audience comparison, approach selection. The more systematic the experimentation, the more informed the final production decisions.

descriptors.strand: Media arts: developing practices and skills
descriptors.title: Reflect to refine production choices
descriptors.description: reflect on their own or others' media arts works and/or practices to refine and inform choices they make during stages of the production process
descriptors.knowledge: Students can document and explain production choices and use Viewpoints questions to evaluate communicative intent. They have used editing software to experiment with sequences. They have not yet applied systematic reflective practice that informs refinement across all stages of production — or developed DSLR manual camera skills through reflective practice.
descriptors.endpoint: Students reflect on their own or others' media arts works and practices to refine and inform choices across stages of the production process.

nodes.label: Analytical reflection on practice
nodes.checkpoint: Students can analyse existing media arts works — examining how camera work, sound, editing, media technologies and mise-en-scène construct representations — and use this analysis to inform their own practice.
criteria: Student analyses at least three technical elements in a media arts work and explains how they construct representations
Student documents at least one analytical finding and explains how it will inform a production decision
nodes.hinge_reason: Analytical reflection is the mechanism that converts existing media arts knowledge into production improvement — without it, students produce technically competent works that are not critically informed, and the 'reflect to refine' command term is not met.

width.minimum: Analyse how at least three technical elements in an existing media arts work construct conventional or alternative representations — and document how at least one finding will inform a decision in their own production.
width.typical: Use Viewpoints questions to examine how camera work, sound, editing and mise-en-scène construct representations in a genre, auteur's work or film movement; document findings; identify which techniques to apply, subvert or challenge in original production; connect analysis to production decisions explicitly.
wider: Examine how camera work, sound, editing and mise-en-scène in a specific film movement or auteur's work construct conventional representations — then design and produce a media arts work that communicates alternative representations to audiences, documenting how each analytical finding informed each production decision

Analyse a media arts work that has been critically recognised for challenging dominant representations — identifying the specific technical and symbolic strategies used, and applying at least two strategies in original production work

modes.reason: Use Viewpoints questions as the analytical framework: 'How has camera work been manipulated to construct this representation? What would change if I used a different approach?' The reasoning chain analysis→finding→application is the core skill.

nodes.label: Reflective practice across production stages
nodes.checkpoint: Students can apply reflective practice across multiple stages of their own production — documenting decisions, evaluating against intent, and refining based on analysis.
criteria: Student documents production decisions at two or more stages of a production
Student describes at least one refinement made as a result of mid-production reflection, with an explanation of the reasoning
