width.minimum: Document production decisions at two or more stages of a production process — evaluating at each stage whether decisions are serving the intended communicative goal, and describing at least one refinement made as a result.
width.typical: Apply systematic reflective practice across pre-production, production and post-production; document and explain creative choices in relation to representations and genre codes; use editing software to experiment with sequences, applying technical codes deliberately; develop manual camera skills (ISO, shutter speed, aperture) through reflective experimentation.
wider: Use editing software to experiment systematically with multiple versions of the same sequence — applying different technical codes (filters, text, music, rhythm, pace) and comparing how each creates meaning for audiences before selecting and justifying the final approach

Develop DSLR manual camera skills through structured reflective practice — documenting ISO, shutter speed and aperture experiments across different lighting conditions, reflecting on how manual control serves intended meaning, and applying findings to original production work

modes.reason: Build reflective practice across production stages — students who only reflect at the end produce works that could have been much stronger with earlier intervention. Practise mid-production reflection as a production skill.

descriptors.title: Investigate media artists
descriptors.description: investigate the ways that media artists use media arts concepts to construct representations in media arts works and practices across cultures, times, places and/or other contexts
descriptors.knowledge: Students can compare media representations across contexts and explain how context shapes values and stereotypes. They have analysed power relationships in representations. They have not yet investigated at the level of evaluating social, cultural and ethical implications — or analysing how media platforms use data to shape audience information.
descriptors.endpoint: Students investigate how media artists use media arts concepts to construct representations across cultures, times, places and contexts — evaluating social, cultural and ethical implications and how audiences are positioned.

nodes.label: Technical and symbolic codes — ideology and positioning
nodes.checkpoint: Students can analyse how technical and symbolic codes communicate social beliefs, values and ideology — and evaluate how audiences are positioned to respond.
criteria: Student can analyse how at least three technical or symbolic codes in a media arts work communicate social beliefs or values
Student can explain how the work positions its audience to respond and whose perspectives are centred or marginalised
nodes.hinge_reason: Understanding how codes communicate ideology and position audiences is the conceptual foundation for this standard at Y9-10 — without it, subsequent evaluation of social, cultural and ethical implications has no analytical grounding.

width.minimum: Analyse how at least three technical or symbolic codes in a media arts work communicate specific social beliefs or values, and explain how the work positions its audience to respond.
width.typical: Analyse how social beliefs and values are communicated through technical and symbolic codes; evaluate how audiences are positioned by representations; investigate stereotypical representations across historical and contemporary contexts; examine how media institutions and practices influence audience perceptions.
wider: Analyse and evaluate how a specific media arts genre has communicated and evolved its ideological positioning across different historical periods — identifying the technical and symbolic code changes that correspond to social changes, and evaluating what this reveals about media's relationship to ideology

Investigate how media platforms use data to influence the breadth and depth of information provided to audiences — examining algorithmic curation through media feeds and evaluating the implications for audience agency, representation and ideological positioning

modes.reason: Students need an explicit analytical framework: 'What values does this code communicate? Who is positioned to agree with this representation? Whose perspective is marginalised?' This is the critical media literacy reasoning chain at Y9-10.

nodes.label: Social, cultural and ethical implications
nodes.checkpoint: Students can evaluate the social, cultural and ethical implications of representations in media arts works — including how representations have changed over time and how media practices perpetuate or challenge prevailing views.
criteria: Student evaluates the social, cultural or ethical implications of representations in at least one media arts context
Student can explain what prevailing views are communicated and what the implications are for the groups represented

width.minimum: Evaluate the social, cultural or ethical implications of representations in one media arts context — identifying what prevailing views are communicated and what the implications are for the groups represented.
width.typical: Analyse and evaluate how representations have changed over time (e.g. gender, multiculturalism, youth in Australian media); research audiences of specific genres and evaluate how codes engage them across media forms; examine the role of media makers in perpetuating and/or challenging prevailing views; justify creative choices in video commentary form.
wider: Analyse and evaluate the social, cultural and ethical implications of changing representations in Australian media over time — deconstructing representations of gender, multiculturalism or youth across decades, evaluating the social forces that shaped each period, and assessing the cumulative impact

Produce a video commentary justifying the technical and symbolic code choices made in an original work — explaining the social and cultural value framework behind choices, communicating alternative points of view, and evaluating how effectively the work challenges prevailing representations

modes.reason: Vary the evaluation contexts — different representation categories, different time periods, different media forms — to ensure students develop genuine evaluative range rather than applying a single analytical lens to a single context.

descriptors.title: First Nations media and identity
descriptors.description: investigate the ways First Nations Australian media artists and/or producers celebrate and challenge multiple perspectives of Australian identity through media arts
descriptors.knowledge: Students can explore how First Nations Australians use media arts to continue and revitalise cultures, and how cultural expressions change over time. They have not yet investigated specifically how First Nations Australian media artists celebrate and challenge multiple perspectives of Australian identity — or analysed how media arts provide a voice through media institutions.
descriptors.endpoint: Students investigate how First Nations Australian media artists and/or producers celebrate and challenge multiple perspectives of Australian identity through media arts, evaluating implications for community debate and audience relationships.

nodes.label: First Nations media arts and Australian identity
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how First Nations Australian media artists and/or producers explore and challenge concepts and histories of Australian identity — identifying specific media arts strategies used.
criteria: Student can identify at least two specific ways a First Nations Australian media artist uses media arts to explore or challenge Australian identity
Student can connect the media arts strategies used to the specific aspects of Australian identity being addressed
nodes.hinge_reason: Understanding how specific First Nations Australian media artists use media arts to address Australian identity is the foundation for evaluation of community debate impact — without it, subsequent analysis of celebration and challenge has no specific evidence base.

width.minimum: Investigate one First Nations Australian media artist or producer's work and explain at least two specific ways they use media arts to explore or challenge a concept or history of Australian identity.
width.typical: Investigate how First Nations Australian media artists explore and challenge concepts and histories of Australian identity; examine how media arts provide a voice through film, television and online platforms; use Viewpoints questions to analyse ideological stance; investigate specific works and practitioners (music videos, feature films, CSAs, advertisements, news reports).
wider: Compare two First Nations Australian media artists or producers who explore Australian identity through different forms (e.g. feature film and social media) — examining how each uses their form to communicate different aspects of lived experience or identity, and evaluating what each form can and cannot communicate

Investigate how First Nations Australian media arts depict issues such as The Stolen Generations, land rights, racism, family or dispossession — examining the specific media arts strategies used and evaluating the potential impact on broader community understanding

modes.reason: Use Viewpoints questions to examine ideological stance: 'What ideology or philosophical stance is taken in this work?', 'What audience relationships does it seek to create?', 'What multiple ways of understanding does it communicate?'

nodes.label: Celebrating and challenging — multiple perspectives
nodes.checkpoint: Students can compare and critique multiple First Nations Australian media artists' use of their practice to celebrate and challenge perspectives about Australian identity — evaluating implications for community debate and audience relationships.
criteria: Student can compare at least two First Nations Australian media artists' approaches to celebrating or challenging Australian identity
Student can evaluate how each approach might affect community debate or audience understanding

width.minimum: Compare how two First Nations Australian media artists celebrate or challenge Australian identity — identifying at least one shared and one different strategy, and evaluating how each might affect community understanding.
width.typical: Compare and critique multiple practitioners; analyse how media arts provide a voice for First Nations Australians through institutions and media forms; evaluate potential impact on audiences and community debate; investigate how First Nations Australians use media arts to highlight care for Country/Place and challenge community debate.
wider: Compare and critique the work of three or more First Nations Australian media artists or producers — examining how each uses their practice to communicate multiple ways of understanding an issue, and evaluating which approaches are most effective at creating productive community debate

Investigate how First Nations Australian media arts representations of Australian identity have changed across different platforms and periods — analysing what forces (institutional, technological, social) have enabled or constrained the range of perspectives expressed

modes.reason: Vary the practitioners, platforms and issues investigated — multiple artists, multiple forms, multiple issues — to ensure students develop a genuinely diverse understanding of First Nations Australian media arts practice, not a single representative example.

descriptors.title: Present and distribute with planning
descriptors.description: present media arts works to audiences and plan approaches for creating relationships with audiences if/when media arts works are distributed in selected personal, community and/or institutional contexts using responsible media practice
descriptors.knowledge: Students can present media arts works in informal and formal settings applying responsible media practices. They can reflect on how different audiences receive the same work. They have not yet planned distribution strategies, investigated classification systems, or engaged with government regulation, self-regulation and institutional media producer relationships.
descriptors.endpoint: Students present media arts works to audiences and plan approaches for creating audience relationships in personal, community and/or institutional distribution contexts using responsible media practice.

nodes.label: Distribution planning and audience relationships
nodes.checkpoint: Students can plan a distribution approach for a media arts work — identifying the target audience, platform, and strategies for creating audience relationships in that distribution context.
criteria: Student can identify a target audience, platform, and at least two audience relationship strategies for a planned distribution
Student can explain how the platform choice serves the intended audience relationship
nodes.hinge_reason: Distribution planning is prerequisite to actual distribution — without a plan that addresses audience relationships, responsible media practice is applied reactively rather than strategically, and the 'plan approaches' command term is not met.

width.minimum: Plan a distribution approach for a media arts work — identifying one platform, the target audience, and at least two strategies for creating audience relationships in that context.
width.typical: Plan distribution approaches across personal, community and institutional contexts; research how different audiences relate to media arts works and how those relationships inform production and distribution; investigate how intended audiences and the communities they form influence the creation of new works.
wider: Investigate the relationships created between intended audiences and media arts works — including the communities formed between audience members — and use this research to plan a distribution strategy that deliberately cultivates specific audience relationships

Plan distribution for a media arts work across two different contexts (e.g. school LMS and community event) — comparing how each context creates different audience relationships and evaluating which best serves the work's purpose

modes.reason: Use structured planning: 'Who is the intended audience? How does this platform create or limit the relationships I want? What responsible practice requirements apply in this context?' Distribution decisions are relationship decisions.

nodes.label: Regulatory and ethical frameworks
nodes.checkpoint: Students can investigate classification systems and regulatory frameworks and apply relevant requirements to production and distribution decisions.
criteria: Student can identify at least one classification or regulatory requirement relevant to their distribution context
Student can explain how that requirement shapes specific production or distribution decisions

width.minimum: Identify one classification or regulatory requirement relevant to a planned distribution (e.g. Australia's classification system for one media platform) and explain how it affects production or distribution decisions.
width.typical: Research Australia's classification system across platforms; investigate differences between government regulation and self-regulation; apply classification thinking to production decisions; produce guidelines for ethical online conduct; apply ICIP rights and copyright requirements to distribution.
wider: Investigate Australia's classification system across different media platforms — analysing the impact of classification requirements on producers and audiences, and applying classification analysis to decisions made in their own production and distribution process

Research differences between government regulation and self-regulation in media production and distribution — comparing how different media producers (sole digital, multi-platform, cross-media, public and private sector) develop audience relationships, and applying findings to plan distribution of original work

modes.reason: Regulatory and ethical frameworks are integrated into distribution decision-making — support students in treating classification, ICIP rights and copyright as distribution design considerations, not external compliance requirements added at the end.

Vary the regulatory and ethical frameworks investigated — classification, ICIP, copyright, government vs self-regulation, platform-specific safety — to build genuine range across the full spectrum of responsible distribution practice.

descriptors.title: Interpret music in styles using style-specific techniques
descriptors.description: interpret music in a variety of forms and styles, manipulating the elements of music and/or compositional devices, and using style-specific vocal/instrumental techniques to communicate ideas, perspectives and/or meaning
descriptors.knowledge: Students have manipulated elements and used compositional devices to communicate ideas (AC9AMU8C01/C02 — Y7-8). They can compose for specific forms, use style-specific devices and notate/document work. The Y9-10 step adds: style-specific vocal/instrumental techniques as a distinct requirement, and accuracy and fluency as explicit performance goals alongside communicative intent.
descriptors.endpoint: Students interpret music in a variety of forms and styles using style-specific vocal/instrumental techniques and compositional devices, demonstrating accuracy, fluency and stylistic understanding in performance.

nodes.label: Identifying stylistic conventions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify the stylistic conventions relevant to music they are learning — including characteristic elements, devices and performance techniques.
criteria: Can identify at least three stylistic conventions relevant to a piece being prepared
Can cite at least one source (composer notes, performer interview, analysis) for each convention identified
nodes.hinge_reason: Applying style-specific techniques without understanding the underlying conventions reduces performance to imitation rather than interpretation. Students who can identify and explain conventions can make deliberate interpretive choices; those who cannot default to their habitual performance approach regardless of style. This underpins all interpretive decisions in the remainder of the standard.

width.minimum: Identify at least three stylistic conventions in one piece of music (e.g. a characteristic rhythmic pattern, a specific dynamic approach, and a typical structural device) from composer, performer or analytical sources.
width.typical: Identify stylistic conventions across multiple pieces and styles using multiple sources (composer notes, performer interviews, analytical commentaries); describe how conventions function in the music; plan how to apply them in performance.
wider: Compare stylistic conventions across two related styles (e.g. classical vs romantic, blues vs jazz) — identify which conventions are shared and which are distinct
Research a specific style's conventions through multiple sources (recordings, interviews, music analysis) and build a reference document for use in rehearsal

modes.reason: Make convention identification systematic before application. For each piece being prepared: identify three conventions, find at least two sources that confirm or complicate them, then map planned applications in specific sections of the score. Analysis before performance.

nodes.label: Applying style-specific techniques for accuracy and fluency
nodes.checkpoint: Students can apply style-specific vocal/instrumental techniques with developing accuracy and fluency, and monitor their own performance against stylistic expectations.
criteria: Applies at least two style-specific techniques with recognisable accuracy in performance
Can describe how each technique serves the style's conventions and communicative goals

width.minimum: Apply at least two style-specific techniques in rehearsal; use listening (own recordings or comparison recordings) to monitor accuracy.
width.typical: Apply style-specific techniques across all relevant aspects of performance — articulation, tone production, rhythmic conventions, ornaments, dynamic conventions; develop stamina and control across the full performance; use recordings and comparison listening to refine accuracy.
wider: Compare performance of the same piece at the start and end of a rehearsal period — document specific technique improvements and identify remaining gaps
Analyse how another performer applies the same style-specific techniques — identify what they do well and develop specific practice strategies to match or adapt

modes.reason: Style-specific technique development requires consistent, targeted repetition. The consolidation investment is in maintaining technique focus across the full rehearsal period — not just in initial learning — so that techniques are maintained under performance conditions, not just in isolated practice.

nodes.label: Performance program with coherent theme or style
nodes.checkpoint: Students can select, interpret and prepare a performance program around a specific theme, style or the work of a composer/performer.
criteria: Selects at least two pieces that cohere around a stated theme, style or composer
Can explain how each piece contributes to the program's overall communicative intention

width.minimum: Select two or more pieces for a thematic or stylistic program; describe how the pieces connect to the theme or style.
width.typical: Select, interpret and practise a performance program around a social/historical theme, music style or composer/performer's work; ensure all pieces in the program cohere around the theme; provide programme information for audiences.
wider: Research the theme or composer's context in depth and use findings to inform specific performance decisions — connect historical or social context to interpretive choices
Present the program with written programme notes for each piece that connect the interpretation to the theme, style or composer's context

modes.reason: Program-building integrates stylistic knowledge, interpretive decision-making, and performance preparation into a coherent artistic statement. The teaching investment is in helping students see the program as a whole, not as individual pieces — how does the sequence communicate the theme?

descriptors.title: Compose using style-specific devices
descriptors.description: compose music, manipulating and combining elements of music and compositional devices relevant to chosen styles and/or forms to communicate ideas, perspectives and/or meaning and notate, document and/or record the music
descriptors.knowledge: Students have composed music using elements and compositional devices to communicate ideas, including for collaborative and cross-curricular purposes (AC9AMU8C01/C02 — Y7-8). The Y9-10 step requires style-specific compositional devices as distinct knowledge, application of aural understanding of key and tonality, and evaluating how context affects audience response.
descriptors.endpoint: Students compose music using style-specific elements, devices and forms to communicate ideas, perspectives and/or meaning, notating, documenting or recording the work.

nodes.label: Aural understanding of key and tonality
nodes.checkpoint: Students can apply an aural understanding of key and tonality when improvising or composing — making tonality-conscious decisions about pitch, harmony and melodic direction.
criteria: Composes or improvises a passage with a recognisable tonal centre
Makes at least one deliberate tonal choice (e.g. avoiding an unstable pitch on a strong beat, or using a characteristic scale pattern from the style)
nodes.hinge_reason: Aural understanding of tonality is foundational to style-specific composition — virtually all Western and many non-Western compositional devices are grounded in key and tonal relationships. Students who compose without tonal awareness produce pitch sequences that conflict with their harmonic intentions. This blocks access to chord progressions, melodic development and style-specific harmonic devices.

width.minimum: Compose or improvise a short passage that demonstrates awareness of key — beginning and ending on stable pitches, with recognisable tonal centre.
width.typical: Apply aural understanding of key and tonality across composition and improvisation — choosing pitches and harmonic progressions that serve tonal coherence; making deliberate tonal choices for expressive effect (e.g. modulation, unexpected chord); recognising and using characteristic scale patterns from the chosen style.
wider: Compose in two or more tonal contexts (e.g. major and minor, or a modal scale and major) — describe how the tonal quality changes the emotional effect
Improvise over a chord progression and adjust pitch choices in response to the harmonies heard — practise aural tracking of tonal centre

modes.reason: Aural tonality understanding is built through repeated listening and singing of scale patterns, common progressions and characteristic melodic movements in the chosen style. Singing before playing or notating keeps the aural foundation primary rather than theoretical.

nodes.label: Style-specific compositional devices
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and apply compositional devices specific to a chosen style (e.g. hooks, riffs, ostinatos, specific chord progressions, characteristic rhythmic patterns) to develop and shape a composition.
criteria: Applies at least two style-specific compositional devices in an original composition
Can identify how each device is characteristic of the style by citing at least one existing example

width.minimum: Apply at least two style-specific devices in a composition; explain how each device is characteristic of the style.
width.typical: Use style-specific compositional devices to develop compositions — hooks, riffs, ostinatos, characteristic progressions, style-specific forms; analyse how these devices are used in existing works and apply findings in original compositions; experiment with ways to combine and manipulate elements using these devices.
wider: Analyse the compositional devices in two or three works in the chosen style and use the findings to compose a new piece — document the analytical process and the compositional decisions it informed
Re-arrange an existing piece in a contrasting style by substituting the original style's devices with the new style's equivalents — compare the effect

modes.reason: Style-specific device application is strongest when grounded in multiple examples from the style. Listening analytically to several works before composing — rather than applying devices from memory or instruction — builds the pattern recognition that makes device use feel natural and stylistically authentic.

nodes.label: Context, audience and compositional purpose
nodes.checkpoint: Students can evaluate how different traditions, styles or contexts affect audience response and use this understanding to compose music designed for a specific audience or purpose.
criteria: Composes a piece with a stated audience or purpose
Can describe at least two specific compositional choices made to serve that audience or purpose, and evaluate whether they succeeded

width.minimum: Compose a piece with a specific audience or purpose in mind; describe at least two compositional choices made to serve that audience or purpose.
width.typical: Evaluate how context and style affect audience response; use this analysis to make deliberate compositional choices (instrumentation, dynamics, structure, style); compose for specific purposes — film/game music, social or historical themes, collaborative song cycles; notate, document or record the completed work.
wider: Compose music for a video game or film sequence — document how each compositional decision serves the narrative or interactive context, and evaluate whether the music achieves its intended effect
Compose a song cycle or set of related pieces exploring a social or historical theme — analyse how the chosen style's conventions carry the theme across the full cycle

modes.reason: Audience-conscious composition integrates tonal understanding, style-specific device knowledge and contextual awareness into a complete compositional act with stated purpose. The teaching investment is in helping students move from 'I composed a piece' to 'I composed this piece for this reason and these choices serve that purpose.'

descriptors.title: Develop, practise and refine aural and instrumental skills
descriptors.description: develop, practise and refine listening/aural skills and style-specific vocal/instrumental skills
descriptors.knowledge: Students have developed ensemble listening skills, vocal and instrumental techniques for expressive effect, and used digital tools for skill development (AC9AMU8D01 — Y7-8). They can make real-time ensemble adjustments and monitor technique using recordings. The Y9-10 step adds: identifying challenging sections and building stamina, mapping and realising dynamic interpretations, and developing technical and expressive facility and control at a higher level.
descriptors.endpoint: Students develop, practise and refine listening/aural skills and style-specific vocal/instrumental skills, demonstrating increasing technical and expressive facility and control.

nodes.label: Identifying challenges and building stamina
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify the technically or musically challenging sections in music they are learning, develop targeted strategies for those sections, and build the stamina to perform the whole work.
criteria: Can identify at least two technically or musically challenging sections in a piece being prepared
Has applied a targeted strategy for each and can describe what they tried and what changed
nodes.hinge_reason: Self-directed practice — identifying challenges and developing strategies without teacher direction — is the foundational skill of independent musicianship. Students who cannot identify and address their own technical weaknesses remain permanently dependent on teacher diagnosis. This is the defining difference between a student who improves in teacher-led rehearsal and one who improves between sessions.

width.minimum: Identify at least two challenging sections in a piece being prepared; develop and apply a different targeted strategy for each.
width.typical: Systematically identify challenges across a piece — technical challenges (speed, range, coordination), musical challenges (expressive nuance, stylistic conventions), and stamina challenges (maintaining quality across the full work); develop and apply targeted practice strategies for each; monitor progress and adjust strategies as needed.
wider: Document a practice log over a rehearsal period — record challenges identified, strategies tried, and progress observed; use the log to inform subsequent practice
Focus specifically on stamina: identify where quality drops across a full-length performance and develop conditioning strategies targeted at those points

modes.reason: Build the diagnostic habit explicitly: before each practice session, students identify one specific challenge to work on, one strategy to try, and how they will know if it worked. After the session, brief reflection: 'Did the strategy work? What did you discover?' This moves practice from running-through to deliberate improvement.

nodes.label: Ensemble skills and collaborative listening
nodes.checkpoint: Students can work collaboratively to develop ensemble skills — listening carefully to establish and maintain balance, intonation and blend across parts.
criteria: Demonstrates at least one real-time ensemble adjustment (not prompted by teacher) during collaborative performance
Can describe what they heard and how they adjusted in response

width.minimum: Demonstrate at least one real-time ensemble adjustment (balance, intonation or blend) made in response to listening to other parts; describe what was heard and how the adjustment was made.
width.typical: Work collaboratively in ensemble contexts to develop balance, intonation and blend — listen for specific parts, adjust dynamics and tuning in real time, respond to other performers' expressive choices; compare ensemble sound across different configurations (duo, trio, larger ensemble).
wider: Record an ensemble rehearsal, listen back together and identify three specific moments where balance or intonation was an issue — develop targeted strategies for each and re-record
Compare ensemble challenges across different ensemble sizes (duo vs quartet vs larger group) — describe how listening demands change with ensemble size

modes.reason: Ensemble listening at Y9-10 requires the individual performance skills to be sufficiently fluent that full attention can go to the group sound. Consolidation here means structured ensemble rehearsal formats that explicitly ask students to monitor specific aspects (balance this rehearsal, intonation next rehearsal) rather than general ensemble playing.

nodes.label: Mapping and realising a dynamic interpretation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can map a planned dynamic interpretation for a piece (identifying loudest and softest points, shaping dynamic arcs) and practise to realise the plan in performance.
criteria: Produces a dynamic interpretation plan for a section or full piece
Can compare a recording of the performance against the plan and describe where the plan was realised and where it was not

width.minimum: Map the dynamic plan for one section of a piece — identify the loudest and softest points and the shape between them; practise to realise the plan and compare a recording with the intended plan.
width.typical: Map a full dynamic interpretation plan for a complete piece — analyse another performance for comparison, identify where the plan differs from default, practise to realise the plan, compare before/after recordings and evaluate the degree of realisation.
wider: Compare dynamic interpretations of the same piece by two different performers — describe how each shapes the dynamic arc differently and what each interpretation communicates
Map a planned interpretation, realise it in performance, then try a contrasting interpretation — compare which communicates the music more effectively and justify the preference

modes.reason: Dynamic mapping makes an interpretive plan visible and testable. The teaching investment is in establishing the habit: plan the interpretation before rehearsing it, then use recording to evaluate the degree to which the plan was realised. This creates a feedback loop between intention and execution that builds expressive control.

descriptors.title: Reflect on own and others' music to inform choices
descriptors.description: use listening, aural skills and understanding of the information provided in scores, charts or lead-sheets to develop interpretations and reflect on the practices of others to inform their own
descriptors.knowledge: Students have developed aural skills for tuning/intonation and used recordings and performance comparisons to develop interpretations (AC9AMU8D02 — Y7-8). They can read from scores and lead-sheets during performance. The Y9-10 step requires using focused listening and aural/memory skills to identify, sing/play and notate musical ideas for future use, and developing real-time intonation skills.
descriptors.endpoint: Students use listening, aural skills and score/chart/lead-sheet information to develop interpretations, and reflect on the practices of others to inform their own compositions and performances.

nodes.label: Developing interpretations from scores and listening
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use both score/chart/lead-sheet information and listening to develop a personal interpretation — identifying what the notation specifies, what it leaves open, and how listening to other performances informs their choices.
criteria: Can distinguish between score-specified and performer-decided aspects of an interpretation
Has a documented interpretive decision for at least two open aspects, each with a stated reason
nodes.hinge_reason: Understanding that scores specify some things and leave others to the performer is the conceptual foundation of music interpretation. Students who treat every marking as fixed cannot develop an interpretation; those who ignore notation produce performances that disregard the composer's intentions. The interplay between what is specified and what is open is where interpretation lives.

width.minimum: Identify at least two interpretive decisions for a piece: one specified by the score/chart and one left open; explain how they decided on the open decision.
width.typical: Use scores, charts and lead-sheets alongside listening to multiple recordings to develop a documented personal interpretation; identify what the notation specifies (pitches, rhythms, dynamics markings) vs what it leaves to the performer (articulation nuance, tempo flexibility, expression); explain choices with reference to both score and listening.
wider: Analyse three recordings of the same piece — document the specific interpretive differences in each and use the analysis to develop a personal interpretation that draws on the strengths of all three
Compare how much interpretive freedom is available in different notation formats (a highly prescriptive score vs a lead-sheet vs a chord chart) — discuss how each format shapes the performer's role

modes.reason: Make the specification/interpretation distinction explicit for each piece studied. Use a two-column annotation: 'What the score specifies' vs 'What I decide.' For open decisions, require at least one listening reference. This makes the interpretive process visible and accountable.

nodes.label: Aural and memory skills for capturing musical ideas
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use focused listening and aural/memory skills to identify, sing or play, and notate or document musical ideas (pitch patterns, intervals, chord progressions) for future use in composition or performance.
criteria: Can identify and notate or record at least one musical idea from listening with sufficient accuracy to reproduce it
Has used at least one captured idea deliberately in a subsequent composition or improvisation

width.minimum: Identify and notate or record at least one musical idea heard during listening (a melodic motif, a chord progression, or a rhythmic pattern) with sufficient accuracy to reproduce it later.
width.typical: Use focused listening to build a personal vocabulary of musical ideas — identifying characteristic pitch patterns, intervals and chord progressions in diverse styles; singing or playing back what is heard; documenting using notation or recording; using captured ideas as raw material for composition or improvisation.
wider: Transcribe a short melody or chord progression by ear, document the process, and use the transcription as the basis for a composition or arrangement
Develop a personal resource of captured musical ideas from multiple styles — organise them by type (melodic, harmonic, rhythmic) and use them deliberately in an original composition

modes.reason: A personal musical vocabulary built through listening is a composing resource that no technique exercise can substitute for. The habit of capturing interesting musical ideas when encountered — rather than passively hearing them — builds the compositional raw material that makes original work richer.

nodes.label: Real-time intonation in performance
nodes.checkpoint: Students can monitor and adjust intonation in real time during ensemble performance, demonstrating developing ability to hear and correct pitch discrepancies without stopping.
criteria: Demonstrates at least one real-time intonation adjustment during ensemble performance
Can describe the aural reference they used to detect and correct the intonation issue

width.minimum: Demonstrate at least one real-time intonation adjustment during ensemble performance; describe what they heard and how they adjusted.
width.typical: Develop and refine real-time intonation skills across ensemble contexts — hearing pitch discrepancies while playing, adjusting immediately, using aural reference points (root of chord, unison pitch) to calibrate; compare real-time adjustment vs stopping and correcting.
wider: Work in a small ensemble specifically on intonation awareness — use slow-tempo practice, tuning drones and unison passages to develop aural sensitivity before applying it in full tempo performance
Develop a personal practice routine for intonation — identify consistent problem pitches or intervals, practise targeted exercises and track improvement through recording comparison

modes.reason: Real-time intonation requires aural sensitivity that is developed through sustained, focused practice — not episodic attention. The consolidation investment is in making intonation awareness a consistent rehearsal focus rather than an occasional correction, so that the aural monitoring becomes automatic rather than deliberate.

descriptors.title: Investigate composers' and performers' use of elements across cultures and times
descriptors.description: investigate and analyse ways that composers and/or performers use the elements of music, compositional devices and/or vocal and instrumental techniques across a range of cultures, times and/or other contexts
descriptors.knowledge: Students have explored how elements of music are combined across cultures and contexts and evaluated personal responses using music terminology (AC9AMU8E01 — Y7-8). They can describe how structural features create effects. The Y9-10 step shifts from exploration to investigation and analysis — specifically examining how composers/performers use elements to influence emotional response, communicate identity, and respond to social and historical contexts.
descriptors.endpoint: Students investigate and analyse ways composers and/or performers use elements of music, compositional devices and/or vocal/instrumental techniques across a range of cultures, times and contexts.

nodes.label: Analysing how elements and devices evoke response
nodes.checkpoint: Students can analyse how a composer or performer uses specific elements and compositional devices to structure a work or evoke a particular emotional response.
criteria: Can identify at least two specific techniques or devices in a piece under analysis
Can explain how each contributes to a specific emotional or communicative effect, with musical reasoning
nodes.hinge_reason: The move from 'describing' to 'analysing' — connecting specific musical choices to specific effects with evidence — is the defining cognitive step of Y9-10 Exploring and Responding. Students who describe without analysis cannot access the investigation required by the descriptor, and cannot meet the demands of senior music analytical writing.

width.minimum: Analyse one piece in depth — identify at least two specific techniques or devices used and explain how each contributes to a particular emotional response.
width.typical: Investigate how composers and performers use elements and devices to structure compositions and evoke emotional responses — examining instrumentation choices, dynamic manipulation, structural devices, expressive techniques; connecting specific musical choices to their emotional and communicative effects; using Viewpoints to guide analysis.
wider: Compare how two composers from different times or cultures use elements to evoke a similar emotional response — analyse what is similar in their approach and what is culturally or historically specific
Use Viewpoints to ask how technology has changed music styles, composition practices, audiences and the music industry — trace one specific technology's influence on compositional choices

modes.reason: Build the analysis habit with an explicit evidence-to-claim structure: 'The composer uses [specific technique] at [specific moment] which creates [specific effect] because [musical reasoning].' The move from observation to analytical claim to musical reasoning is the progression to make explicit. Viewpoints questions provide a useful scaffold.

nodes.label: Music in times of conflict, change and social context
nodes.checkpoint: Students can investigate how music is used in times of conflict and social change — analysing what compositional and performative choices carry political, social or historical messages.
criteria: Can identify the social or historical context of a piece of music and connect it to specific compositional choices
Can analyse how those choices carry the work's social or political message, with musical evidence

width.minimum: Investigate one piece of music connected to a specific historical or social context; analyse at least two compositional choices that carry the work's message.
width.typical: Compare how people in a range of times, places and contexts have used music in times of conflict and change — examining how specific compositional and performative choices carry political or social messages; investigating why music might be described as 'experimental' in its response to social context; discussing how music influences personal and social identity.
wider: Investigate how music used in two different historical or political conflicts uses similar or different compositional strategies to carry its message — compare the musical choices and their social contexts
Analyse how music influences personal or social identity — use this analysis to inform the creation of a piece designed to communicate a specific social or community message

modes.reason: Musical responses to conflict and social change span many different historical and cultural contexts — each adds a new example of how the same musical purpose (communicating protest, grief, solidarity) is realised through different compositional choices. Breadth of examples is what enables genuine analytical comparison.

nodes.label: Experimental music and sound installations
nodes.checkpoint: Students can investigate why music might be described as 'experimental' and analyse how elements of music are manipulated in sound designs for installations or site-specific artworks.
criteria: Can explain why a piece might be described as experimental with at least two musical reasons
Can describe how at least one element of music is manipulated in an unusual or context-specific way

width.minimum: Identify at least two reasons why a specific piece of music might be described as experimental; describe how at least one element of music is manipulated in an unusual way.
width.typical: Investigate the concept of experimental music — how composers combine techniques from different cultural or historical contexts, how elements are manipulated in installations or site-specific works, how the space and physical context shape the music; discuss what distinguishes experimental music from conventional practice and what it aims to achieve.
wider: Investigate how a specific experimental composer combines techniques from two or more cultural or historical traditions — describe what personal style emerges and what makes it distinct from each source tradition
Investigate how elements of music are manipulated in a sound installation — analyse how the physical space, listener movement and context shape the musical experience

modes.reason: Experimental music challenges students' assumptions about what music is and does. Guided questioning — 'Why do you think this was made this way?', 'What is the composer trying to achieve that conventional approaches could not?', 'What does the space add to the music?' — builds the analytical flexibility to engage with unfamiliar sonic contexts.

descriptors.title: First Nations Australians celebrating and challenging Australian identity
descriptors.description: investigate ways that First Nations Australian performers and composers are celebrating and/or challenging multiple perspectives of Australian identity
descriptors.knowledge: Students have explored how First Nations Australians use music to continue and revitalise culture — including diverse contemporary styles, language revitalisation, and cultural knowledge-sharing in performance (AC9AMU8E02 — Y7-8). The Y9-10 step specifically concerns Australian national identity — how First Nations Australian artists engage with, celebrate and challenge perspectives on what Australia is and means.
descriptors.endpoint: Students investigate ways First Nations Australian performers and composers celebrate and/or challenge multiple perspectives of Australian identity, evaluating innovations and the motivations behind music that advocates for social change.

nodes.label: Contributing to contemporary Australian music
nodes.checkpoint: Students can evaluate innovations in the ways First Nations Australian composers and performers are contributing to Australian contemporary music, including inter-cultural collaborations.
criteria: Can identify at least one innovative contribution by a First Nations Australian artist to contemporary Australian music
Can describe what makes the contribution innovative and how it relates to First Nations Australian identity or perspective

width.minimum: Identify at least one First Nations Australian artist whose work makes an innovative contribution to contemporary Australian music; describe what is innovative about their contribution.
width.typical: Investigate innovations across a range of First Nations Australian contemporary music contributions — artists working in orchestral, chamber, pop, hip-hop, country, and electronic contexts; inter-cultural collaborations that draw on First Nations Australian and non-Indigenous traditions; evaluate what each contributes to Australian contemporary music and what makes each innovative.
wider: Investigate a specific inter-cultural collaboration between a First Nations Australian artist and a non-Indigenous artist or ensemble — describe what each tradition contributes, what is new in the collaboration, and how each artist has talked about the process
Compare how two or three First Nations Australian artists in different genres each contribute to Australian contemporary music — what does each do that no other tradition could?

modes.reason: The breadth of First Nations Australian contributions to contemporary Australian music is the point — students who only encounter one or two examples cannot develop a picture of the full scope of these contributions. Each new genre or collaboration context reveals a different dimension of what First Nations Australian artists bring to Australian contemporary music.

nodes.label: Music that advocates, educates and challenges
nodes.checkpoint: Students can investigate and evaluate the intentions of First Nations Australian songwriters, composers and performers who use music to share knowledge, educate, protest or advocate for change.
criteria: Can identify the advocacy purpose of a First Nations Australian music work
Can analyse at least two compositional choices that carry that purpose, and evaluate their effectiveness with musical reasoning
nodes.hinge_reason: Evaluating intentionality — understanding that artistic choices in advocacy music are purposeful and can be assessed for effectiveness — is the critical analytical step here. Students who can only identify the message without analysing how the music carries it remain at a surface engagement level. The ability to connect compositional choices to advocacy purposes is the analytical skill that distinguishes Y9-10 Exploring and Responding.

width.minimum: Investigate one piece of music by a First Nations Australian artist that advocates for a specific cause or challenges a perspective on Australian identity; identify the intended message and at least two compositional choices that carry it.
width.typical: Investigate how First Nations Australian songwriters and performers use music to share knowledge, educate, protest, advocate for change, or express opinions — including music challenging action on climate change, environmental protection, social justice and racism; evaluate the intentions and effectiveness of specific works; discuss how genre and style choices affect the reach and impact of the music.
wider: Evaluate the effectiveness of a specific advocacy work — does the music achieve its stated purpose? What compositional choices help? What might be done differently?
Compare two pieces with similar advocacy aims but different stylistic approaches — which is more effective for which audience, and why?

modes.reason: Build an evaluation framework for advocacy music: 'What is the intended message? Who is the intended audience? Which musical choices serve that message for that audience? How effective are those choices, and what evidence supports that evaluation?' This connects musical analysis to purpose and audience — the two dimensions that make advocacy music analytically interesting.

nodes.label: Mapping First Nations Australian music geographically
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use an annotated map of First Nations Australian language groups to identify where specific composers and performers are working and connect their music to their cultural and geographic context.
criteria: Can locate at least two First Nations Australian artists on a language group map
Can describe how each artist's work connects to their Country/Place or cultural context

width.minimum: Locate at least two First Nations Australian artists on a language group map; describe how each artist's work connects to their Country/Place or language group.
width.typical: Use and annotate a map of First Nations Australian language groups to identify where composers and performers are working; research and present descriptions of specific artists' music and its cultural and geographic context; make connections between Country/Place, language group and musical practice.
wider: Compare two First Nations Australian artists from different regions and language groups — how does the specificity of their Country/Place shape their music differently?
Research a First Nations Australian artist whose work directly references their language group or Country/Place — investigate how the specific geographic and cultural context is present in the music

modes.reason: Geographic mapping integrates the understanding of music as culturally and geographically situated with the investigation of specific artists and their work. The map makes visible the diversity of First Nations Australian cultures that the music represents — and challenges any residual assumption that First Nations Australian music is a single tradition from a single place.

descriptors.title: Rehearse and present planned performances
descriptors.description: rehearse and present planned performances in a range of physical and/or virtual spaces
descriptors.knowledge: Students can perform in a range of forms in informal and formal settings, use peer feedback systematically, and perform via digital platforms (AC9AMU8P01 — Y7-8). They can adapt performance decisions to context. The Y9-10 step adds: performing in a range of physical and virtual spaces as a distinct requirement, recording and evaluating systematically, and performing own compositions with accompanying scores or visual material.
descriptors.endpoint: Students rehearse and present planned performances in a range of physical and/or virtual spaces, recording and evaluating performances using digital tools, and reflecting on personal and audience responses.

nodes.label: Planning performances for specific spaces
nodes.checkpoint: Students can plan and adapt performances for specific physical and virtual spaces — making decisions about staging, presentation format and audience interaction suited to each context.
criteria: Can identify at least two performance decisions that are specific to the space or platform chosen
Adapts at least one aspect of the performance (staging, introduction, or format) in response to the specific context

width.minimum: Plan a performance for at least one specific space (physical or virtual); identify at least two decisions that are specific to that space.
width.typical: Plan and present performances in multiple physical and/or virtual spaces — making context-specific decisions about staging, introduction format, audience interaction, audio/visual requirements; compare how performing in different spaces (classroom, concert hall, assembly, online platform) changes the performance decisions.
wider: Present the same performance in both a physical and a virtual space — compare how the audience interaction, staging and performance decisions differ between the two contexts
Research the specific technical requirements of a venue or platform before performing — use the research to inform preparation decisions

modes.reason: Physical and virtual performance contexts each impose genuinely different demands. Students who have only ever performed in one context default to its conventions when placed in another. Each new performance context encountered builds a more flexible and adaptive approach to performance planning.

nodes.label: Recording, evaluating and improving across performances
nodes.checkpoint: Students can record multiple performances, evaluate them systematically using digital tools, and identify specific improvements made between performances.
criteria: Compares at least two recordings of the same piece and identifies at least one specific improvement and one remaining area for development
Can explain what drove the improvement (what they practised or changed)
nodes.hinge_reason: Systematic self-evaluation using recordings — identifying specific changes between performances rather than vague impressions — is the metacognitive practice that drives independent musical improvement. Students who cannot evaluate their own recordings specifically remain dependent on teacher diagnosis. This is the primary skill that distinguishes students who continue to improve without regular teacher instruction from those who plateau.

width.minimum: Record at least two performances of the same piece at different stages; compare them and identify at least one specific improvement and one remaining area for development.
width.typical: Use digital tools to record and systematically evaluate multiple performances — comparing before/after recordings; identifying specific improvements in technique, expression, intonation and stylistic accuracy; documenting what drove improvements; reflecting on personal responses to the performances.
wider: Build a performance portfolio of recordings with written evaluations for each — trace the arc of development across the portfolio and identify the most significant improvements
Evaluate multiple performances from the perspective of both performer and audience — describe how each perspective reveals different aspects of the performance

modes.reason: Build a structured recording evaluation protocol: listen once for overall impression, once for technique, once for expression, once for stylistic accuracy. After each focused listen, document one specific observation. The structure prevents students from listening generally and concluding 'it was good/bad' without specific evidence.

nodes.label: Performing own compositions with contextual material
nodes.checkpoint: Students can perform their own compositions and reflect on personal and audience responses — presenting scores, programme notes or visual material that support audience understanding.
criteria: Performs an original composition with contextual information for the audience
Reflects on at least one aspect of personal or audience response and connects it to a future compositional or performance decision

width.minimum: Present a performance of an original composition with at least brief contextual information (a title, a description of the piece's intention, or a programme note); reflect on one aspect of the audience's or their own response.
width.typical: Perform original compositions with accompanying scores or visual material; provide programme notes that explain the compositional intention and choices; present in both physical and virtual contexts where possible; compare personal response to the performance with observed audience response; use reflection to inform future compositions.
wider: Present a themed performance program of original works — provide programme notes for each piece and evaluate how well the program communicated its intended theme or message
Compare an original composition performance with a performance of repertoire by another composer — reflect on how the experience of performing your own work differs and what you learn from each

modes.reason: Performing original compositions integrates composition, performance, interpretation and reflection into a complete artistic act. The teaching investment is in supporting students to see the performance of their own work as a complete feedback loop: the audience response (or their own listening) generates information that feeds the next compositional decision.

descriptors.title: Evaluate critical feedback in visual arts practice
descriptors.description: evaluate critical feedback when planning, developing and refining their visual arts practice
descriptors.knowledge: Students have created planned artworks using coordinated visual choices and can explain their decisions (AC9AVA8C01/AC9AVA8C02, implied from progression). They have engaged with peer and teacher feedback at an informal level. They have not yet systematically evaluated feedback, tracked its influence on decision-making, or distinguished between seeking impressions and confirming intended responses.
descriptors.endpoint: Students evaluate critical feedback from teachers, peers and audiences when planning, developing and refining their visual arts practice — documenting how feedback influences decisions.

nodes.label: Seeking impressions without leading
nodes.checkpoint: Students can seek feedback in a way that uncovers genuine audience impressions rather than confirming their own intended response.
criteria: Seeks feedback on a work without revealing the intended meaning first
Records what the audience perceived and compares this with the intended response
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who lead audiences toward their intended meaning receive confirmation rather than feedback — the gap between intention and reception is diagnostic only if the seeking process is neutral. Without this, subsequent evaluation of feedback is based on affirming data, not useful critique.

width.minimum: Seek feedback on one work in progress without revealing the intended meaning first; record what the audience perceived.
width.typical: Develop and use feedback-seeking strategies that uncover meaning and interpretation without confirming or leading the audience; compare audience impressions with intended response; use the gap as a diagnostic tool.
wider: Design a structured feedback protocol for the class — develop questions that elicit genuine impression without leading, test it on peer works, and evaluate the protocol's effectiveness
Seek feedback from an audience outside the class (community group, exhibition visitors) — compare impressions from different audience types and reflect on what this reveals

modes.reason: The distinction between 'seeking impressions' and 'leading the audience' is subtle and requires explicit instruction and practice. Scaffolding the feedback protocol — what questions to ask and what not to say — builds the skill.

nodes.label: Evaluating and responding to feedback
nodes.checkpoint: Students can evaluate feedback from teachers and peers and document how it influences their decisions — accepting, adapting or consciously setting aside feedback with reasoning.
criteria: Evaluates at least one piece of feedback on a work in progress
Documents a decision made in response — including whether it was accepted, adapted or set aside, with a reason

width.minimum: Evaluate at least one piece of feedback on a work in progress; document one decision made in response to it — including whether they accepted, adapted or set it aside and why.
width.typical: Evaluate and respond to feedback from multiple sources across multiple works; document decisions and reasoning in written, oral or multimedia journal; track changes made as a result of feedback; use self-assessment with Viewpoints questions alongside external feedback.
wider: Collaborate with a community group or external agency to generate ideas and receive feedback on an artwork project — evaluate how external feedback differs from peer/teacher feedback
Develop a systematic reflective process — use Viewpoints questions to self-assess work in progress alongside external feedback and document the relationship between the two

modes.reason: Evaluating feedback requires weighing its validity against intentions — students need a reasoning framework (Does this align with my intent? Is this a perception issue or an execution issue? Should I change the work or my communication of it?) rather than simply accepting all feedback.

nodes.label: Structuring ideas and tracking development
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use structured documentation (sketches, maquettes, annotated digital images, journals) to experiment with ways of developing ideas and to track the evolution of a work.
criteria: Uses at least one structured documentation form to show how an idea evolved through two or more stages
Connects at least one documented change to a feedback evaluation

width.minimum: Use at least one structured documentation form (sketch series, annotated images, journal) to show how an idea evolved through at least two stages.
width.typical: Experiment with and evaluate ways of structuring ideas in sketches, studies, maquettes, annotated digital images and journals; use documentation to track development and refine directions; connect documentation to feedback evaluation.
wider: Create a virtual or scale model of an exhibition of a researched artist — use this structure to communicate your understanding of the artist's intentions and refine it based on feedback
Plan and document a substantial creative project from initial idea through to completed work — use the documentation to evaluate the role of feedback at each stage

modes.reason: Documentation, feedback evaluation and iterative refinement come together here — students demonstrate a coherent creative process where external critique informs internal development at every stage.

descriptors.title: Create artworks reflecting personal expression
descriptors.description: select and manipulate visual conventions, visual arts processes and/or materials to create artworks that reflect personal expression, and represent and/or challenge, ideas, perspectives and/or meaning
descriptors.knowledge: Students can plan and create artworks with coordinated visual choices and can evaluate feedback in their practice. They make deliberate aesthetic decisions. They have not yet developed a sustained personal voice, self-initiated research process, or created artworks that deliberately challenge established perspectives.
descriptors.endpoint: Students select and manipulate visual conventions, processes and materials to create artworks that reflect personal expression and represent or challenge ideas, perspectives and meaning.

nodes.label: Researching and developing personal approaches
nodes.checkpoint: Students can research approaches to their subject or concept and develop a direction that reflects a personal point of view — not just reproducing a known style.
criteria: Researches at least two approaches to representing a subject or concept
Identifies one that reflects a personal point of view and gives a specific reason
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who research only to imitate rather than to find a personal direction produce technically competent work without personal expression — the descriptor explicitly requires expression, and without self-directed research the work stays in exemplar convergence.

width.minimum: Research at least two approaches to representing a subject or concept; identify one that resonates with a personal point of view and explain why.
width.typical: Research approaches to representing subjects and concepts from particular viewpoints; annotate research with own images and written evaluations; develop a personal direction distinct from direct imitation; document the development of personal expression.
wider: Investigate how artists across cultures represent similar themes from distinctly different viewpoints — analyse how personal, cultural and contextual factors shape the approach; develop a response that reflects your own position
Explore how visual arts can represent personal experiences — investigate how other artists have approached self-awareness, emotional awareness or wellbeing; develop your own approach

modes.reason: Developing a personal point of view from research requires explicit reasoning — 'Why does this approach resonate? What does it allow me to do that others don't?' Without this reasoning scaffold, students default to whichever approach looks most achievable.

nodes.label: Creative problem-solving and resolution
nodes.checkpoint: Students can initiate and use creative problem-solving to resolve visual and conceptual challenges throughout the making process.
criteria: Identifies at least one creative challenge in a work in progress
Documents at least two possible solutions before choosing one, with reasoning

width.minimum: Identify at least one creative challenge in a work in progress and document at least two possible solutions before choosing one.
width.typical: Use creative problem-solving throughout the making process; document challenges and multiple possible resolutions; make and justify choices; track how problems were resolved in final documentation.
wider: Create an artwork that represents a current global or local issue — research how other artists have addressed similar themes; develop a distinct visual argument; evaluate whether the work challenges or represents the issue
Create a site-specific 3D work — document how site conditions posed challenges and how you resolved them through sculptural techniques, space and form

modes.reason: Creative problem-solving is context-dependent — the problems differ across media, concepts and sites. Students who have only problem-solved in one context develop narrow strategies. A range of challenge types builds genuine creative resourcefulness.

nodes.label: Personal expression in completed artworks
nodes.checkpoint: Students can create artworks in which personal expression is evident — using materials, techniques and conventions in intentional, interpretative and personal ways to represent or challenge ideas, perspectives and meaning.
criteria: Creates an artwork that reflects a personal position or perspective
Uses at least two visual choices in ways that are interpretative — not merely technical — and can explain what personal meaning they carry

width.minimum: Create one artwork that reflects a personal position and uses at least two visual choices (convention, material, technique) in ways that are intentional and interpretative.
width.typical: Create artworks that realise planned intentions and communicate personal expression; use materials, techniques and conventions interpretatively; create works in response to specific subjects, themes or ideas; represent or challenge perspectives through visual means.
wider: Create artworks that deliberately challenge an established perspective or assumption — use research and documentation to show how the challenge is constructed visually
Apply painting techniques to create the illusion of texture and form in a landscape — document how technical decisions serve the expressive intent

modes.reason: Research, problem-solving and personal voice come together in the completed work. The integration is evidenced when the artwork reflects something distinctive — not a competent generic response but a personal interpretative position.

descriptors.strand: Visual arts: developing practices and skills
descriptors.title: Experiment to refine skills and develop personal expression
descriptors.description: experiment with visual conventions, visual arts processes and materials to refine skills and develop personal expression
descriptors.knowledge: Students can experiment with and document visual arts processes and reflect on discoveries to make informed choices (AC9AVA8D01, implied from progression). They have developed documentation habits. They have not yet investigated a medium in depth for comprehensive understanding, or begun identifying an emerging personal style.
descriptors.endpoint: Students experiment with visual conventions, processes and materials to refine skills and develop personal expression, using deep investigation and documentation to identify their own artistic voice.

nodes.label: In-depth investigation of a medium
nodes.checkpoint: Students can investigate a medium or form in depth — exploring its material properties and technical processes comprehensively, developing understanding of what it can do.
criteria: Investigates at least two technical processes of one medium
Documents what the medium can and cannot do based on the investigation
nodes.hinge_reason: Comprehensive medium understanding is the foundation for technical refinement — students who have only surface-level material knowledge cannot make the nuanced choices that distinguish personal expression from generic making. Depth here enables everything downstream.

width.minimum: Investigate one medium's material properties and at least two technical processes associated with it; document discoveries.
width.typical: Experiment comprehensively with a medium's material properties and technical processes; investigate how these properties enable specific visual effects; document and evaluate the investigation; develop understanding of the full range of what the medium can do.
wider: Investigate artists through their sketchbooks — uncover their experimental processes and find connections between their practice and the development of their personal expression

Use line analysis (drawing lines, shapes and arrows over photocopies of artworks) to decode compositional techniques — use a coding system for rule of thirds, movement, repetition and visual hierarchy; apply findings to your own work

modes.reason: In-depth investigation of a single medium requires extended practice — not one lesson but sustained engagement. The consolidation is not about drilling a single technique but about building comprehensive knowledge through varied experimentation within one form.

nodes.label: Interrogating multiple approaches
nodes.checkpoint: Students can interrogate multiple approaches to representing a topic — using different media to express different interpretations or emotions.
criteria: Uses at least two different media to represent the same topic
Describes what each approach expresses differently — not just what it looks like but what it communicates

width.minimum: Use at least two different media to represent the same topic differently; describe what each approach expresses.
width.typical: Interrogate multiple approaches to the same activity using diverse media; produce several works on the one topic each exploring a different emotion or interpretation; compare approaches and document what each reveals.
wider: Develop an 'inspiration' journal — collect photographs, found objects, media experiments, thoughts and ideas from everyday life; use Viewpoints questions to identify what you are drawn to and why

Investigate artists from a different cultural context (e.g. a country in the Asia region) through accounts of their influences — reflect on how their accounts inform your understanding of what can shape your own practice

modes.reason: Using a single approach to represent a topic produces one reading. The comparison across multiple media reveals how mode shapes meaning — students who only use one approach cannot see the expressive choices available to them.

nodes.label: Developing personal expression
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and document an emerging personal style — patterns in what they are drawn to, how they work, and what visual choices feel distinctively their own.
criteria: Identifies at least one pattern in their practice that could characterise an emerging personal style
Can explain what they are drawn to and connect it to choices visible in their work

width.minimum: Identify at least one pattern in their visual arts practice that could characterise an emerging personal style.
width.typical: Use Viewpoints questions to interrogate an inspiration journal and documented practice to identify emerging preferences and style characteristics; document personal style development; ask 'What am I drawn to and why is this important to me?'
wider: Annotate photocopies of artworks you admire with compositional analysis — identify patterns in what you respond to and connect these to patterns in your own making
Investigate the development of a visual arts form you work in — trace how personal expression has developed within this form historically and reflect on where your own practice sits

modes.reason: Medium investigation, multi-approach interrogation and emerging preferences come together in the identification of personal expression. The integration is the recognition: 'Here is what my practice is becoming and why.'

descriptors.strand: Visual arts: developing practices and skills
descriptors.title: Reflect on influences on visual arts practice
descriptors.description: reflect on the way they and other visual artists respond to influences to inspire, develop and resolve choices they make in their own visual arts practice
descriptors.knowledge: Students have begun identifying an emerging personal style and have investigated artists from diverse contexts. They can make informed choices based on documented experimentation. They have not yet systematically reflected on how personal, cultural and contextual influences shape their own practice, or used investigation of others' influences to understand their own.
descriptors.endpoint: Students reflect on the ways they and other visual artists respond to influences — using this understanding to inspire, develop and resolve choices in their own visual arts practice.

nodes.label: Identifying personal influences
nodes.checkpoint: Students can investigate and reflect on the role of their own culture, family and personal experiences as influences on their visual arts practice.
criteria: Identifies at least one personal influence (cultural, familial or experiential)
Explains how it has shaped at least one aspect of their practice — a choice, direction or recurring concern
nodes.hinge_reason: Personal influence reflection is the foundation for this descriptor — students who cannot identify their own influences cannot meaningfully compare them with other artists' influences, and cannot use influence understanding to resolve making choices.

width.minimum: Identify at least one personal influence (cultural background, family, personal experience) and explain how it has shaped one aspect of their practice.
width.typical: Investigate how culture, family and personal experiences influence what they are drawn to, what they make and how they make it; document reflections in journal form; connect personal influences to specific choices visible in their work.
