wider: Explore current issues of personal importance (local or global) as a starting point for artwork — document how the issue connects to your own experiences and values, and how this shapes your visual response
Investigate how your visual arts practice can explore and represent personal experiences — research how other artists have approached self-awareness and emotional awareness; develop your own approach

modes.reason: Influence reflection is not automatic — students need structured prompts ('What experiences have shaped what I make? What would be absent from my work without my background?') to surface influences that are invisible precisely because they are familiar.

nodes.label: Investigating other artists' influences
nodes.checkpoint: Students can investigate how other artists respond to their own influences — examining accounts of their practices to understand the many factors that can shape a visual arts practice.
criteria: Investigates at least one artist's accounts of their influences
Explains how at least one influence is visible in specific choices in the work

width.minimum: Investigate one artist's accounts of their influences and explain how at least one influence is visible in their work.
width.typical: Investigate a diverse range of visual artists — including artists from different countries and contexts (e.g. the Asia region) — through accounts of the influences on their work; analyse how influences shape specific artistic choices; connect this understanding to your own practice.
wider: Investigate First Nations Australian artists and their reflections on how personal and community experiences shape their visual arts practice — reflect on what these accounts suggest about how you might represent your own experiences
Analyse how artists structure artworks to represent ideas — use Viewpoints questions to unpack the relationship between the artist's influences and their compositional and material choices

modes.reason: Students who investigate only one type of artist (e.g. Western contemporary) develop a narrow model of what influences can be. A diverse range — including cross-cultural and First Nations — expands their understanding of the range of factors that can shape making.

nodes.label: Using influence understanding to resolve choices
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use their understanding of personal and external influences to inspire, develop and resolve choices in their own visual arts practice.
criteria: Identifies at least one making choice that was inspired or resolved by understanding a personal or external influence
Explains the connection — not just 'I was influenced by X' but how the influence shaped the specific choice

width.minimum: Identify at least one making choice that was directly inspired or resolved by understanding a personal or external influence.
width.typical: Reflect on, evaluate and resolve choices in artworks as they progress — through informal discussion, journal reflection or multimedia evaluation; connect choices to identified influences; use understanding of how other artists respond to influences to inform own resolutions.
wider: Explore a current global or local issue as a starting point — research how artists have used their influences to address similar issues; reflect on how your own background shapes your response and use this to resolve a making choice
Compare your own influence reflections with those of artists you have investigated — identify parallels and differences and explain what this reveals about your own practice

modes.reason: Personal influence reflection and external artist investigation come together in the resolution of a specific making choice. The integration is evidenced when the student can trace a decision back to an understood influence — their own or inspired by another artist's approach.

descriptors.title: Artists develop personal expression across cultures and contexts
descriptors.description: investigate the ways that artists across cultures, times, places and/or other contexts develop personal expression in their visual arts practice to represent, communicate and/or challenge ideas, perspectives and/or meaning
descriptors.knowledge: Students can compare how artists from different contexts communicate ideas and examine multiple perspectives on artworks (AC9AVA8E01, implied from progression). They have developed critical questioning skills. They have not yet produced extended critical analysis, selected from multiple critical viewpoints, or investigated the historical development of a visual arts form.
descriptors.endpoint: Students investigate how artists across cultures, times, places and other contexts develop personal expression to represent, communicate and challenge ideas, perspectives and meaning.

nodes.label: Analysing personal expression in context
nodes.checkpoint: Students can analyse how an artist's personal expression is shaped by their cultural, historical and contextual position — and how this shapes what the artwork represents, communicates or challenges.
criteria: Identifies at least one aspect of an artist's cultural, historical or contextual position
Explains how it shapes the personal expression visible in the work — what it represents, communicates or challenges
nodes.hinge_reason: Contextual analysis of personal expression is the foundation for all comparative and evaluative work in this descriptor. Students who can only describe personal expression without connecting it to context cannot make the comparative claims the descriptor requires.

width.minimum: Analyse one artwork: identify one aspect of the artist's context and explain how it shapes the personal expression visible in the work.
width.typical: Analyse artworks from multiple cultural and historical contexts; examine how lived experience, cultural forces and historical position shape personal expression; compare approaches to a shared theme (portraiture, identity, freedom, social change) across artists from different contexts.
wider: Compare how artists representing the same historical event from different cultural positions develop different personal expressions — analyse how the differences reflect their respective contexts
Investigate how linear versus circular timelines shift meaning in art — examine this with reference to First Nations Australian ways of knowing, being and doing

modes.reason: Contextual analysis requires a reasoning framework — students need to move from 'the artist painted X' to 'the artist painted X because of Y cultural/historical position and this is why the work challenges/represents Z'. Without the framework, analysis stays descriptive.

nodes.label: Multiple critical viewpoints
nodes.checkpoint: Students can select different critical viewpoints (formal, contextual, socio-political, cultural) to develop different explanations of the same artwork or artist's approach.
criteria: Applies at least two different critical viewpoints to the same artwork
Explains how each produces a different understanding of what the work represents, communicates or challenges

width.minimum: Apply two different critical viewpoints to the same artwork; explain how each produces a different understanding.
width.typical: Select different critical viewpoints to develop explanations about artists' approaches and works across different times and contexts; analyse and compare how the same artwork looks different through different critical lenses; develop extended evaluative accounts.
wider: Debate the interpretive value of different critical viewpoints applied to the same artist or artwork — evaluate which viewpoint illuminates most for a particular purpose and audience
Investigate the development of a visual arts form over time — trace how globalisation, cultural practices and material discoveries have shaped how personal expression is possible within that form

modes.reason: Students who apply only one critical viewpoint develop a partial understanding of how artworks communicate and challenge. A range of critical lenses (formal, contextual, socio-political) reveals that meaning is not singular.

nodes.label: Extended critical account
nodes.checkpoint: Students can produce an extended written, oral or multimedia account that investigates how an artist or artists develop personal expression to represent, communicate or challenge ideas across cultures, times or places.
criteria: Produces an extended account of at least one artist that discusses personal expression and communicative intent
The account applies at least one critical viewpoint and connects the artist's context to specific aspects of the work

width.minimum: Produce an extended account (written, oral or multimedia) of at least one artist — discussing how personal expression serves their communicative or challenging intent.
width.typical: Create extended essays, pod/vodcasts, debates or reviews that analyse how artists develop personal expression; apply multiple critical viewpoints; compare artists across contexts; evaluate the role of cultural, historical and personal forces.
wider: Produce a comparative essay or debate about two artists from different cultural contexts representing the same theme — evaluate whose approach more effectively challenges assumptions and explain why

Investigate First Nations Australian ways of knowing and circular timelines as a framework for understanding how personal expression in First Nations visual arts challenges linear Western art historical narratives

modes.reason: Contextual analysis and multiple critical viewpoints come together in the extended account — students demonstrate sustained critical thinking about how personal expression functions across cultures, times and places.

descriptors.title: First Nations artists celebrate and challenge Australian identity
descriptors.description: investigate the ways that First Nations Australian artists celebrate and challenge multiple perspectives of Australian identity through their artworks and visual arts practice
descriptors.knowledge: Students have explored how First Nations Australian arts continue and revitalise cultures, and engaged with site-specific and community-based works (AC9AVA8E02, implied from progression). They understand arts as ongoing cultural practice. They have not yet engaged with First Nations Australian visual arts as explicitly political, activist or identity-challenging, or investigated 'first contacts' and colonisation from multiple perspectives within this frame.
descriptors.endpoint: Students investigate ways that First Nations Australian artists celebrate and challenge multiple perspectives of Australian identity through their artworks and visual arts practice.

nodes.label: Visual arts as activism
nodes.checkpoint: Students can investigate how First Nations Australian artists use visual communication as a tool for activism — expressing calls for change through artworks, protest posters and street art.
criteria: Examines at least one example of First Nations Australian visual art as activism
Explains what change is being called for and how at least one visual choice communicates the message
nodes.hinge_reason: The activist dimension is the key new conceptual territory at Y9-10 compared to earlier bands. Students who only understand First Nations Australian arts as cultural continuation and celebration cannot engage with the challenging and political dimensions the descriptor requires.

width.minimum: Examine one example of First Nations Australian visual art as activism (protest poster, street art, campaign); explain what change is being called for and how visual choices communicate the message.
width.typical: Research artworks, protest posters and street art by First Nations Australian artists used as activism; analyse how visual communication tools express calls for change; investigate the relationship between visual choices and activist purpose.
wider: Investigate how First Nations Australian artists are caring for Country/Place through visual arts campaigns — explore how environmental activism is visualised and who the intended audience is
Compare protest posters by First Nations Australian artists from different historical periods — analyse how visual communication strategies have evolved and what stays constant

modes.reason: Students may not have encountered First Nations Australian visual arts as explicitly political. Structured investigation (what change is being called for? who is the intended audience? how do visual choices serve the activist purpose?) builds the analytical framework needed.

nodes.label: Multiple perspectives on Australian identity
nodes.checkpoint: Students can investigate how First Nations Australian artists present multiple perspectives of Australian identity — including perspectives that challenge dominant narratives about 'first contacts' and colonisation.
criteria: Investigates at least one First Nations Australian artwork that presents a perspective on Australian identity
Explains how it celebrates or challenges a specific aspect of how Australian identity has been understood

width.minimum: Investigate one First Nations Australian artwork that presents an alternative perspective on Australian identity or history; explain how it challenges a dominant narrative.
width.typical: Compare and analyse artworks by diverse First Nations Australian artists that celebrate and challenge concepts and histories of Australian identity; investigate 'first contacts' from multiple perspectives; examine how artists present multiple ways of understanding shared histories.
wider: Analyse how First Nations Australian artists use their practices to challenge and inform community debate about 'first contacts' between First Nations Peoples and British or European colonisers — compare with other cultural perspectives
Investigate contemporary First Nations Australian designers who are challenging concepts and histories of Australian identity in commercial and applied design contexts

modes.reason: Students who examine only one perspective on Australian identity cannot understand how First Nations Australian artists challenge narratives. Engaging with both the dominant narrative and the challenge — and with multiple First Nations perspectives — is essential.

nodes.label: Cultural continuation, development and community voice
nodes.checkpoint: Students can investigate how First Nations Australian visual arts provide opportunities to continue and develop culture, communicate lived experiences, and care for Country/Place and people.
criteria: Identifies at least two distinct purposes served by First Nations Australian visual arts (from continuation, challenge, Country care, lived experience communication)
Demonstrates understanding that these purposes are not separate but often simultaneous in a single artwork or practice

width.minimum: Identify at least two distinct ways First Nations Australian visual arts serve community or cultural purposes (continuation, challenge, caring for Country, communicating lived experience).
width.typical: Explore the full range of ways First Nations Australian visual arts function — cultural continuation, community development, lived experience communication, Country/Place care, identity declaration and political challenge; synthesise understanding across multiple artists and forms.
wider: Work with representatives of the First Nations Australian community to explore how local groups are caring for Country/Place — investigate how visual arts campaigns highlight environmental issues for local and broader audiences

Investigate how the digital age has expanded opportunities for First Nations Australian artists and designers to continue and develop culture — explore specific examples of online, social media or digital art contexts

modes.reason: Activism, identity challenge and cultural continuation come together in a complete understanding of First Nations Australian visual arts as simultaneously political, cultural and community-directed — serving multiple purposes at once.

descriptors.title: Evaluate exhibits and curate exhibitions
descriptors.description: evaluate art exhibits to inform the curation and exhibition of their own and/or others' artworks and/or visual arts practice
descriptors.knowledge: Students can prepare artworks for formal display, create exhibition materials and make deliberate presentation decisions for different audiences (AC9AVA8P01, implied from progression). They have produced artist statements and curated class exhibitions. They have not yet evaluated existing exhibitions as a research base for their own curatorial decisions, or planned exhibitions that communicate a broader curatorial argument.
descriptors.endpoint: Students evaluate art exhibitions to inform the curation and exhibition of their own and/or others' artworks and visual arts practice.

nodes.label: Evaluating exhibitions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can visit or investigate exhibitions (physical or virtual) and evaluate the curatorial and presentational choices made — analysing how these choices create meaning and communicate artists' intentions.
criteria: Identifies at least two curatorial choices in an exhibition
Explains how each choice serves the exhibition's purpose or communicates the artist's/curator's intentions
nodes.hinge_reason: Exhibition evaluation is the research base for the student's own curation — students who evaluate superficially cannot derive curatorial principles to apply to their own work. The depth of evaluation determines the quality of the curatorial reasoning that follows.

width.minimum: Visit or investigate one exhibition; identify at least two curatorial choices (spatial arrangement, sequencing, labelling, lighting, grouping) and explain how each serves the exhibition's purpose.
width.typical: Visit and evaluate exhibitions in physical or virtual galleries, museums or community sites; analyse how artists and curators work together; investigate how curatorial choices create visual narrative and communicate intention; produce written, oral or multimedia evaluations.
wider: Create a virtual or scale model of an exhibition of a researched artist — use this to communicate your understanding of the artist's intentions and refine based on peer feedback
Evaluate an exhibition of contemporary First Nations Australian art — analyse how the curatorial choices reflect Indigenous Cultural and Intellectual Property rights and community protocols

modes.reason: Curatorial analysis requires a systematic framework — students need to analyse spatial arrangement, sequencing, labelling and audience flow as deliberate choices, not just notice what they see. Structured evaluation tools build this analytical capacity.

nodes.label: Planning and curating exhibitions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can plan and curate an exhibition of their own or others' work — making deliberate decisions about selection, arrangement, sequence and spatial narrative.
criteria: Plans an exhibition with deliberate decisions about selection, arrangement and sequence
Articulates at least one curatorial argument — what the exhibition communicates and why specific choices serve it

width.minimum: Plan a class exhibition: make deliberate decisions about which works to include, how to sequence them and one spatial arrangement choice; explain the reasoning.
width.typical: Plan and curate exhibitions of own work and/or others' works; make deliberate decisions about selection, arrangement and spatial narrative; consider Indigenous Cultural and Intellectual Property rights where relevant; develop a coherent curatorial argument.
wider: Plan and curate a community installation or an imagined exhibition of artworks by researched artists — develop and present the curatorial argument in written or multimedia form
Plan an exhibition that explicitly engages with Indigenous Cultural and Intellectual Property rights — research the relevant considerations and document how they shaped curatorial decisions

modes.reason: Students who curate only a single class exhibition have limited experience of how curatorial decisions change across different contexts (community installation, imagined artist retrospective, physically constrained space). A range of curatorial contexts builds genuine curatorial capability.

nodes.label: Exhibition materials and curatorial voice
nodes.checkpoint: Students can develop exhibition materials — didactic panels, artist statements, branding, press statements — that communicate the curatorial argument and serve the audience.
criteria: Develops at least two exhibition materials that communicate the curatorial argument
The materials are tailored to the intended audience and context — not generic labels

width.minimum: Develop at least two exhibition materials (e.g. a curatorial statement and an artist label) that communicate the curatorial argument.
width.typical: Develop a comprehensive set of exhibition materials — didactic panels, artist or curatorial statements, advertising, branding and press statements; evaluate their effectiveness for the intended audience; construct explanations of how artists communicate ideas and meaning.
wider: Develop a full exhibition materials set for a class show — labels, introduction, advertising, press statement and review — and evaluate each element's effectiveness with peer feedback
Create a written, oral or multimedia response to an exhibition of work — connect the curatorial evaluation to the student's own approach in a planned or realised exhibition

modes.reason: Exhibition evaluation, curatorial planning and materials development come together in a complete exhibition practice — where the materials serve the curatorial argument and both reflect the student's understanding of how artworks communicate to audiences.
